items.title: The Kedi language
items.text:
A language for typed programs with natural language. Learn the syntax, follow the runtime, and find the rules behind your programs.

Start with installation

Illustrative output Paris

items.title: Why Typed LLM Programs
items.text:
Prompts are useful for fuzzy transformations; Python is useful for deterministic logic. Kedi keeps both in one dataflow without pretending they are the same thing.

This definition is a fragment: it does not call a model until the procedure is invoked. The first program supplies model selection, command-line inputs, and a complete executable entry point.

~Ticket(category: str, urgency: int)

@classify(message: str) -> Ticket:
  >> The classification of support message <message> is [ticket: Ticket].
  = `ticket`

<message> is a substitution: Kedi renders an existing value into the prompt. [ticket: Ticket] is an output capture: the adapter asks the model for a value matching the generated schema. = `ticket` returns the native Ticket object. Writing = <ticket> instead would stringify it.

Use output capture whenever a model result participates in the program's dataflow, including plain text. A str capture still gives the adapter an explicit output contract:

@summarize(message: str) -> str:
  >> A two-sentence summary of <message> is [summary: str].
  = <summary>

Raw capture is an escape hatch for deliberately unstructured text, not the default form of a Kedi model call.

Typed does not mean factually correct. Validation checks the declared contract; it cannot prove that a model's answer is true. Deterministic checks, evidence, and evaluation address different questions.

items.title: Choose a Starting Point
items.text:
• New to Kedi: begin with Learn Kedi.
  • Learning the DSL: use the Language Reference.
  • Embedding Kedi in Python: use the Python API.
  • Building tool-using or delegated agents: use Agents and Orchestration.
  • Looking up exact syntax or behavior: use the Reference.

After the first program, use Projects and Execution to split it across files, then choose a task from the Cookbook. You do not need tools, profiles, or delegated agents to use typed templates.

items.title: Language, Python API, and Model Integrations
items.text:
The same runtime semantics are available through two authoring surfaces:

  • .kedi files are best for workflows where prompts, types, procedures, tests, and profiles should be visible together.
  • @kedi.query and @kedi.bind are best when Python owns the public function signature and Kedi provides the implementation.

Adapters are boundary implementations, not alternative Kedi dialects. The language semantics stay stable, while capability validation reports whether a selected backend supports structured output, tools, MCP, approvals, or subagents.

items.title: Documentation Conventions
items.text:
Code blocks marked kedi are Kedi source. Backticks have two different roles:

  • single backticks, such as `items`, evaluate a Python expression;
  • triple backtick blocks execute multiline Python.

The documentation distinguishes:

  • substitution (<value>), which reads and renders a value;
  • output capture ([value: Type]), which asks the model to produce a value;
  • native return (= `value`), which preserves the Python object;
  • rendered return (= <value>), which returns text.

Those choices are called out in examples because replacing one with another can change types, validation, or whether a model response is retained.

items.title: Kedi A2A Structured Output Extension v1
items.text:
Extension URI: https://docs.kedi-lang.org/a2a/extensions/structured-output/v1/

This optional A2A extension lets a Kedi client request a JSON-Schema result from a Kedi-served agent. Generic A2A text invocation remains unchanged.
path: Kedi A2A Structured Output Extension v1

items.title: Agent Card Declaration
items.text:
An implementation supporting per-request schemas advertises an AgentExtension with the extension URI and these parameters:

{
  "version": 1,
  "mode": "request-schema",
  "schemaDialect": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "maxSchemaBytes": 32768,
  "resultArtifactName": "kedi-structured-output",
  "schemaEncodings": ["json-utf8", "protobuf-value"],
  "resultEncodings": ["json-utf8", "protobuf-value"]
}

Clients accept mode values fixed and request-schema. Kedi's v1 server publishes request-schema. The extension is optional for raw text requests.
path: Kedi A2A Structured Output Extension v1

items.title: Request
items.text:
For a structured request, the client must:

  1. include the extension URI in Message.extensions;
  2. request the application/json output mode; and
  3. place this object in SendMessageRequest.metadata:
{
  "kediStructuredOutput": {
    "version": 1,
    "resultEncoding": "json-utf8",
    "schemaJson": "{\"type\":\"object\",\"properties\":{\"answer\":{\"type\":\"string\"}},\"required\":[\"answer\"],\"additionalProperties\":false}",
    "schema": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "answer": {"type": "string"}
      },
      "required": ["answer"],
      "additionalProperties": false
    }
  }
}

schemaJson is the authoritative JSON document when present. Unlike numeric values inside protobuf Struct, a JSON string preserves integer constraints and enum values larger than 2**53. The schema object is a legacy fallback; Kedi includes it only when its numbers can pass through protobuf doubles without changing their values. Invalid schemaJson never falls back to schema. Requests with only the legacy schema object remain supported.

The UTF-8 JSON encoding of the schema must not exceed the advertised limit. Kedi validates the schema before invoking the served adapter. Remote $ref and $id resolution are unsupported, schema nesting is bounded, and invalid schemas fail the task rather than reaching a model.
path: Kedi A2A Structured Output Extension v1

items.title: Successful Result
items.text:
The completed task contains one final artifact with:

  • name kedi-structured-output;
  • the extension URI in Artifact.extensions;
  • media type application/json; and
  • for resultEncoding: json-utf8, one raw part containing the UTF-8 JSON document that validates against the request schema. JSONRPC represents the bytes as base64, not as free-form model text.

Kedi clients request json-utf8. This preserves nested integer and floating-point types, including large integer identifiers, across streaming, task retrieval, and persisted results. It does not coerce floats into integers or relax capture validation. Non-finite numbers and malformed JSON are rejected.

When resultEncoding is absent or protobuf-value, the server uses the legacy data part. It rejects results that would lose numeric value in this encoding. Legacy protobuf results do not preserve the distinction between 78 and 78.0; both peers must support json-utf8 for lossless typed results. Updated clients still read legacy data parts. If both forms are present in one artifact, the raw JSON part takes precedence, and malformed raw JSON cannot fall back to data.

The server validates the result before completing the task. The client validates it again before assigning Kedi captures. Progress data, unrelated artifacts, and plain text are never interpreted as the typed result.
path: Kedi A2A Structured Output Extension v1

items.title: Failure Behavior
items.text:
• A structured request to a peer that does not advertise the extension fails before the task is sent.
  • A missing, malformed, oversized, wrongly named, or schema-invalid result fails without partial capture assignment.
  • The extension does not authorize tools, transfer local configuration, or imply support for Kedi artifacts.
  • v1 does not define repair-model retries, partial structured fields, remote schema references, or usage/cost accounting.

The task and context lifecycle otherwise follows A2A v1 semantics.
path: Kedi A2A Structured Output Extension v1

items.title: Adapter Development
items.text: An agent adapter is the boundary between Kedi's runtime and a model framework or agent harness. Every >> template, << raw invoke, claim, delegation, and tool call a program makes passes through it. This section is the complete contract for writing one.

items.title: Kedi Renders, the Adapter Transports
items.text:
Kedi decides what the model sees and what a result must look like:

  • the rendered prompt and the instruction text: profile instructions, template rules, claim rules, and capability, skill, and artifact instructions;
  • the output contract: a field schema for template captures, a Python type for claims and typed raw invokes, a wrapped JSON Schema for structured children;
  • the tools, already wrapped with approval, required-tool tracking, artifact admission, and telemetry;
  • validation of every returned value, budgets, limits, history, and conversation commits.

The adapter maps that onto its backend and back: messages, tool calls, structured output, provider state, and usage. It must not write task prompts of its own. See Prompts and Instructions.

A backend that is not written in Python connects through a JSON-RPC bridge: a process that speaks Kedi's adapter protocol on its stdio.

items.title: Kinds
items.text:
kind Selected with Typical backend "agent-framework" > adapter: or compile_program(adapter=...) a model framework where Kedi supplies the tools and the loop is in-process (Pydantic AI, LangChain) "agent-harness" > agent: or compile_program(agent=...) an agent runtime with its own tools, sandbox, and loop (Codex, Claude Agent SDK, ACP, A2A)

Kedi rejects an instance passed through the wrong parameter.

items.title: The Surface
items.text:
Only the first row is required. Every other protocol is optional and is switched on by an AdapterCapabilities flag; Kedi checks the flag before it relies on the protocol, and the LSP uses the same flags for diagnostics.

Protocol Methods Capability Page AgentAdapter invoke, invoke_sync, produce, produce_sync supports_structured_output Call Lifecycle, Structured Output SupportsProfileOverride default_model, profile_override supports_profile_override, supports_model_override, supports_effort, supports_settings, settings Profiles, Models, and Settings SupportsTemplatePromptMode template_prompt_mode — Prompts and Instructions SupportsToolRegistration tool_scope, register_tool supports_tool_registration, supports_deferred_tools, supports_capabilities Tools native approvals approval_ceiling and the adapter's approval hook supports_native_approvals, supports_native_approval_handler Approvals hooks HookRegistrationMixin, hooked_agent_run, tool hook dispatch hooks Hooks MCP profile mcp_servers supports_mcp MCP, Skills, and Capability Tools CodeMode execute_code controls supports_codemode CodeMode artifacts registered artifact tools, native admission supports_artifacts, supports_native_artifacts Artifacts SupportsSubagentExecution subagent_scope, subagent_run_kwargs, produce_subagent, telemetry_model_name supports_subagents, supports_background_subagents, supports_live_subagent_input, supports_subagent_interrupt Subagents SupportsConversationState conversation_scope supports_stateful_history, supports_history_replay, supports_history_processing Conversations and History compaction and caching history codecs, compaction backends supports_native_compaction Compaction and Prompt Caching multimodal input PromptDraft.media supports_media_input Multimodal Input budgets usage reporting, run-budget admission supports_request_budget, supports_tool_attempt_budget Budgets and Usage events AgentEventSink, stream events supports_stream_events Events, Streaming, and Telemetry

Every capability is None (unknown), True, or False. Kedi treats only True as support. The Capability Reference lists every field, what Kedi does differently because of it, and the error it raises when a program needs a capability the adapter lacks.

items.title: Reading Order
items.text:
1. Reference Adapter: a complete, tested adapter that every later page extends.
  2. Call Lifecycle, Prompts and Instructions, Rendered Request and Structured Output: what each call receives and must return.
  3. The pages for the protocols your backend can support.
  4. Concurrency and Event Loops and Testing an Adapter before you ship.

The Python on these pages runs in the documentation test suite. A python title="name.py" block is part of the module it names.

items.title: Approvals
items.text: Every tool call is approved before it runs. The policy comes from the program (> approval: allow, deny, or a handler) and from the tool's risk. Who applies it depends on one capability, supports_native_approvals.

items.title: The Two Models
items.text:
Kedi-wrapped approval (default) Native approval Capability supports_native_approvals unset or False supports_native_approvals=True tool.fn already applies the policy runs the tool without asking Children Kedi applies every ancestor's policy to the child's tools the adapter applies request.approval_ceiling Backend-native tools (shell, file edits, provider tools) not covered: the adapter must not expose them the adapter's approval hook covers them Use when the backend only calls tools Kedi registered the backend executes its own tools, or the framework has an approval step of its own

An adapter without native approvals needs no approval code at all: calling tool.fn asks the policy, and the reference adapter returns a denial to the model. Advertise native approvals only when the adapter applies policies to every tool the backend can run.

items.title: Requests and Decisions
items.text:
kedi.agent_adapter.approvals.policy:

Type Fields ApprovalPolicy mode ("allow" / "deny") or handler (a callable, sync or async); built with ApprovalPolicy.allow(), .deny(), .dynamic(handler) ApprovalRequest tool_name, arguments (validated, read-only), risk (read_only, mutating, sensitive), adapter_shortname, description, metadata, reason, tool_reason_enabled ApprovalDecision decision (allow, deny, edit), edit_arguments, reason; built with .allow(), .deny(reason=), .edit(arguments, reason=)

Resolution rules, the same for both models:

  1. read_only tools are allowed without asking.
  2. No policy (None) denies mutating and sensitive tools.
  3. A static mode allows or denies.
  4. A handler decides. An edit replaces the arguments; they are validated again, and an edit that raises the risk is asked again.
  5. A denial raises ToolApprovalDenied("Tool '<name>' was denied: <reason>").

items.title: Native Approvals
items.text:
With native approvals, Kedi registers unwrapped tools and the adapter applies the policies for every call, in this order:

  1. every policy in approval_ceiling (empty for a top-level call, the ancestors' policies inside subagent_scope), root first;
  2. the tool's own policy: tool_approval_policy(tool, profile.approval, arguments) resolves tool.approval, a capability policy, or the profile's policy.

Each policy receives the arguments approved by the previous one:

native_approvals.py
import json
from collections.abc import Generator
from contextlib import contextmanager
from contextvars import ContextVar
from dataclasses import replace
from typing import Any

from kedi.agent_adapter import ToolSpec
from kedi.agent_adapter.approvals.policy import ApprovalPolicy, ToolApprovalDenied
from kedi.agent_adapter.tools.errors import correctable_tool_error
from kedi.agent_adapter.tools.execution import (
    resolve_tool_arguments_async,
    validate_tool_arguments,
)
from kedi.agent_adapter.tools.specs import tool_approval_policy

from backend import ToolCall
from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter


class NativeApprovalAdapter(ChatAdapter):
    capabilities = replace(ChatAdapter.capabilities, supports_native_approvals=True)

    def __init__(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self._ceiling: ContextVar[tuple[ApprovalPolicy | None, ...]] = ContextVar(
            f"chat_ceiling_{id(self)}", default=()
        )

    @contextmanager
    def approval_ceiling(
        self, policies: tuple[ApprovalPolicy | None, ...]
    ) -> Generator[None, None, None]:
        token = self._ceiling.set(tuple(policies))
        try:
            yield
        finally:
            self._ceiling.reset(token)

    async def _approve(self, tool: ToolSpec, arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
        local = tool_approval_policy(tool, self.active_profile.approval, arguments)
        approved = arguments
        for policy in (*self._ceiling.get(), local):
            approved = await resolve_tool_arguments_async(
                tool, approved, policy=policy, adapter_shortname=self.shortname
            )
        return approved

    async def _execute(self, tools: dict[str, ToolSpec], call: ToolCall) -> str:
        tool = tools.get(call.name)
        if tool is None:
            return await super()._execute(tools, call)
        try:
            arguments = await self._approve(tool, validate_tool_arguments(tool, call.arguments))
        except ToolApprovalDenied as exc:
            return json.dumps({"ok": False, "error": exc.message})
        except Exception as exc:
            message = correctable_tool_error(tool, exc)
            if message is None:
                raise
            return json.dumps({"ok": False, "error": message})
        return await super()._execute(tools, ToolCall(call.id, call.name, arguments))

The adapter enters approval_ceiling(request.approval_ceiling) in its subagent_scope, next to the tool and profile scopes. Backend-native tools need the same loop in the backend's approval callback, with an ApprovalRequest built for the native operation.

Native adapters also own two details Kedi handles for wrapped tools:

  • Interactive handlers. A handler may block for a person's answer. In async code, await resolve_tool_arguments_async; a handler that implements SupportsAsyncApprovalResolution.resolve_async is then asked without blocking the event loop. Advertise supports_native_approval_handler only when the backend's own approval prompt can drive such a handler.
  • Approval reasons. With the tool_reason setting, the model supplies a reason with each call, and the reason reaches ApprovalRequest.reason. List tool_reason in capabilities.settings only when the adapter adds the reason argument to tool schemas and passes it to the request; see kedi.agent_adapter.approvals.reason.

items.title: Running It
Artifacts
items.text: A tool can return more data than a model should read at once: a log file, a search dump, a large table. Kedi stores such a result as an artifact and gives the model a compact reference and tools to read it in bounded pieces. The program itself still receives native values; artifacts only change what the model sees.

items.title: What Kedi Does
items.text:
For every call with tools, when artifacts are enabled (the default):

  1. it adds the artifacts.instructions part, which explains references and the retrieval tools, to instructions;
  2. it registers the artifact management tools with the call's other tools: read_artifact, search_artifacts, release_artifact, and run_artifact_code, plus query_artifact when query_artifacts is enabled;
  3. it wraps each tool's fn: when a successful result serializes to more than the policy's threshold (100 kB by default), the result is stored in the session's artifact store and fn returns the reference instead.

A reference is a JSON object (ArtifactRef.model_dump(mode="json")):

Field Content ref_id the opaque id the model passes to read_artifact logical_type, media_type what the value is summary, preview a short description and the first preview_chars characters size_bytes, char_count the stored size created_at, expires_at lifetime under ttl sensitive whether the value must not be echoed usage_hint how to read the rest

items.title: The Adapter's Part
items.text:
Advertise supports_artifacts=True when the adapter:

  • registers every tool Kedi passes, including the management tools;
  • returns each fn result to the model as is: a reference stays a reference, and the adapter never fetches, expands, or truncates it;
  • keeps every tool-call id paired with its result: a later read_artifact call is a new tool call with a new result, not an edit of the old message;
  • leaves storage to Kedi: no artifact store or manager of its own, and no re-running of the source tool to get the full value.

The constructor requires supports_structured_output and supports_tool_registration alongside it. Without supports_artifacts, a call with tools fails with ArtifactCapabilityError: Active adapter does not support Kedi artifact references and tools, unless the program disables artifacts for the profile:

> artifacts:
    enabled: false

A disabled profile sends every tool result to the model in full.

The reference adapter satisfies all four rules without artifact-specific code: it registers what it is given and serializes whatever fn returns.

items.title: Native and MCP Tool Results
items.text:
Kedi wraps only the tools it registers. Results from backend-native tools (a harness's file or shell tools, provider built-ins) and from MCP servers the adapter connects itself bypass that wrapper. To bring them under the same policy, admit each result before it enters model-visible history:

from kedi.agent_adapter.tools.execution import admit_current_artifact_result

model_visible = await admit_current_artifact_result(
    result, tool_name=native_name, call_id=call_id
)

The function returns the reference for a large result, the result unchanged for a small one, and the result unchanged outside a Kedi request (no active artifact scope). Send model_visible to the model in place of result. Advertise supports_native_artifacts=True only when every native and MCP result goes through it.

items.title: Failures
items.text:
Situation Result the session's session_quota or max_artifacts is exhausted fn returns an error object for the model instead of the reference; the run continues a result is too large to admit at all ToolOutputTooLargeError propagates from fn the model reads an unknown or expired ref_id the management tool fails with a correctable error the model can read

A failed admission never falls back to sending the full payload.

items.title: Running It
items.text:
run_artifacts.py
import asyncio
import json

from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program

from backend import BackendRequest, Reply, ToolCall
from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter

SOURCE = """
@read_log(day: str) -> str:
  ###
  Return the audit log of one day.
  ###
  > tool:
    risk: read_only
  = `"line " * 1000 + "APPROVED BY ada"`

> artifacts:
    threshold: 1kb
> use: read_log
[answer] << Who approved the change on 2026-11-20?
= <answer>
"""


class Script:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.results: list[dict] = []

    async def complete(self, request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
        self.results = [json.loads(m["content"]) for m in request.messages if m["role"] == "tool"]
        if not self.results:
            return Reply(tool_calls=(ToolCall("c1", "read_log", {"day": "2026-11-20"}),))
        if len(self.results) == 1:
            ref = self.results[0]["result"]
            arguments = {"ref_id": ref["ref_id"], "pattern": "APPROVED BY"}
            return Reply(tool_calls=(ToolCall("c2", "read_artifact", arguments),))
        return Reply(text=json.dumps(self.results[1]["result"]))


backend = Script()
runtime = compile_program(parse_program(SOURCE), adapter=ChatAdapter(backend, model="m1"))
try:
    answer = runtime.run_main()
finally:
    asyncio.run(runtime.aclose())

ref = backend.results[0]["result"]
assert set(ref) >= {"ref_id", "preview", "size_bytes", "usage_hint"}
assert ref["size_bytes"] > 1000 and "APPROVED" not in ref["preview"]
assert "APPROVED BY ada" in answer

The model received a reference instead of 5 kB of log, then found the line it needed with one bounded read.

items.title: Budgets and Usage
items.text: Kedi limits what a run may spend in three ways: run budgets cap the number of model requests and tool attempts, a size ceiling rejects requests that cannot fit the context window, and subagent usage limits cap each child. All three depend on the adapter telling Kedi what it does, at the moment it does it.

items.title: Reporting Usage
items.text:
After every completed backend request, report it:

from kedi.agent_adapter.invocation import InvocationUsage, report_invocation

report_invocation(
    InvocationUsage(
        requests=1,
        tool_calls=len(reply.tool_calls),
        input_tokens=usage.input_tokens,
        cache_read_tokens=usage.cache_read_tokens,
        cache_write_tokens=usage.cache_write_tokens,
        output_tokens=usage.output_tokens,
        total_tokens=usage.total_tokens,
        cost_usd=usage.cost,  # a Decimal, or None when unknown
    )
)
Field Meaning requests model requests completed (normally 1 per report) tool_calls business tool calls the adapter admitted for that response; never structured-output protocol calls, such as an output function that carries a typed answer input_tokens all input tokens, including cached ones cache_read_tokens, cache_write_tokens the cached part of the input, when the provider reports it output_tokens, total_tokens as reported by the provider cost_usd the provider's cost, when it reports one; leave None rather than estimating

Kedi routes the report to everything observing the call: the request-size reservation, model and agent telemetry, checkpoints, kedi explain usage, and a child's usage limits. Report the figures the provider returns, and never estimate one. A token count the provider does not return is None, which means unknown; 0 means it measured zero. When a response carries no usage at all, report InvocationUsage.unmeasured(). A sum that includes an unknown count is unknown, and telemetry leaves unknown counts off its spans instead of recording 0. A report outside a Kedi call is ignored.

Set supports_token_usage=True only when every report carries the provider's token counts. Kedi refuses a child's token limits, before the child runs, on an adapter without it.

items.title: Run Budgets
items.text:
> budget:
    request_limit: 10
    tool_attempt_limit: 20
Dimension Counted Who counts Capability requests every actual model generation: tool-loop turns, output repairs, retries, fallback models the adapter calls admit_run_operation("request") before each one supports_request_budget tool attempts each start of a Kedi tool body, and each of its retries Kedi, inside tool.fn supports_tool_attempt_budget

kedi.run_budget.admit_run_operation(dimension) charges the innermost budget and every enclosing one, and raises RunBudgetExceeded: Run request budget exhausted (limit N, consumed N) once a limit is reached. Call it immediately before sending the request, after any local validation, so a refused request is never sent. Let RunBudgetExceeded propagate; it is never a correctable tool error.

Rules for advertising the capabilities:

  • supports_request_budget: the adapter admits every physical request, including its own retries. The provider SDK must not retry on its own: with a finite request limit, disable SDK retries (max_retries=0) or reject the run. Kedi's helper kedi.run_budget.assert_no_hidden_model_retries(model) performs that check for SDK clients that expose max_retries.
  • supports_tool_attempt_budget: every tool the backend can run is a Kedi tool called through fn. Kedi refuses tool-attempt budgets for calls with MCP servers or external tools, whose attempts it cannot see.

Without the capability, a budget fails before the call: Adapter '<shortname>' cannot enforce request run budget for this execution.

items.title: The Request Size Ceiling
items.text:
Before each call, Kedi estimates the request (one token per byte of prompt, instructions, tool schemas, output schema, media, and history) and rejects it when the estimate exceeds 85 % of the context window minus a 16,384-token output reserve. The window is 200,000 tokens unless the profile sets context_limit. A stateful adapter can make the history part of the estimate exact by implementing SupportsHistoryTokenEstimate:

from collections.abc import Mapping
from typing import Any

def estimate_history_tokens(self, state: Mapping[str, Any]) -> int:
    """Estimate the model-visible content of a resume_state, without metadata."""

Usage reported during the call is checked against the reservation as it arrives.

items.title: Subagent Usage Limits
items.text: A child's request, tool-call, and token limits are enforced from the same reports; see Subagents.

items.title: Running It
items.text:
run_budgets.py
import asyncio
import json

from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program
from kedi.run_budget import RunBudgetExceeded

from backend import BackendRequest, Reply, ToolCall
from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter


class Script:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.requests = 0

    async def complete(self, request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
        self.requests += 1
        if not any(m["role"] == "tool" for m in request.messages):
            return Reply(tool_calls=(ToolCall("c1", "lookup", {"city": "Paris"}),))
        return Reply(text="done")


def run(budget: str) -> tuple[object, Script]:
    backend = Script()
    source = f"""
@lookup(city: str) -> str:
  ###
  Look up a city.
  ###
  > tool:
    risk: read_only
  = `city`

> budget:
    {budget}
> use: lookup
[answer] << Look up Paris.
= <answer>
"""
    runtime = compile_program(parse_program(source), adapter=ChatAdapter(backend, model="m1"))
    try:
        return runtime.run_main(), backend
    except Exception as error:
        return error, backend
    finally:
        asyncio.run(runtime.aclose())


value, backend = run("request_limit: 2")
assert value == "done" and backend.requests == 2

error, backend = run("request_limit: 1")
assert isinstance(error, RunBudgetExceeded) or isinstance(
    getattr(error, "original", None), RunBudgetExceeded
), error
assert "Run request budget exhausted (limit 1, consumed 1)" in str(error)
assert backend.requests == 1

error, _backend = run("tool_attempt_limit: 0")
assert "Run tool_attempt budget exhausted (limit 0, consumed 0)" in str(error), error

A second request was refused before it reached the backend, and a tool attempt beyond the limit ended the run instead of reaching the model as a tool error.

items.title: Call Lifecycle
items.text: Every model call a program makes goes through the same sequence. This page lists it step by step, with the adapter methods Kedi calls at each point, and ends with a test that records the order on the reference adapter.

items.title: Which Statement Calls What
items.text:
Kedi statement Entry point Arguments [x] << ... (untyped raw invoke) invoke_sync prompt, instructions [x: T] << ... (typed raw invoke) produce_sync template, output_type=T, instructions >> ... [x] ... [y: T] ... (template capture) produce_sync template, output_schema, instructions > if: <claim> and > loop: <claim> conditions produce_sync template, output_type (an annotated bool), instructions a child run started by delegate_task invoke or produce_subagent (async) see Subagents

Kedi calls only keyword arguments. Accept unknown ones with **kwargs: new keywords are added over time, and an adapter must not fail on one it ignores.

  • prompt and template are the prompt Kedi rendered, not the source template. A template capture's prompt starts with Kedi's field list; a claim's prompt is Claim: <text>.
  • instructions is the complete instruction text for the call, or None when there is none. See Prompts and Instructions.
  • produce_sync receives exactly one of output_schema (a mapping from each output name to its resolved Kedi type) and output_type (a Python type). See Structured Output.

items.title: The Sequence
items.text:
For one call, Kedi:

  1. Resolves the call. It freezes the active profile, resolves the adapter from > adapter: / > agent: or the compiled default, and resolves the call's tools: the profile's Kedi tools, deferred capability tools, skill tools, artifact tools, and delegation tools, each wrapped for approval, required-tool tracking, artifact admission, and telemetry.
  2. Checks the adapter against the profile. > requires: capabilities, > fallback:, history processors, tool_reason, native compaction, CodeMode, and hook events are checked against capabilities. If the adapter does not implement SupportsProfileOverride, a profile that sets a model, effort, MCP servers, settings, compaction, or CodeMode fails with AgentProfileOverrideUnsupported. These checks raise before any model work.
  3. Opens a tool scope. For an adapter with SupportsToolRegistration, it enters tool_scope() and calls register_tool(spec) for each tool, even when the call has none. The empty scope keeps a nested call from inheriting its caller's tools.
  4. Enters the profile. For an adapter with SupportsProfileOverride, it enters profile_override(profile).
  5. Checks multimodal input. A prompt with images, audio, video, or documents and an adapter without supports_media_input fails with MediaError: Adapter '<shortname>' does not accept media input.
  6. Runs the prompt hook. For an adapter based on HookRegistrationMixin, user_prompt_submit hooks run now and may replace the prompt text. See Hooks.
  7. Assembles the request. The prompt, instruction parts, tool definitions, output contract, and conversation coordinates become one immutable AgentRunRequest.
  8. Opens the conversation turn. With history enabled, it reserves the next turn in the conversation; > history: enabled on an adapter without supports_stateful_history and SupportsConversationState fails with Adapter '<shortname>' does not support stateful history. See Conversations and History.
  9. Checks the run budget and request size. An active > budget: needs the matching budget capability. Kedi estimates the request's tokens from the prompt, instructions, tool schemas, output schema, media, and history, and reserves them against the profile's context limit. See Budgets and Usage.
  10. Enters the request scopes: required-tool tracking, artifact admission, the adapter's conversation_scope(conversation) when history is on, and the model-call telemetry span.
  11. Observes usage. Every report_invocation from the adapter now feeds the request-size reservation, telemetry, and checkpoints.
  12. Calls the adapter: invoke_sync(prompt=..., instructions=...) or produce_sync(template=..., output_schema=... | output_type=..., instructions=...).
  13. Checks required tools. If a tool marked required_before_output did not return successfully, the result is rejected with RequiredToolCallError.
  14. Validates the value. For a template capture, every output name must be present (LLM did not return required key: <name>). Each explicitly typed field ([x: T]), each typed raw invoke, and each claim is validated and converted with TypeAdapter(T).validate_python. Untyped fields ([x]) are kept as returned.
  15. Commits. With history, the turn is committed with the adapter's continuation state only now, after the value was accepted. On any exception the turn is cancelled and the continuation state is discarded.

Steps 13 to 15 belong to Kedi; an adapter never commits history or validates the final value itself.

items.title: Threads and Loops
items.text:
A template capture or claim runs as a job on Kedi's execution engine, so produce_sync is usually called on a worker thread, possibly for several blocks at once. Raw invokes run on the calling thread. In both cases:

  • keep per-call state in ContextVars or in the scopes Kedi opens, never in plain attributes;
  • run async work with kedi.agent_adapter.execution.run_sync, which uses Kedi's shared event loop; see Concurrency and Event Loops.

items.title: Recording the Sequence
items.text:
This adapter records each method Kedi calls on it:

run_lifecycle.py
import asyncio
from collections.abc import Generator, Sequence
from contextlib import contextmanager
from typing import Any

from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program

from backend import BackendRequest, Reply, ToolCall
from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter


class TracingAdapter(ChatAdapter):
    def __init__(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.events: list[str] = []

    @contextmanager
    def tool_scope(self, tools: Sequence[object] = ()) -> Generator[None, None, None]:
        self.events.append("enter tool_scope")
        with super().tool_scope(tools):
            yield
        self.events.append("exit tool_scope")

    def register_tool(self, tool: Any) -> None:
        if tool.name == "population":
            self.events.append("register population")
        super().register_tool(tool)

    @contextmanager
    def profile_override(self, profile: Any) -> Generator[None, None, None]:
        self.events.append("enter profile_override")
        with super().profile_override(profile):
            yield
        self.events.append("exit profile_override")

    def produce_sync(self, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        self.events.append(f"produce_sync {sorted(kwargs)}")
        return super().produce_sync(**kwargs)


class Backend:
    async def complete(self, request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
        if not any(m["role"] == "tool" for m in request.messages):
            return Reply(tool_calls=(ToolCall("c1", "population", {"city": "Paris"}),))
        return Reply(data={"count": 2_100_000})


SOURCE = """
@population(city: str) -> int:
  ###
  Return the population of a city.
  ###
  > tool:
    risk: read_only
  = `2_100_000`

> use: population
>> Paris has [count: int] inhabitants.
= `count`
"""

adapter = TracingAdapter(Backend(), model="m1")
runtime = compile_program(parse_program(SOURCE), adapter=adapter)
try:
    assert runtime.run_main() == 2_100_000
finally:
    asyncio.run(runtime.aclose())

assert adapter.events == [
    "enter tool_scope",
    "register population",
    "enter profile_override",
    "produce_sync ['instructions', 'output_schema', 'template']",
    "exit profile_override",
    "exit tool_scope",
], adapter.events

The scopes are strictly nested: tools are registered before the profile is entered, both are open while the adapter runs, and both close in reverse order after it returns.

items.title: Capability Reference
items.text: AdapterCapabilities (kedi.agent_adapter.AdapterCapabilities) is the adapter's declaration of what it implements. Kedi reads it before relying on an optional protocol, > requires: checks it before any model I/O, and the language server and kedi explain read it for built-in adapters.

items.title: Values
items.text:
Most fields are bool | None:

Value Meaning Kedi True implemented and tested relies on it False not implemented refuses programs that need it None unknown, for example until a remote peer is asked refuses it, unless the name is in negotiated_capabilities

Declare only what the adapter really implements, not what the underlying SDK could do. A capability that Kedi relies on but the adapter only approximates fails in ways Kedi cannot detect.

items.title: Fields
items.text:
Field Means the adapter Kedi, when it is True When a program needs it and it is not True supports_structured_output constrains answers to a JSON Schema — > requires: structured_output fails supports_tool_registration implements tool_scope / register_tool registers each call's tools tools on an adapter without the protocol: AgentToolOverrideUnsupported: Active adapter does not support tool registration supports_capabilities applies > capability: bundles — (Kedi merges a bundle's instructions and tools into the profile; using one adds an implicit capabilities requirement) MissingAdapterCapabilityError for capabilities supports_deferred_tools activates defer: true capability tools on demand registers tools with a pending deferred_capability MissingAdapterCapabilityError for deferred_tools supports_mcp connects profile MCP servers — (mcp_servers reaches the adapter through the profile either way) > requires: mcp fails; the adapter must refuse servers it cannot open supports_profile_override implements SupportsProfileOverride — (the protocol, not the flag, is checked at run time) > requires: profile_override fails supports_model_override honors > model: — > requires: model_override fails supports_model_fallback tries > fallback: models on transient failures passes fallback_models > fallback: fails with MissingAdapterCapabilityError for model_fallback supports_effort honors > effort: — > requires: effort fails supports_settings honors the names in settings — > requires: settings fails settings the accepted setting names allows tool_reason, and names Kedi does not know, only when listed tool_reason is not supported by adapter '<shortname>'; adapter '<shortname>' does not take the settings <names> supports_codemode runs the CodeMode controls, or, on a JSON-RPC bridge, its backend's own code mode allows > codemode: CodeMode is not supported by adapter '<shortname>' supports_native_approvals applies approval policies itself stops wrapping tools with approval; passes approval_ceiling to children — supports_native_approval_handler drives an interactive approval handler natively — > requires: native_approval_handler fails supports_subagents runs children (SupportsSubagentExecution) offers delegate_task and continue_subagent AgentSubagentUnsupported: Active adapter does not support Kedi subagent delegation supports_background_subagents lets children run while the parent continues offers background, wait_subagent, cancel_subagent, subagent_status background: true fails as a tool error supports_live_subagent_input delivers input to running children offers send_subagent_input, send_parent_message > requires: live_subagent_input fails supports_subagent_interrupt stops and restarts a child attempt accepts interrupt: true > requires: subagent_interrupt fails supports_artifacts passes Kedi tool results through unchanged and registers artifact tools adds the artifact contract to calls with tools a call with tools fails: ArtifactCapabilityError: Active adapter does not support Kedi artifact references and tools supports_native_artifacts admits adapter-native and MCP tool results before they enter history — > requires: native_artifacts fails supports_stateful_history continues native conversations (SupportsConversationState) enters conversation_scope and keeps continuation state > history: enabled fails: Adapter '<shortname>' does not support stateful history supports_history_replay rebuilds the full causal message sequence from Kedi history — > requires: history_replay fails supports_history_processing runs history processors allows processors and conditions MissingAdapterCapabilityError for history_processing supports_native_compaction compacts history natively allows compaction: native native compaction is not supported by adapter '<shortname>' supports_stream_events emits streaming events — > requires: stream_events fails supports_request_budget admits each model request against the run budget allows > budget: request_limit Adapter '<shortname>' cannot enforce request run budget for this execution supports_token_usage reports the provider's token counts with each invocation (see Reporting Usage) — a child with token limits fails before it runs: Adapter '<shortname>' reports no token usage, so the subagent <limits> cannot be enforced supports_tool_attempt_budget admits each tool attempt against the run budget allows > budget: tool_attempt_limit (not with MCP or external tools) Adapter '<shortname>' cannot enforce tool_attempt run budget for this execution supports_media_input accepts multimodal input: places prompt images, audio, video, and documents in the request allows multimodal prompts MediaError: Adapter '<shortname>' does not accept media input supports_image_output returns an Image for [img: Image] << ...: one the model draws, or one of the request's media it names allows image output the model can only name an attached image; a request with none fails: MediaError: Adapter '<shortname>' cannot produce images supports_audio_output returns an Audio for [speech: Audio] << ..., from a model that speaks; the request carries no media and no tools allows speech output MediaError: Adapter '<shortname>' cannot produce speech supports_native_structured_output False: the backend cannot take an output schema natively adds the protocol.output part to render() (see Rendered Request) — supports_native_tool_calling False: the backend cannot take tool definitions natively adds the protocol.tools part to render(): the tool catalog and the call format — hooks dispatches the listed hook events (HookCapabilities) runs profile hooks Agent hooks are not supported by adapter '<shortname>', or Agent hook events <names> are not supported supported_json_schema_formats enforces these JSON Schema formats the language server flags other formats for built-in adapters — negotiated_capabilities checks these None capabilities itself, before remote work lets > requires: pass for them —

A — in the third column means Kedi changes nothing at run time; the flag still answers > requires:, the language server, and kedi explain.

items.title: Invariants
items.text:
The constructor enforces two dependencies:

  • supports_artifacts=True requires supports_structured_output=True and supports_tool_registration=True;
  • supports_native_artifacts=True requires supports_artifacts=True.

items.title: > requires: and Negotiation
items.text:
> requires:
    structured_output
    tool_registration

Kedi checks each requirement against capability_status(name):

  • True passes;
  • False fails with MissingAdapterCapabilityError: Adapter '<shortname>' does not satisfy required capability '<name>';
  • None fails too, unless the name is in negotiated_capabilities. An adapter that can only learn a capability from its peer, such as an A2A adapter reading an Agent Card, lists it there and must refuse the request itself, before starting remote work, when the peer turns out not to support it.

items.title: Built-in Shortnames
items.text: The language server and kedi explain resolve capabilities from the adapter registry, by shortname. An adapter passed as an instance (compile_program(adapter=...)) is known only at run time, so its capabilities produce run-time errors, not editor diagnostics.

items.title: Running It
CodeMode
items.text: With > codemode: enabled, the model does not call the profile's tools one by one. It gets three control tools and writes short Python programs that call the application tools inside a sandbox (Monty). Kedi provides the sandbox, the catalog, the limits, and the tool boundary; the adapter swaps the tools it exposes for the controls.

items.title: The Controls
items.text:
Tool Purpose search_tools browse the catalog of application tools; returns names and a cursor get_tool_schema return exact schemas for chosen tools and make them callable in the sandbox execute_code run one bounded code cell; tools are awaited: result = await lookup(city="Paris")

The application tools (procedures, Python tools, MCP tools the adapter connected, artifact and skill tools) stay behind the controls. Each nested call still goes through the tool's wrapped fn, so approval, hooks, artifact admission, budgets, and telemetry apply per call.

items.title: Implementing It
items.text:
Kedi checks supports_codemode before the call: CodeMode is not supported by adapter '<shortname>'. The adapter reads the policy from the active profile and builds a bridge for the run:

Step Call read the policy settings = normalize_codemode_settings(profile.codemode) from kedi.agent_profile; None or enabled=False means no CodeMode build the run's bridge CodeModeToolSpecBridge(tools, limits=CodeModeLimits(**settings.limit_values()), policies=..., adapter_shortname=..., preload_tools=settings.preload_tools) from kedi.agent_adapter.codemode expose the controls declare bridge.control_tools to the backend instead of the application tools add the instructions append_codemode_instructions(instructions, enabled=True, preloaded_tools=bridge.preloaded_tools) close await bridge.close() when the run ends, also on error

policies are the approval policies the bridge applies to each nested call. Kedi's wrapped tools already apply theirs, so an adapter without native approvals passes (); an adapter with native approvals passes the same chain it applies to direct calls (see Approvals).

CodeMode needs inline approval: a handler that would defer a decision cannot suspend a partially executed cell. The controls are sequential and never produce artifacts; their results go to the model as they are.

codemode_adapter.py
from dataclasses import replace
from typing import Any

from kedi.agent_adapter.codemode import (
    CodeModeLimits,
    CodeModeToolSpecBridge,
    append_codemode_instructions,
)
from kedi.agent_profile import normalize_codemode_settings

from backend import Reply
from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter


class CodeModeAdapter(ChatAdapter):
    capabilities = replace(ChatAdapter.capabilities, supports_codemode=True)

    async def _run(self, **kwargs: Any) -> tuple[Reply, list[dict[str, Any]]]:
        settings = normalize_codemode_settings(self.active_profile.codemode)
        if settings is None or not settings.enabled:
            return await super()._run(**kwargs)
        bridge = CodeModeToolSpecBridge(
            self._tools.get(),
            limits=CodeModeLimits(**settings.limit_values()),
            policies=(),
            adapter_shortname=self.shortname,
            preload_tools=settings.preload_tools,
        )
        kwargs["instructions"] = append_codemode_instructions(
            kwargs.get("instructions"), enabled=True, preloaded_tools=bridge.preloaded_tools
        )
        token = self._tools.set(bridge.control_tools)
        try:
            return await super()._run(**kwargs)
        finally:
            self._tools.reset(token)
            await bridge.close()

items.title: Running It
items.text:
run_codemode.py
import asyncio
import json

from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program

from backend import BackendRequest, Reply, ToolCall
from codemode_adapter import CodeModeAdapter

SOURCE = """
@population(city: str) -> int:
  ###
  Return the population of a city.
  ###
  > tool:
    risk: read_only
  = `{"Paris": 2_100_000, "Lyon": 520_000}[city]`

> codemode: enabled
> use: population
[answer] << What is the combined population of Paris and Lyon?
= <answer>
"""

CODE = 'a = await population(city="Paris")\nb = await population(city="Lyon")\na + b'


class Script:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.tools: list[list[str]] = []

    async def complete(self, request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
        self.tools.append(sorted(tool["name"] for tool in request.tools))
        results = [json.loads(m["content"]) for m in request.messages if m["role"] == "tool"]
        if not results:
            arguments = {"tool_names": ["population"]}
            return Reply(tool_calls=(ToolCall("c1", "get_tool_schema", arguments),))
        if len(results) == 1:
            return Reply(tool_calls=(ToolCall("c2", "execute_code", {"code": CODE}),))
        return Reply(text=str(results[1]["result"]))


backend = Script()
runtime = compile_program(parse_program(SOURCE), adapter=CodeModeAdapter(backend, model="m1"))
try:
    assert runtime.run_main() == "2620000"
finally:
    asyncio.run(runtime.aclose())

assert backend.tools[0] == ["execute_code", "get_tool_schema", "search_tools"]

The model saw only the three controls; one execute_code cell called the procedure twice through its wrapped fn and combined the results.

items.title: Compaction and Prompt Caching
items.text: A long conversation outgrows the context window and gets expensive to resend. Two mechanisms address that: compaction shortens the history, and prompt caching lets the provider reuse an unchanged prefix. Both depend on the adapter's native history, so both are adapter work that Kedi configures and checks.

items.title: Native Compaction
items.text:
A program asks for compaction in its history settings:

> history:
    enabled: true
    compaction_mode: native
    compaction_threshold: `100_000`

compaction_mode is native or disabled. With native, the provider or harness compacts the history itself: OpenAI and Anthropic context management, Codex thread limits, Claude Agent SDK session compaction. Kedi does not replace an unsupported provider with a summarizer of its own.

Kedi checks before the call:

Condition Error compaction_mode: native without history CompactionSettingsError: native compaction requires history to be enabled the adapter does not advertise supports_native_compaction CompactionSettingsError: native compaction is not supported by adapter '<shortname>'

The adapter receives the policy as profile.compaction, a kedi.agent_profile.compaction.CompactionSettings with mode and an optional threshold in input tokens, in profile_override. It must:

  • map the policy to the backend: enable the provider's compaction and pass threshold when the backend has one;
  • refuse what it cannot honor: a backend with no configurable threshold must reject an explicit threshold (Kedi's Claude adapter does), instead of silently using its own;
  • treat disabled as "add no compaction": it does not switch off compaction that a harness performs internally;
  • mark rewritten history: when a turn's history was compacted, set conversation.cache_prefix_changed = True so Kedi starts a new cache epoch (see below);
  • store the compacted history in result_state like any other turn (see Conversations and History).

items.title: Prompt Caching
items.text:
Providers cache a request prefix that repeats exactly: tool definitions, instructions, and earlier turns. Kedi keeps its side stable:

  • instruction parts are ordered from the most to the least stable and do not change between calls with the same profile and tools (see Prompts and Instructions);
  • each conversation lane has a cache_key, available as AdapterConversationContext.cache_key in conversation_scope and as request.conversation.cache_key on the assembled request.

The adapter's part:

  • send tools, then instructions, then the history, in the same order and serialization on every request;
  • pass cache_key to the provider's cache-routing option when it has one (Kedi's Pydantic AI adapter sends it as OpenAI's prompt_cache_key);
  • apply provider cache-control markers only to stable content;
  • never change earlier history silently. When a processor, compaction, or a reset rewrites it, set cache_prefix_changed = True. Kedi then increments the conversation's cache_epoch, derives a new cache_key, and drops the state of other adapters in the conversation, whose history no longer matches.

items.title: Running It
items.text:
run_compaction.py
import asyncio
from collections.abc import Generator
from contextlib import contextmanager
from dataclasses import replace
from typing import Any

from kedi.agent_adapter import AdapterConversationContext
from kedi.agent_profile.compaction import CompactionSettingsError
from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program

from backend import BackendRequest, Reply
from stateful_adapter import StatefulAdapter


class CompactingAdapter(StatefulAdapter):
    capabilities = replace(StatefulAdapter.capabilities, supports_native_compaction=True)

    def __init__(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.policies: list[object] = []
        self.cache_keys: list[str] = []

    @contextmanager
    def profile_override(self, profile: Any) -> Generator[None, None, None]:
        self.policies.append(profile.compaction)
        with super().profile_override(profile):
            yield

    @contextmanager
    def conversation_scope(
        self, conversation: AdapterConversationContext
    ) -> Generator[None, None, None]:
        self.cache_keys.append(conversation.cache_key)
        with super().conversation_scope(conversation):
            yield


class Echo:
    async def complete(self, request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
        return Reply(text="ok")


SOURCE = """
> history:
    enabled: true
    compaction_mode: native
    compaction_threshold: `50_000`
[a] << First.
[b] << Second.
= <b>
"""


def run(source: str, adapter: StatefulAdapter) -> None:
    runtime = compile_program(parse_program(source), adapter=adapter)
    try:
        runtime.run_main()
    finally:
        asyncio.run(runtime.aclose())


adapter = CompactingAdapter(Echo(), model="m1")
run(SOURCE, adapter)
assert {(p.mode, p.threshold) for p in adapter.policies} == {("native", 50_000)}
first_key, second_key = adapter.cache_keys
assert first_key and first_key == second_key

try:
    run(SOURCE, StatefulAdapter(Echo(), model="m1"))
except Exception as error:
    assert "native compaction is not supported by adapter 'chat'" in str(error), error
else:
    raise AssertionError("native compaction needs supports_native_compaction")

items.title: Concurrency and Event Loops
items.text: One adapter instance serves a whole program. Kedi calls it from several threads at once, runs children in background tasks, and nests calls inside tool calls. This page states the rules that keep those calls apart and keep provider clients working.

items.title: Where Calls Come From
items.text:
Call Thread Concurrency template captures and claims an engine worker thread independent blocks run at the same time raw invokes (<<) the thread running the program one at a time per program thread a child (invoke, produce_subagent) a task on Kedi's event loop several children, and background children, at once a nested call from a tool inside the outer call's tool execution while the outer call waits for the tool

Calls of one conversation are the exception: Kedi runs them strictly in turn order (see Conversations and History).

items.title: State
items.text:
• Keep per-call state in ContextVars or in objects Kedi passes (the conversation context, the child request). Kedi copies the context into worker threads and tasks, so a value set inside a scope is visible to everything that call does, and to nothing else.
  • Never keep the active tools, profile, child request, or conversation in a plain attribute. A second block running at the same time would see them.
  • Instance attributes are for configuration and for objects shared safely by all calls, such as an async provider client.

items.title: One Event Loop
items.text:
Kedi runs all model work that overlaps in time on one shared event loop. That is what lets provider connection pools and background children work across calls (docs/EVENT_LOOPS.md in the Kedi repository has the full design). For an adapter:

  1. Run async work from sync entry points with run_sync (kedi.agent_adapter.execution.run_sync). Never call asyncio.run, start a thread with its own loop, or keep a private loop for model work.
  2. Never block the loop. Inside coroutines, use async clients. A blocking call stalls every concurrent call and child; if a backend only offers a blocking client, run it with asyncio.to_thread.
  3. Bind clients to the loop that uses them. Create async clients lazily inside the running loop, or use clients that do so. A client created on one loop and used on another fails with errors such as "attached to a different loop" or "Event loop is closed".
  4. Hold locks only around state changes, never across an await of a model request, an approval, or a tool.
  5. An async host keeps its loop. When a host runs Kedi inside use_async_owner_loop(), Kedi uses the host's loop; run_sync follows, and the adapter must not close it.

items.title: Resources
items.text: runtime.aclose() releases the runtime's sessions, children, and artifacts; it does not close the adapter. Whoever created the adapter owns it. Give an adapter that holds connections or processes close() and aclose() methods and call them when the adapter is no longer needed. Resources that belong to one conversation go in the conversation's cleanup instead.

items.title: Running It
items.text:
run_concurrency.py
import asyncio
import threading

from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program

from backend import BackendRequest, Reply
from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter


class Slow:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.active = 0
        self.peak = 0
        self.prompts: list[str] = []

    async def complete(self, request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
        with self.lock:
            self.active += 1
            self.peak = max(self.peak, self.active)
        self.prompts.append(request.messages[-1]["content"])
        await asyncio.sleep(0.3)
        with self.lock:
            self.active -= 1
        field = "city" if "capital" in request.messages[-1]["content"] else "river"
        return Reply(data={field: "answer"})


SOURCE = """
>> The capital of France is [city].
>> The longest river in France is [river].
= `(city, river)`
"""

backend = Slow()
runtime = compile_program(parse_program(SOURCE), adapter=ChatAdapter(backend, model="m1"))
try:
    assert runtime.run_main() == ("answer", "answer")
finally:
    asyncio.run(runtime.aclose())

assert backend.peak == 2
assert sum("capital" in p for p in backend.prompts) == 1
assert sum("river" in p for p in backend.prompts) == 1

The two independent blocks reached the backend at the same time, each with its own prompt and output schema, through one adapter instance.

items.title: Conversations and History
items.text: With > history: enabled, consecutive calls of a profile form one conversation: each call sees the earlier turns. Kedi owns the conversation: turn order, commit and rollback, persistence, and cache identity. The adapter owns the native form of the history, the messages its backend needs to continue, and stores it in state Kedi hands it.

items.title: The Protocol
items.text:
kedi.agent_adapter.SupportsConversationState:

from contextlib import AbstractContextManager
from kedi.agent_adapter import AdapterConversationContext

def conversation_scope(
    self, conversation: AdapterConversationContext
) -> AbstractContextManager[None]: ...

Advertise supports_stateful_history=True. Without both, > history: enabled fails before the call: Adapter '<shortname>' does not support stateful history.

items.title: One Turn
items.text:
For each call in a conversation, Kedi:

  1. reserves the next turn; calls of one conversation run strictly in order, even when the program runs blocks in parallel;
  2. builds an AdapterConversationContext with the adapter's state from the last committed turn as resume_state;
  3. enters conversation_scope(context) around the call (see Call Lifecycle, step 10);
  4. after a successful call, commits context.result_state as the adapter's state, together with the prompt and the result as portable turns;
  5. after a failed or cancelled call, discards result_state and keeps the previous state.

The adapter reads resume_state at the start of the call and writes result_state before it returns. It never commits anything itself.

items.title: The Context
items.text: Field Use resume_state the adapter's state from the last committed turn of this lane; empty for the first turn result_state write the state the next turn should resume from session_id, turn_sequence the conversation and the turn number cache_key, cache_epoch pass cache_key to provider prompt caching; it changes when the epoch does cache_prefix_changed set to True when this turn rewrote earlier history (for example native compaction); Kedi then rotates the cache epoch cleanup a callable that releases a live resource kept across turns, such as a remote session; Kedi calls it when the state is replaced or the conversation closes require_explicit_completion(), mark_completed() for backends that report completion asynchronously: call the first at the start and the second when the backend confirms the turn, and Kedi commits only then

items.title: Lanes
items.text: Kedi keys the adapter's state by a lane: a fingerprint of the adapter class and shortname, its default model, and the profile's model, fallback models, effort, settings, MCP servers, and tool definitions. When any of them changes between turns, the new turn gets an empty resume_state: native history recorded for one model and tool set is not replayed into another. The portable turns are still recorded and persisted by Kedi.

items.title: What to Store
items.text:
resume_state and result_state are persisted with interactive sessions and snapshots. Store only JSON-compatible values: serialized messages, a remote thread id, a digest of the instructions. Keep live clients, streams, and SDK objects out; hold those in cleanup's closure.

Store the complete causal message sequence, including tool calls and their results in order. Provider-native tool calls and results stay native messages; never flatten them into user-prompt text.

items.title: Implementing It
items.text:
stateful_adapter.py
from collections.abc import Generator, Sequence
from contextlib import contextmanager
from contextvars import ContextVar
from dataclasses import replace
from typing import Any

from kedi.agent_adapter import AdapterConversationContext

from backend import Reply
from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter


class StatefulAdapter(ChatAdapter):
    capabilities = replace(ChatAdapter.capabilities, supports_stateful_history=True)

    def __init__(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self._conversation: ContextVar[AdapterConversationContext | None] = ContextVar(
            f"chat_conversation_{id(self)}", default=None
        )

    @contextmanager
    def conversation_scope(
        self, conversation: AdapterConversationContext
    ) -> Generator[None, None, None]:
        token = self._conversation.set(conversation)
        try:
            yield
        finally:
            self._conversation.reset(token)

    async def _run(
        self,
        *,
        prompt: str,
        instructions: str | None,
        output_schema: dict[str, Any] | None,
        history: Sequence[dict[str, Any]] = (),
        max_requests: int | None = None,
    ) -> tuple[Reply, list[dict[str, Any]]]:
        conversation = self._conversation.get()
        if conversation is not None and not history:
            history = conversation.resume_state.get("messages", [])
        reply, messages = await super()._run(
            prompt=prompt,
            instructions=instructions,
            output_schema=output_schema,
            history=history,
            max_requests=max_requests,
        )
        if conversation is not None:
            conversation.result_state["messages"] = messages
        return reply, messages

The class adds history at the one place every call passes through. Writing result_state on the way out is safe even when Kedi later rejects the value (a missing field, a required tool that never ran): Kedi commits it only after accepting the result.

items.title: History Processing
items.text:
> history: may name a history processor, a callable that receives the native message list before each model request and returns a shorter or rewritten one. Advertise supports_history_processing=True only when the adapter runs processors through Kedi's runner, kedi.agent_adapter.history_processing.HistoryProcessorRunner:

Step Call construct once HistoryProcessorRunner(processor, codec, condition) with a HistoryMessageCodec for your message type per call with runner.run_scope(conversation): around the run before each model request outcome = await runner.process(messages, model_id=model); send outcome.messages after a successful run runner.capture(messages, stored_messages) to record the lineage of the saved history before sending runner.prepare_transport() tells whether to reset a server-side continuation and which cache key to use

The codec has two methods: clone(messages) returns an independent copy, and inspect(messages) returns a HistorySnapshot describing each message's role, tool-call pairing, and fingerprint, so the runner can protect tool-call groups and unfinished turns from being cut apart. Kedi's Pydantic AI and LangChain adapters (PydanticHistoryMessageCodec, LangChainHistoryMessageCodec) are the reference implementations.

items.title: Running It
items.text:
run_conversations.py
import asyncio

from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program

from backend import BackendRequest, Reply
from stateful_adapter import StatefulAdapter


class Recorder:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.requests: list[BackendRequest] = []

    async def complete(self, request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
        self.requests.append(request)
        return Reply(text=f"answer to {request.messages[-1]['content']}")


def run(source: str, backend: Recorder) -> None:
    runtime = compile_program(parse_program(source), adapter=StatefulAdapter(backend, model="m1"))
    try:
        runtime.run_main()
    finally:
        asyncio.run(runtime.aclose())


def users(request: BackendRequest) -> list[str]:
    return [m["content"] for m in request.messages if m["role"] == "user"]


backend = Recorder()
run("> history: enabled\n[a] << First.\n[b] << Second.\n= <b>\n", backend)
first, second = backend.requests
assert users(first) == ["First."]
assert users(second) == ["First.", "Second."]
assert second.messages[1] == {"role": "assistant", "content": "answer to First."}

backend = Recorder()
run(
    "> history: enabled\n[a] << First.\n> model: m2\n[b] << Second.\n= <b>\n",
    backend,
)
assert users(backend.requests[1]) == ["Second."]

The second request carries the first turn. A different model starts a new lane, so its first request carries no native history.

items.title: Errors, Retries, and Cancellation
items.text: An adapter meets three kinds of failure: a tool call fails, a backend request fails, or the run is cancelled. Kedi decides which failures the model may see and correct, which ones are retried, and which ones end the program. The adapter follows those decisions with three helpers.

items.title: Tool Failures
items.text:
When tool.fn(**arguments) raises, the adapter must pick one of three paths:

Failure Path Example ToolApprovalDenied (approval policy) or HookDeniedError (pre_tool_use hook) return exc.message to the model as a failed tool result Tool 'delete_file' was denied: static deny policy correctable_tool_error(tool, exc) returns a message return that message to the model Tool lookup failed: ValueError: unknown city. Correct the arguments if they caused this, or continue without this result. correctable_tool_error(tool, exc) returns None re-raise; the program call fails a RuntimeError in a procedure, RunBudgetExceeded, run cancellation

kedi.agent_adapter.tools.errors.correctable_tool_error(tool, exc) is the classification Kedi's built-in adapters use. It returns Kedi's model-facing message for:

  • application tools (Kedi procedures and Python tools) that raise ValueError, LookupError, or OSError: rejected input, a missing record, unreachable data;
  • Kedi's own tool families: subagent delegation and lifecycle, dynamic workflows, artifact management, filesystem and terminal tools, CodeMode controls, and capability activation;

and None for budget exhaustion (RunBudgetExceeded), cancellation, failures after a tool already returned, and every other exception. Do not write your own classification or your own message; a message from this function is the text the model should read.

Kedi's errors (KediExecutionError and its subclasses, including both denial types) render a Kedi stack trace in str(exc). Send exc.message, the plain message, to the model.

The reference adapter's _execute implements exactly this table. A framework with a tool-retry envelope (Pydantic AI's ModelRetry, LangChain's ToolMessage with an error status) carries the same message through that envelope instead of a JSON result.

items.title: Request Failures
items.text:
A backend request can fail transiently: a rate limit, an overloaded server, a timeout. Retry only the request, never the whole run, and never a tool call:

from kedi.agent_adapter.request_retry import wait_for_request_retry

attempt = 0
while True:
    try:
        return await backend.complete(request)
    except Exception as error:
        attempt += 1
        if not await wait_for_request_retry(error, attempt=attempt, retries=retries):
            raise

wait_for_request_retry(error, attempt=, retries=):

  • returns False when attempt > retries or the error is not transient;
  • treats an error as transient when it has an integer status_code of 408, 429, or 5xx, so keep the provider's exception (or give yours a status_code);
  • waits for the provider's Retry-After (read from error.response.headers, following __cause__), or for exponential backoff from 0.5 s, and returns True;
  • returns False instead of waiting longer than 30 seconds.

Kedi's built-in adapters default to two retries and read the request_retries setting; request_retry_limit(settings, default) validates that setting. Report usage only for requests that completed.

When the request finally fails, raise. Kedi wraps the exception in a KediExecutionError with the Kedi source location and keeps the original as error.original, so the retry policy of the job-manager engine can still classify a 429 or a timeout. Never turn a failed request into an empty result, and never fall back to a text request after a structured one failed.

items.title: Cancellation
items.text:
A run is cancelled when the program's caller cancels it, when a parent cancels a child, when a CodeMode or workflow sandbox stops, or when an interrupt supersedes a child attempt. Cancellation arrives as asyncio.CancelledError in the adapter's coroutine, or as RunCancelled when synchronous work checks check_run_cancelled().

  • Let both propagate. Do not catch BaseException or asyncio.CancelledError to return a value.
  • Release what the call owns in finally: streams, sessions, subprocesses. run_sync gives the cancelled coroutine time to clean up.
  • A cancelled call must not write continuation state (result_state) or report a result; Kedi discards the turn.
  • A cancellation request is not proof that a remote side effect was undone. Do not report one as reversed.

items.title: Error Messages
items.text:
Raise errors that name the adapter and the failing part:

Situation Raise a profile field the adapter does not support AgentProfileOverrideUnsupported from profile_override an MCP transport the backend cannot open ValueError naming the transport, before the request the backend returned no text or no structured value RuntimeError naming the adapter a protocol or stream error from the backend the provider's exception, or one chained to it with from

items.title: Running It
Events, Streaming, and Telemetry
items.text: A host can follow a run while it happens: the notebook shows a child's progress, an A2A server forwards messages, a UI renders the model's text. Kedi defines the event model and delivers events to the host. The adapter tells Kedi when the backend produced a message and when a run changed state.

items.title: The Events
items.text:
kedi.agent_adapter:

Event Fields Published AgentRunStateEvent run_id, parent_run_id, agent_name, adapter, sequence, state (started, completed, failed, cancelled) when a run starts and ends AgentMessageEvent run_id, parent_run_id, agent_name, adapter, sequence, message_id, phase (commentary, final), content, segment_index, segment_count when a model message is complete

commentary is text the model produced on its way, such as "Let me look that up" before a tool call; final is the answer. run_id and parent_run_id tie a child's events to the delegation that started it.

A host observes events by binding a dispatcher around the work:

from kedi.agent_adapter import AgentEventDispatcher, bind_agent_event_dispatcher

dispatcher = AgentEventDispatcher(print)  # a callback or an AgentEventSink
with bind_agent_event_dispatcher(dispatcher):
    runtime.run_main()
dispatcher.close()  # delivers what is still queued

The dispatcher delivers on its own thread, so a slow sink never blocks the model loop; AsyncAgentEventQueue adapts it to an asyncio consumer.

items.title: The Adapter's Part
items.text:
Wrap each backend run in agent_event_run(shortname) from kedi.agent_adapter.events and report messages to the resolver it yields:

Resolver call When (entering the context) publishes started append_delta(message_id, text) a streamed chunk of a message arrived complete_message(message_id, text=None) a message is complete; without text the deltas are joined mark_tool_boundary() the model called a tool: pending messages become commentary mark_message_boundary() a new message started without a tool call complete_run(final_text=) a text call succeeded: publishes the answer as final, then completed (leaving the context) publishes completed, failed, or cancelled from how the block exited

The resolver is None when no host observes the run; skip the calls then. Publish final only for text calls (invoke): a structured call's result is a value, not a message. Advertise supports_stream_events=True when the adapter publishes messages this way.

event_adapter.py
import itertools
from contextvars import ContextVar
from dataclasses import replace
from typing import Any

from kedi.agent_adapter.events import AgentMessageResolver, agent_event_run

from backend import BackendRequest, Reply
from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter


class EventAdapter(ChatAdapter):
    capabilities = replace(ChatAdapter.capabilities, supports_stream_events=True)

    def __init__(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self._resolver: ContextVar[AgentMessageResolver | None] = ContextVar(
            f"chat_events_{id(self)}", default=None
        )
        self._message_ids = itertools.count(1)

    async def _run(self, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        with agent_event_run(self.shortname) as resolver:
            token = self._resolver.set(resolver)
            try:
                reply, messages = await super()._run(**kwargs)
            finally:
                self._resolver.reset(token)
            if resolver is not None and kwargs.get("output_schema") is None and reply.text:
                resolver.complete_run(final_text=reply.text)
            return reply, messages

    async def _complete(self, request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
        reply = await super()._complete(request)
        resolver = self._resolver.get()
        if resolver is not None and reply.tool_calls:
            if reply.text:
                resolver.complete_message(f"message-{next(self._message_ids)}", reply.text)
            resolver.mark_tool_boundary()
        return reply

items.title: Telemetry
items.text:
Kedi creates the spans: the agent call, each model call, each tool call (from the wrapped fn), approvals, hooks, and children. The adapter contributes:

  • usage, through report_invocation (see Budgets and Usage);
  • the model name, through default_model() and, for children, telemetry_model_name(), used when the profile sets no model;
  • errors, by raising the provider's exception, which the spans record.

Do not open spans for operations Kedi already traces.

items.title: Running It
items.text:
run_events.py
import asyncio

from kedi.agent_adapter import (
    AgentEventDispatcher,
    AgentMessageEvent,
    AgentRunStateEvent,
    bind_agent_event_dispatcher,
)
from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program
