Running It
items.text:
run_chat.py
import asyncio
from collections.abc import Callable

from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program

from backend import BackendRequest, Reply
from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter


class ScriptedBackend:
    """A test backend: each request is answered by a function of that request."""

    def __init__(self, answer: Callable[[BackendRequest], Reply]) -> None:
        self.answer = answer
        self.requests: list[BackendRequest] = []

    async def complete(self, request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
        self.requests.append(request)
        return self.answer(request)


def run(source: str, backend: ScriptedBackend) -> object:
    runtime = compile_program(parse_program(source), adapter=ChatAdapter(backend, model="m1"))
    try:
        return runtime.run_main()
    finally:
        asyncio.run(runtime.aclose())

runtime.aclose() releases the runtime's resources after the run; it is not model work, so asyncio.run is correct there.

A template capture with a tool:

run_chat.py
from backend import ToolCall

SOURCE = """
@population(city: str) -> int:
  ###
  Return the population of a city.
  ###
  > tool:
    risk: read_only
  = `2_100_000`

> use: population
>> Paris has [count: int] inhabitants.
= `count`
"""


def answer(request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
    tool_results = [m for m in request.messages if m["role"] == "tool"]
    if not tool_results:
        return Reply(tool_calls=(ToolCall("c1", "population", {"city": "Paris"}),))
    return Reply(data={"count": 2_100_000})


backend = ScriptedBackend(answer)
assert run(SOURCE, backend) == 2_100_000
first = backend.requests[0]
assert first.model == "m1"
assert "<TemplateInstructions>" in (first.instructions or "")
assert first.output_schema is not None and "count" in first.output_schema["properties"]
assert "population" in {tool["name"] for tool in first.tools}

items.title: Rendered Request
items.text: Kedi renders every piece of text a model reads; the adapter transports it. current_request().render() returns that text for the call in progress as one value. It is the supported way for a custom adapter to build its backend request.

items.title: Reading the Request
items.text:
from kedi.agent_adapter import current_request

rendered = current_request().render()

current_request() is valid inside invoke, produce and their _sync forms when Kedi makes the call. It raises RuntimeError outside a Kedi call, and when Kedi calls invoke, produce or produce_subagent to run a subagent child: the child runs inside its parent's request. has_current_request() says which case applies, so an adapter that also runs children falls back to the call's arguments:

from kedi.agent_adapter import current_request, has_current_request

if has_current_request():
    rendered = current_request().render()
else:
    ...  # build the request from prompt or template, instructions and output_schema
Field Contents system the instruction parts joined with a blank line, verbatim; None when there are none instruction_parts the same parts, each with identity, source and content user the rendered prompt: the prompt or template argument media the prompt's attachments (see Multimodal Input) output_json_schema the output schema Kedi built, with the model description and field descriptions; None for text output_tool_name final_result when there is an output schema, for a backend that takes the output as a tool call tools each tool's name, Kedi description, input and return schema, and required_before_output; parameters and returns give the schemas as plain JSON objects prompt_kind raw, template or claim call_kind invoke or produce

Send system as the system or developer text, user with its media as the user turn, the output schema as the backend's structured-output contract and tools as its tool definitions. Without protocol parts, system is the same text as the instructions argument.

items.title: Backends Without Native Structured Output or Tool Calling
items.text:
Some backends cannot take an output schema or tool definitions natively; a small local model that only answers in text, for example. Declare it in the capabilities:

AdapterCapabilities(
    supports_structured_output=True,
    supports_tool_registration=True,
    supports_native_structured_output=False,
    supports_native_tool_calling=False,
)

supports_structured_output stays True: Kedi still asks the adapter for structured values. The two new flags tell Kedi to render the contracts as text. render() then appends Kedi-owned instruction parts after the others:

Identity Present when Contents protocol.output supports_native_structured_output=False and the call has an output schema <OutputProtocol>: answer with a JSON value matching the schema, and the schema itself protocol.tools supports_native_tool_calling=False and the call has tools <ToolProtocol>: the call format, the final format, and <Tools>, each tool's description and schemas

The model answers with one JSON object per turn:

  • {"action": "call_tool", "callId": "c1", "name": "lookup", "arguments": {...}} to call a tool;
  • {"action": "final", "data": ...} with the output value, or {"action": "final", "text": "..."} for a text call.

The adapter parses that object and runs tools as usual. It never writes this text itself; the wording is versioned (PROTOCOL_VERSION in kedi.agent_adapter.request.prompts). The protocol parts are not part of the instructions argument, so hooks and telemetry see the instructions they always saw.

An adapter that adds tools during the run, from MCP servers for example, passes its final tool set so the catalog names them too:

from kedi.agent_adapter.request import tool_definition

rendered = current_request().render(tools=tuple(tool_definition(spec) for spec in specs))

items.title: Corrections
items.text:
Corrections are Kedi's text too. kedi.agent_adapter.request.prompts has one function for each:

Function Send it as a user turn when output_correction(error) the answer fails the output schema; error is the validation error required_tools_correction(missing, attempted=...) the model answers before a tool with required_before_output completed; attempted is whether it tried protocol_correction(detail) the answer is not one protocol action; detail is your parse error

Take required tools from ToolDefinition.required_before_output. Do not infer them from the prompt.

items.title: Scenario
items.text:
The adapter below forwards the rendered request to a text-only backend and parses its JSON action.

rendered_adapter.py
from __future__ import annotations

import json
from typing import Any

from pydantic import TypeAdapter

from kedi.agent_adapter import AdapterCapabilities, AgentAdapterKind, current_request
from kedi.agent_adapter.request.prompts import output_correction


class PromptedAdapter:
    """A backend that reads text and answers with one JSON action."""

    kind: AgentAdapterKind = "agent-framework"
    shortname = "prompted"
    capabilities = AdapterCapabilities(
        supports_structured_output=True,
        supports_native_structured_output=False,
        supports_native_tool_calling=False,
    )

    def __init__(self, answers: list[str]) -> None:
        self.answers = answers
        self.sent: list[dict[str, Any]] = []

    def invoke_sync(self, *, prompt: str, **_: Any) -> str:
        return str(self._answer(None))

    def produce_sync(self, *, template: str, output_type: Any = None, **_: Any) -> Any:
        return self._answer(TypeAdapter(output_type))

    def _answer(self, validator: TypeAdapter[Any] | None) -> Any:
        rendered = current_request().render()
        messages = [{"role": "user", "content": rendered.user}]
        for answer in self.answers:
            self.sent.append({"system": rendered.system, "messages": list(messages)})
            action = json.loads(answer)
            if validator is None:
                return action["text"]
            try:
                return validator.validate_python(action["data"])
            except ValueError as error:
                messages += [
                    {"role": "assistant", "content": answer},
                    {"role": "user", "content": output_correction(error)},
                ]
        raise RuntimeError("no valid answer")
run_rendered_request.py
from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program

from rendered_adapter import PromptedAdapter

adapter = PromptedAdapter(['{"action": "final", "data": "three"}', '{"action": "final", "data": 3}'])
runtime = compile_program(
    parse_program("[count: int] << How many sides has a triangle?\n= `count`\n"), adapter=adapter
)
assert runtime.run_main() == 3

first, second = adapter.sent
assert first["system"].startswith("<OutputProtocol>\n")
assert '<OutputSchema>{"type": "integer"}</OutputSchema>' in first["system"]
assert first["messages"] == [{"role": "user", "content": "How many sides has a triangle?"}]
correction = second["messages"][-1]["content"]
assert correction.startswith("The structured output does not match the required schema:")

The first answer fails the schema, so the adapter sends Kedi's correction and the second answer is accepted.

items.title: Structured Output
items.text: produce and produce_sync return values, not text. Kedi says what the value must look like in one of two ways, the adapter asks the backend for it, and Kedi validates what comes back.

items.title: The Two Contracts
items.text:
Argument Sent for Value output_schema template captures (>> ... [a] ... [b: T] ...) dict[str, ResolvedKediType]: one entry per output name, in template order output_type typed raw invokes ([x: T] << ...) and claims a Python type: T, or Annotated[bool, Field(description=...)] for a claim

Exactly one of them is set. ResolvedKediType is Kedi's resolved form of a field type, including Annotated descriptions, constraints, Literal choices, custom ~Types, and generics. Do not interpret it yourself; turn it into a JSON Schema with Kedi's helpers.

items.title: Building the JSON Schema
items.text:
from pydantic import TypeAdapter
from kedi.agent_adapter.output_schema import build_output_model

if output_schema is not None:
    schema = build_output_model(output_schema).model_json_schema()
else:
    schema = TypeAdapter(output_type).json_schema()

build_output_model builds the Pydantic model Kedi's own adapters send:

  • one field per output name, with the field's type, description, and constraints;
  • names that Pydantic cannot use as attributes (a leading underscore, model_..., or a BaseModel member) become internal field names with the Kedi name as the alias, so the JSON property is still the Kedi name;
  • fixed-length tuples are expressed with items instead of prefixItems, which most model APIs reject;
  • for template captures in completion mode, a model description that tells the model to return only the replacement values.

Call it inside produce: the description depends on the active request.

items.title: Non-Object Roots
items.text:
A claim's schema is a bare boolean, and a typed raw invoke's schema is whatever T is: {"type": "integer"}, an array, an enum. Many structured output APIs accept only an object at the root. For such a backend, wrap the schema in one property and unwrap the answer:

object_root.py
from typing import Any

from pydantic import TypeAdapter

from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter
from kedi.agent_adapter.output_schema import build_output_model


class ObjectRootAdapter(ChatAdapter):
    async def produce(
        self,
        *,
        template: str,
        output_schema: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
        output_type: Any = None,
        instructions: str | None = None,
        **_: Any,
    ) -> Any:
        if output_schema is not None:
            schema = build_output_model(output_schema).model_json_schema()
            reply, _messages = await self._run(
                prompt=template, instructions=instructions, output_schema=schema
            )
            return reply.data
        value_schema = TypeAdapter(output_type).json_schema()
        wrapped = {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"result": value_schema},
            "required": ["result"],
            "additionalProperties": False,
        }
        reply, _messages = await self._run(
            prompt=template, instructions=instructions, output_schema=wrapped
        )
        return reply.data["result"]

Move $defs to the wrapper's root if your backend does not resolve references below the root.

items.title: Return Values
items.text:
Call Return output_schema a mapping, or an object with one attribute per output name output_type the value

Return the decoded JSON. Then Kedi:

  1. reads every output name from the result; a missing one fails the call with LLM did not return required key: <name>;
  2. validates and converts each explicitly typed field ([x: T]), each typed raw invoke, and each claim with TypeAdapter(T).validate_python, so a JSON object becomes the program's ~Type instance and "3" becomes 3 for an int;
  3. keeps untyped fields ([x]) exactly as returned. Their schema type is string; return a string.

Do not convert values into Kedi types inside the adapter, and do not return provider message or response objects.

items.title: JSON Schema Formats
items.text: supported_json_schema_formats declares which JSON Schema format values the backend enforces, for example frozenset({"date", "date-time"}). The Kedi language server uses it for built-in adapters to flag field types that would produce an unsupported format (K-ADAPTER-SCHEMA-FORMAT). Leave it None when the backend accepts any format; Kedi still validates the returned value against the full type.

items.title: Advertising Structured Output
items.text: Set supports_structured_output=True only when the backend constrains the answer to the schema, including nested objects, lists, unions, and constraints. An adapter that only asks for JSON in the prompt does not support structured output and must not write such a prompt either (see Prompts and Instructions). A program can demand the capability with > requires: structured_output, which fails before any model call when the adapter does not advertise it.

items.title: Running It
items.text:
run_structured_output.py
import asyncio
from collections.abc import Callable

from kedi.errors import KediExecutionError
from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program

from backend import BackendRequest, Reply
from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter
from object_root import ObjectRootAdapter


class Recorder:
    def __init__(self, answer: Callable[[BackendRequest], Reply]) -> None:
        self.answer = answer
        self.requests: list[BackendRequest] = []

    async def complete(self, request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
        self.requests.append(request)
        return self.answer(request)


def run(source: str, answer: Callable[[BackendRequest], Reply], adapter_type=ChatAdapter):
    backend = Recorder(answer)
    runtime = compile_program(parse_program(source), adapter=adapter_type(backend, model="m1"))
    try:
        return runtime.run_main(), backend.requests
    finally:
        asyncio.run(runtime.aclose())


CAPTURE = """
~Airport(code: str, runways: int)

>> [city] has [airports: list[Airport]] and [population: int] inhabitants.
= `(city, airports, population)`
"""

value, [request] = run(
    CAPTURE,
    lambda _r: Reply(
        data={
            "city": "Paris",
            "airports": [{"code": "CDG", "runways": 4}],
            "population": "2100000",
        }
    ),
)
city, airports, population = value
assert city == "Paris"
assert airports[0].code == "CDG" and airports[0].runways == 4
assert population == 2_100_000
schema = request.output_schema
assert list(schema["properties"]) == ["city", "airports", "population"]
assert schema["properties"]["population"]["type"] == "integer"
assert "replacement values" in schema["description"]

A missing field fails the call:

run_structured_output.py
try:
    run(CAPTURE, lambda _r: Reply(data={"city": "Paris", "airports": []}))
except KediExecutionError as error:
    assert "LLM did not return required key: population" in str(error)
else:
    raise AssertionError("a missing field must fail")

A claim through a backend that needs an object root:

run_structured_output.py
CLAIM = """
[answer] = `'no'`
> if: Paris is in France
  [answer] := yes
= <answer>
"""

value, [request] = run(CLAIM, lambda _r: Reply(data={"result": True}), ObjectRootAdapter)
assert value == "yes"
assert request.output_schema["properties"]["result"]["type"] == "boolean"
assert "claim is established" in request.output_schema["properties"]["result"]["description"]

items.title: Subagents
items.text:
A profile with > subagent: name lets its model delegate tasks to child profiles. Kedi owns delegation: the delegation tools, budgets, run records, validation of child results, continuation history, cancellation, and the approval and sandbox limits that children inherit. The adapter owns one thing: running a child task on its backend when Kedi asks.

This page adds that capability to the reference adapter.

items.title: What Kedi Does and What the Adapter Does
items.text: Step Owner Offer delegate_task and the other control tools to the parent model Kedi, through register_tool Check max_agents, depth, concurrency, and the parent's allowed children Kedi Evaluate the child profile and resolve the child's adapter Kedi Resolve the child's tools and instructions, apply inherited approval and cwd/sandbox limits Kedi Isolate the child's profile, tools, and conversation Adapter, in subagent_scope Run the child task and return text or a JSON object Adapter, in invoke / produce_subagent Report each backend request Adapter, with report_invocation Validate the child result and feed corrections back to the model Kedi supplies the validator and the feedback text; the adapter runs the retry Record the run, enforce usage limits, publish the result to the parent Kedi

items.title: How Delegation Reaches the Parent
items.text:
Delegation needs nothing from the parent adapter beyond tool registration. When the active profile declares children, Kedi adds these tools to the call's tool set and registers them with register_tool, like any other tool:

Tool Offered when Purpose delegate_task always start a child; final_schema requests a JSON result continue_subagent always continue a completed child conversation wait_subagent, cancel_subagent, subagent_status the adapter advertises supports_background_subagents manage children started with background: true send_subagent_input, send_parent_message the adapter advertises supports_live_subagent_input message a running child or its parent run_workflow the profile uses > workflow: dynamic run generated orchestration code; children still run through Kedi

All of them are async ToolSpec functions with risk: read_only. Starting an isolated child is not itself a mutation; the child's own tools carry the risk. The adapter executes them like every other tool, which is why the reference adapter awaits awaitable tool results.

Capability checks happen before the parent runs:

Condition Error The parent's adapter does not advertise supports_subagents AgentSubagentUnsupported: Active adapter does not support Kedi subagent delegation The model passes background: true without supports_background_subagents the tool call fails with The active adapter does not support background subagents The child's adapter does not implement the protocol below KediExecutionError: Adapter '<shortname>' does not implement Kedi child execution

A child profile may select a different adapter (> adapter: or > agent:); the child's adapter, not the parent's, runs the child.

items.title: How Kedi Runs a Child
items.text:
For each child run, Kedi:

  1. evaluates the child profile and applies the inherited cwd/sandbox limits;
  2. resolves the child's adapter and checks the protocol;
  3. resolves the child's tools, already wrapped with the child's approval policy and every ancestor's policy (see Approvals);
  4. renders the child's instructions;
  5. calls subagent_run_kwargs(limits) with the remaining usage limits and adds instructions to the result;
  6. enters subagent_scope(request);
  7. calls await invoke(prompt=task, **run_kwargs) for a text child, or await produce_subagent(template=task, output_schema=schema, **run_kwargs) when a result schema applies;
  8. validates the result, records it, and returns it to the parent's tool call.

Kedi calls the async entry points. A child runs on Kedi's shared event loop, never through invoke_sync.

items.title: The Protocol
items.text:
kedi.agent_adapter.subagents.SupportsSubagentExecution:

class SupportsSubagentExecution(Protocol):
    shortname: str

    def telemetry_model_name(self) -> str | None: ...

    def subagent_scope(
        self, request: SubagentExecutionRequest
    ) -> AbstractContextManager[None]: ...

    def subagent_run_kwargs(self, limits: SubagentUsageLimits) -> Mapping[str, Any]: ...

    async def invoke(self, *, prompt: str, **kwargs: Any) -> str: ...

    async def produce_subagent(
        self, *, template: str, output_schema: dict[str, Any], **kwargs: Any
    ) -> Mapping[str, Any]: ...

Add supports_subagents=True to the capabilities. An optional class attribute, supports_native_subagent_resume, changes how continuations are sent; see Continuations.

items.title: The Request
items.text:
subagent_scope receives a SubagentExecutionRequest:

Field Type What the adapter does with it profile AgentProfile Apply it for the child's calls, as profile_override does: model, and any other field the adapter supports. tools tuple[ToolSpec, ...] Replace the parent's tools with exactly these. They include the child's Kedi tools, its artifact and skill tools, and its own delegation tools when it has children. instructions str \| None Also passed to invoke / produce_subagent as instructions; send it as the system message. approval_ceiling tuple[ApprovalPolicy \| None, ...] Only for adapters with supports_native_approvals: apply every policy, in order, to native and Kedi tools. Otherwise Kedi has already applied them. usage_limits SubagentUsageLimits The same limits passed to subagent_run_kwargs. output_state SubagentOutputState \| None Pass to accept_subagent_output so a profile > output: type is validated natively. conversation SubagentConversationContext Native continuation state: read resume_state, write result_state.

items.title: Implementing the Protocol
items.text:
subagent_adapter.py
from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Generator, Mapping, Sequence
from contextlib import contextmanager
from contextvars import ContextVar
from dataclasses import replace
from typing import Any

from jsonschema.validators import validator_for

from kedi.agent_adapter.output_schema import OutputCorrection
from kedi.agent_adapter.subagents import (
    SubagentConversationContext,
    SubagentExecutionRequest,
    SubagentUsageLimits,
    accept_subagent_output,
)

from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter


class SubagentChatAdapter(ChatAdapter):
    capabilities = replace(
        ChatAdapter.capabilities,
        supports_subagents=True,
        supports_background_subagents=True,
    )
    supports_native_subagent_resume = True

    def __init__(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self._child: ContextVar[SubagentExecutionRequest | None] = ContextVar(
            f"chat_child_{id(self)}", default=None
        )

    def telemetry_model_name(self) -> str | None:
        return self.active_profile.model or self._model

telemetry_model_name names the model in the child's run record and spans when the child profile does not set > model:.

items.title: Scoping a Child
items.text:
subagent_adapter.py
    @contextmanager
    def subagent_scope(self, request: SubagentExecutionRequest) -> Generator[None, None, None]:
        with self.tool_scope(request.tools), self.profile_override(request.profile):
            token = self._child.set(request)
            try:
                yield
            finally:
                self._child.reset(token)

    @contextmanager
    def tool_scope(self, tools: Sequence[object] = ()) -> Generator[None, None, None]:
        # A Kedi model call made by one of the child's tools opens a new tool scope.
        # It is not the child's own turn, so it must not see the child request.
        token = self._child.set(None)
        try:
            with super().tool_scope(tools):
                yield
        finally:
            self._child.reset(token)

Two details matter:

  • Replace, do not extend, the tools. tool_scope(request.tools) sets the child's tool set; the parent's tools, including its own delegate_task, must not be visible to the child.
  • Mark only the child's own turn. The child request lives in a ContextVar, so it would be inherited by anything the child's tools do. A Kedi procedure used as a tool may run its own >> template, and Kedi enters tool_scope() before every program call. Clearing the child request in tool_scope keeps that nested call an ordinary call.

items.title: Usage Limits
Text Children
items.text:
subagent_adapter.py
    async def invoke(
        self,
        *,
        prompt: str,
        instructions: str | None = None,
        max_requests: int | None = None,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ) -> str:
        child = self._child.get()
        if child is None:
            return await super().invoke(prompt=prompt, instructions=instructions, **kwargs)
        reply, messages = await self._run(
            prompt=prompt,
            instructions=instructions,
            output_schema=None,
            history=resume_messages(child.conversation),
            max_requests=max_requests,
        )
        if reply.text is None:
            raise RuntimeError("The child returned no text")
        save_messages(child.conversation, messages)
        return reply.text

Without a result schema the child's text becomes the delegation's task_summary, and final_result is None.

items.title: Structured Children
items.text:
A child returns structured data when the parent passes final_schema to delegate_task, or when the child profile declares > output: Type. Kedi wraps the schema before calling produce_subagent:

{
  "type": "object",
  "title": "KediSubagentResult",
  "properties": {
    "task_summary": {
      "type": "string",
      "maxLength": 1000,
      "description": "Briefly state what you did, key decisions, and any limitations."
    },
    "final_result": {"...": "the requested schema"}
  },
  "required": ["task_summary", "final_result"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}

Send output_schema to the backend as given and return the decoded object. Kedi validates it against the schema after produce_subagent returns; an invalid result fails the child. To let the model correct itself instead, run Kedi's validator in a retry loop:

subagent_adapter.py
    async def produce_subagent(
        self,
        *,
        template: str,
        output_schema: dict[str, Any],
        instructions: str | None = None,
        max_requests: int | None = None,
        **_: Any,
    ) -> Mapping[str, Any]:
        child = self._child.get()
        if child is None:
            raise RuntimeError("produce_subagent runs only inside subagent_scope")
        validator = validator_for(output_schema)(output_schema)
        history = resume_messages(child.conversation)
        prompt = template
        for _attempt in range(3):
            reply, messages = await self._run(
                prompt=prompt,
                instructions=instructions,
                output_schema=output_schema,
                history=history,
                max_requests=max_requests,
            )
            try:
                accepted = accept_subagent_output(reply.data, validator, child.output_state)
            except OutputCorrection as correction:
                history, prompt = messages, str(correction)
                continue
            save_messages(child.conversation, messages)
            return accepted
        raise RuntimeError("The child did not return a valid result after 3 attempts")

accept_subagent_output(output, validator, output_state):

  • checks the JSON Schema and raises OutputCorrection listing up to eight violations, ending with "Return a corrected object with task_summary and final_result as root siblings.";
  • with an output_state, also validates final_result against the child profile's > output: type, and returns the value serialized back to JSON;
  • returns the object to accept.

The correction message is Kedi's text. Send it to the model as the next user turn; do not write your own. Each retry is a backend request and counts against the child's limits.

items.title: Continuations
items.text:
continue_subagent(run_id, task) starts a new run in the same child conversation. Kedi sends the earlier turns in one of two ways:

supports_native_subagent_resume What the adapter receives absent or False prompt begins with "Continue the same child task using this verified prior conversation state:", followed by the earlier tasks and results as JSON, then the new task. The adapter needs no state. True prompt is the new task only. The adapter restores its own history from conversation.resume_state.

With native resume, the adapter keeps its message history in the conversation context:

subagent_adapter.py
def resume_messages(conversation: SubagentConversationContext) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    return list(conversation.resume_state.get("messages", []))


def save_messages(
    conversation: SubagentConversationContext, messages: list[dict[str, Any]]
) -> None:
    conversation.result_state["messages"] = messages
  • resume_state is the state your adapter wrote at the end of the previous successful run of this conversation; it is empty for the first run.
  • Write result_state only once the run has succeeded. Kedi commits it after validating the result, and drops it when the run fails or is cancelled, so a failed attempt never becomes history.
  • Both are plain dictionaries that Kedi persists with interactive sessions. Store JSON-compatible values only; keep live clients and SDK objects out.

items.title: Running It
Background Children
items.text:
Advertise supports_background_subagents only when a child can run while the parent's call continues. Kedi starts a background child as a task on its shared event loop and returns the handle to the parent's tool call. Two things make that safe:

  • the synchronous entry points use run_sync, so the parent call and the background child share Kedi's loop, and the child survives the tool call that started it;
  • all per-run state lives in ContextVars and in the request objects, so the parent's next model request and the child's requests do not see each other's tools, profile, or conversation.

items.title: Approvals in Children
items.text:
A child can never be more permissive than its ancestors. Every ancestor's approval policy applies to the child's tools, in order from the root, followed by the child's own policy; an ancestor without > approval: contributes Kedi's default policy, which denies non-read-only tools.

  • Adapters without supports_native_approvals need to do nothing. Kedi wraps the child's tools with all of these policies before they reach subagent_scope.
  • Adapters with supports_native_approvals receive the ancestor policies as request.approval_ceiling and must apply them, then the child profile's policy, to every tool the child can call, including backend-native tools.

items.title: Live Input and Interrupts
items.text:
Two further capabilities let a parent talk to a running child:

Capability Effect supports_live_subagent_input Kedi offers send_subagent_input and send_parent_message. Input sent while a child runs is queued for that child. supports_subagent_interrupt send_subagent_input may set interrupt: true, which stops the child's current attempt so it restarts with the new input.

Kedi's coordinator already handles input between attempts: when a child finishes while input is queued, Kedi starts another attempt of the same run with the input appended, after restoring resume_state from that attempt's result_state. To deliver input during an attempt, or to stop one, wrap the backend run in controlled_attempt:

from kedi.agent_adapter.subagents.control import controlled_attempt, current_live_input

control = current_live_input()
if control is None:
    reply, messages = await run_child()
else:
    reply, messages = await controlled_attempt(
        control,
        run_child(),
        deliver=deliver_now,  # optional: inject AgentInput items into the running backend
        stop=stop_backend,    # optional: ask the backend to stop the current turn
    )

controlled_attempt raises RunInterrupted when the attempt is superseded; let it propagate, because Kedi restarts the attempt. deliver receives AgentInput items, whose render() text is what the model should see; return False when they could not be delivered, and Kedi hands them to the next attempt instead. Advertise these capabilities only when the attempt really stops and restarts; a backend that cannot be interrupted must leave supports_subagent_interrupt unset.

items.title: Errors
items.text: Situation What happens invoke / produce_subagent raises The child run fails; the parent's tool call returns the failure to the parent model. produce_subagent returns a non-object TypeError: Subagent structured output must be an object, got <type> The object violates the wrapped schema jsonschema.ValidationError; the child fails. Use accept_subagent_output to correct instead. A reported request exceeds the child's limits KediExecutionError: Subagent request limit N exceeded: observed M The parent cancels a child The child's task receives asyncio.CancelledError; release backend resources and re-raise.

items.title: Testing an Adapter
items.text: An adapter is correct when real Kedi programs behave the same on it as on Kedi's own adapters. Test it the way the pages in this section do: replace the provider with a scripted backend, run programs through compile_program, and assert on what the backend received and what the program returned.

items.title: Scripted Backends
items.text:
A scripted backend answers each request with a function of that request and records it:

class ScriptedBackend:
    def __init__(self, answer):
        self.answer = answer
        self.requests = []

    async def complete(self, request):
        self.requests.append(request)
        return self.answer(request)

Decide the answer from the request, not from a counter: the tool results already in messages, the tools offered, whether output_schema is set. A script that keys on content keeps working when Kedi adds a correction turn or runs blocks in a different order.

items.title: What to Cover
items.text:
Write one scenario per row that applies to your adapter:

Area Scenario Page text [x] << ... returns the text Call Lifecycle structured output a capture with a custom type and a typed field; a claim; a typed raw invoke Structured Output prompt contract instructions and the prompt arrive verbatim and once Prompts and Instructions tools a tool call, an invalid argument, an approval denial, a fatal tool error Tools, Errors retries a transient failure is retried; a 400 is not Errors profiles > model: and a supported setting reach the backend; unsupported fields are refused Profiles hooks prompt edit, argument edit, denial Hooks artifacts a large result becomes a reference and can be read Artifacts children text, structured with a correction, continuation, background, and an ancestor deny Subagents history the second turn carries the first; a new lane starts empty Conversations budgets a request limit stops the second request Budgets concurrency two blocks run at once and stay apart Concurrency

Every capability you advertise needs at least one scenario that fails when the capability is broken. A capability with no scenario should not be advertised.

items.title: Parity With a Built-in Adapter
items.text:
Run the same program through Kedi's Pydantic AI adapter, driven by a FunctionModel that plays the same script, and compare what the program saw:

run_testing.py
import asyncio
import json

from pydantic_ai.messages import ModelRequest, ModelResponse, TextPart, ToolCallPart, ToolReturnPart
from pydantic_ai.models.function import FunctionModel

from kedi.agent_adapter import PydanticAdapter
from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program

from backend import BackendRequest, Reply, ToolCall
from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter

SOURCE = """
@population(city: str) -> int:
  ###
  Return the population of a city.
  ###
  > tool:
    risk: read_only
  = `{"Paris": 2_100_000}[city]`

> instructions: Use the tool for numbers.
> use: population
>> Paris has [count: int] inhabitants.
= `count`
"""


def run(adapter: object) -> object:
    runtime = compile_program(parse_program(SOURCE), adapter=adapter)
    try:
        return runtime.run_main()
    finally:
        asyncio.run(runtime.aclose())


class Script:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.instructions: list[str | None] = []

    async def complete(self, request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
        self.instructions.append(request.instructions)
        results = [json.loads(m["content"]) for m in request.messages if m["role"] == "tool"]
        if not results:
            return Reply(tool_calls=(ToolCall("c1", "population", {"city": "Paris"}),))
        return Reply(data={"count": results[0]["result"]})


pydantic_instructions: list[str | None] = []


async def function_model(messages, info) -> ModelResponse:
    pydantic_instructions.append(info.instructions)
    returns = [
        part
        for message in messages
        if isinstance(message, ModelRequest)
        for part in message.parts
        if isinstance(part, ToolReturnPart)
    ]
    if not returns:
        return ModelResponse(parts=[ToolCallPart("population", {"city": "Paris"}, tool_call_id="c1")])
    [output] = info.output_tools
    return ModelResponse(parts=[ToolCallPart(output.name, {"count": returns[0].content})])


script = Script()
assert run(ChatAdapter(script, model="m1")) == 2_100_000
assert run(PydanticAdapter(FunctionModel(function_model))) == 2_100_000
assert script.instructions[0] == pydantic_instructions[0], (script.instructions[0], pydantic_instructions[0])

Both adapters returned the same value, and the custom adapter sent the model exactly the instruction text Kedi's own adapter sends.

items.title: Conformance Check
items.text:
kedi adapter check MODULE:CLASS runs Kedi programs through your adapter and checks what reached the model against what Kedi rendered (see Rendered Request). CLASS.for_conformance(base_url) returns an adapter whose backend talks to the kit's local recording endpoint, which speaks three protocols:

Route Protocol {base_url}/v1/chat/completions OpenAI Chat Completions {base_url}/v1/messages Anthropic Messages {base_url}/kedi/webgpu the WebGPU bridge payload

Send requests with stream off; the endpoint refuses streamed ones. The kit creates a fresh adapter for every run and closes it afterwards with aclose() or close() when the adapter has one, so for_conformance may start processes or open clients.

Each scenario runs one Kedi call in two variants with different text:

Scenario Program invoke a raw invoke with profile instructions produce a template capture of nested types with field descriptions claim a template condition tool-allow, tool-deny a tool the model calls once, with approval: allow or deny media an image prompt; runs only with supports_media_input request-budget request_limit: 1 with a tool call, then with a failing first request; runs only with supports_request_budget subagent a > task child with its own instructions and a task capture; the kit checks the child's request, which reaches the adapter through invoke or produce_subagent; runs only with supports_subagents

Build the factory's client without SDK retries (max_retries=0). With retries on, Kedi cannot count every request, refuses request_limit, and the request-budget scenario fails.

For every recorded request the kit checks that:

  • each instruction part is in the system text exactly once, and the prompt is in the user turn exactly once;
  • the output schema's descriptions and each tool's description arrive unchanged;
  • the program returns the scripted value, and a tool's result reaches the model only when approval allows the call;
  • a request the budget refuses never reaches the endpoint: the second request of the tool call fails with RunBudgetExceeded, and a failed first request is not retried behind the budget's back;
  • text Kedi did not write is the same in both variants. A fixed harness prompt passes and the report lists it; text that depends on the request, such as "Fill these fields: …", fails.

--json prints the report as JSON. The command exits 1 when a check fails. For a JSON-RPC bridge, kedi adapter check --bridge COMMAND also runs the protocol's conformance fixtures; see JSON-RPC Bridges. PydanticAdapter, LangChainAdapter and WebGPUAdapter have for_conformance; the Claude and Codex harness adapters reach their models through their CLIs, so this endpoint cannot record them:

kedi adapter check kedi.agent_adapter:PydanticAdapter

From Python, check_adapter takes the factory directly. The backend below gives the Reference Adapter an OpenAI-compatible transport, and the reference adapter passes:

http_backend.py
from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import json
import urllib.request
from typing import Any

from backend import BackendRequest, Reply, ToolCall


class HttpBackend:
    """The scripted backend's contract over an OpenAI-compatible endpoint."""

    def __init__(self, base_url: str) -> None:
        self.url = f"{base_url}/v1/chat/completions"

    async def complete(self, request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
        messages: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
        if request.instructions:
            messages.append({"role": "system", "content": request.instructions})
        for message in request.messages:
            if "tool_calls" in message:
                calls = [
                    {
                        "id": call["id"],
                        "type": "function",
                        "function": {"name": call["name"], "arguments": json.dumps(call["arguments"])},
                    }
                    for call in message["tool_calls"]
                ]
                messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": None, "tool_calls": calls})
            else:
                messages.append(message)
        body: dict[str, Any] = {"model": request.model, "messages": messages}
        if request.tools:
            body["tools"] = [{"type": "function", "function": tool} for tool in request.tools]
        if request.output_schema is not None:
            body["response_format"] = {
                "type": "json_schema",
                "json_schema": {"name": "output", "schema": request.output_schema},
            }
        response = await asyncio.to_thread(self._post, body)
        message = response["choices"][0]["message"]
        calls = tuple(
            ToolCall(call["id"], call["function"]["name"], json.loads(call["function"]["arguments"]))
            for call in message.get("tool_calls") or ()
        )
        if calls or request.output_schema is None:
            return Reply(text=message.get("content"), tool_calls=calls)
        return Reply(data=json.loads(message["content"]))

    def _post(self, body: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
        post = urllib.request.Request(
            self.url, data=json.dumps(body).encode(), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}
        )
        with urllib.request.urlopen(post, timeout=30) as response:
            return json.load(response)
run_conformance.py
from kedi.agent_adapter.conformance import check_adapter

from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter
from http_backend import HttpBackend
from multimodal_adapter import MultimodalAdapter

for adapter in (ChatAdapter, MultimodalAdapter):
    report = check_adapter(lambda base_url: adapter(HttpBackend(base_url), model="m1"))
    assert report.passed, report.render()
    statuses = {result.name: result.status for result in report.results}
    assert statuses["media"] == ("passed" if adapter is MultimodalAdapter else "skipped")

items.title: Running the Section's Examples
items.text: The scenarios on these pages are executable. tests/test_adapter_development_examples.py in the documentation repository assembles every python title="..." block into its module and runs each run_*.py scenario in a fresh interpreter. Copying the modules into your test suite is a working starting point.

items.title: Tools
items.text: Kedi decides which tools a call may use and wraps each one with its safety and bookkeeping. The adapter declares those tools to the backend, executes the calls the model makes, and returns the results to the model. It implements two methods.

items.title: The Protocol
items.text:
kedi.agent_adapter.SupportsToolRegistration:

from collections.abc import Sequence
from contextlib import AbstractContextManager
from kedi.agent_adapter import ToolSpec

def tool_scope(self, tools: Sequence[object] = ()) -> AbstractContextManager[None]: ...

def register_tool(self, tool: ToolSpec) -> None: ...

Advertise supports_tool_registration=True. Without the protocol, a profile with tools fails before the call with AgentToolOverrideUnsupported: Active adapter does not support tool registration (requested tools=...).

items.title: Scopes
items.text:
For every model call, Kedi enters tool_scope() and then calls register_tool once per tool (see Call Lifecycle). For a child run the adapter enters tool_scope(request.tools) itself (see Subagents). A scope must:

  • start from exactly the given tools, not from the enclosing scope's: an empty tool_scope() means no tools until Kedi registers them;
  • replace a tool registered again under the same name;
  • restore the enclosing scope on exit, also on error;
  • be isolated per task and thread: parallel blocks, background children, and nested calls each have their own scope.

A ContextVar holding a tuple gives all four, as in the reference adapter. Kedi's own adapters use kedi.agent_adapter.tools.scope.ToolScope, which implements the same rules and can be used directly:

from kedi.agent_adapter.tools.scope import ToolScope

self._scope = ToolScope()

def tool_scope(self, tools=()):
    return self._scope.tool_scope(tools)

def register_tool(self, tool):
    self._scope.register_tool(tool)

# the active tools: self._scope.scoped_tools

items.title: What a ToolSpec Carries
items.text:
Field Use in the adapter name the tool name the model sees and calls description the tool description, sent unchanged json_schema the JSON Schema of the arguments; None means an object without properties return_schema the JSON Schema of the result, for backends that accept output schemas on tools fn the callable to execute, already wrapped by Kedi; keyword arguments only sequential True: never run this call concurrently with another call of the same turn metadata source (kedi, mcp, external, ...) and kind (subagent, artifact_management, filesystem, ...) for routing and telemetry; required_before_output risk, risk_resolver, approval, capability_policy inputs to Kedi's approval; the adapter needs them only with native approvals (see Approvals) argument_validator used through validate_tool_arguments, below artifact_result, result_admitter, retry_policy, proc, deferred_capability Kedi-internal; applied inside fn

Declare to the backend exactly name, description, and json_schema; do not rename tools, merge descriptions, or simplify schemas. For a Kedi procedure, Kedi builds the description from the procedure's ### docstring and its return type (Double a number. Returns `int` instance.), and the schema from its typed parameters.

items.title: Executing a Call
items.text:
arguments = validate_tool_arguments(tool, call.arguments)
result = tool.fn(**arguments)
if inspect.isawaitable(result):
    result = await result
  1. Validate. kedi.agent_adapter.tools.execution.validate_tool_arguments applies the tool's argument_validator: it binds the arguments to the tool's signature, fills defaults, and checks each value against its declared type, building ~Type instances from objects. Types are checked strictly: "4" is not accepted for an int. A rejected argument raises ToolArgumentError, a ValueError, which follows the correctable path below, so the model reads which parameter was wrong and can call the tool again.
  2. Call fn with keyword arguments. Kedi has wrapped it, so the call:
  3. asks the approval policy and may edit the arguments or raise ToolApprovalDenied (adapters without native approvals);
  4. marks a required_before_output tool as attempted and returned;
  5. runs the tool's own retries (> tool: retries:); never retry a tool call in the adapter;
  6. admits a large result as an artifact and returns its reference instead (see Artifacts);
  7. records the tool span and the run's tool history.
  8. Await an awaitable result. Delegation, lifecycle, workflow, and many procedure tools are coroutines.
  9. Return the result to the model as the backend's tool-result message, serialized with pydantic_core.to_jsonable_python(result, fallback=str). Keep the tool-call id paired with its result.
  10. On failure, follow Errors, Retries, and Cancellation: denials and correctable errors go back to the model, everything else propagates.

When the backend returns several tool calls in one turn, they may run concurrently, except calls to sequential tools, which must run alone.

items.title: Tools That Must Run Before the Answer
items.text:
A tool with metadata["required_before_output"] is True must return successfully before the model's final answer is accepted. Kedi checks it after the adapter returns and rejects the result with RequiredToolCallError: Required tool <name> was not called; the adapter response cannot be accepted. Kedi's dynamic workflow tool, run_workflow, is such a tool.

To give the model a chance to recover instead, check the state before accepting a final answer:

from kedi.agent_adapter.tools.scope import current_required_tool_calls

state = current_required_tool_calls()
missing = set() if state is None else state.names - state.returned

When missing is not empty, keep the turn going and ask the model to call the tools.

items.title: Deferred and Capability Tools
items.text: A > capability: with defer: true registers tools whose deferred_capability names a capability the model has not loaded yet. Only adapters that advertise supports_deferred_tools receive them; Kedi refuses the program for every other adapter. See MCP, Skills, and Capability Tools.

items.title: Running It
items.text:
run_tools.py
import asyncio
import json

from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program

from backend import BackendRequest, Reply, ToolCall
from chat_adapter import ChatAdapter

SOURCE = """
@double(n: int) -> int:
  ###
  Double a number.
  ###
  > tool:
    risk: read_only
  = `n * 2`

> use: double
[answer] << Double four.
= <answer>
"""


class Script:
    def __init__(self, arguments: dict) -> None:
        self.arguments = arguments
        self.requests: list[BackendRequest] = []

    async def complete(self, request: BackendRequest) -> Reply:
        self.requests.append(request)
        results = [json.loads(m["content"]) for m in request.messages if m["role"] == "tool"]
        if not results:
            return Reply(tool_calls=(ToolCall("c1", "double", self.arguments),))
        return Reply(text=json.dumps(results[0]))


def run(arguments: dict) -> tuple[dict, BackendRequest]:
    backend = Script(arguments)
    runtime = compile_program(parse_program(SOURCE), adapter=ChatAdapter(backend, model="m1"))
    try:
        return json.loads(runtime.run_main()), backend.requests[0]
    finally:
        asyncio.run(runtime.aclose())


result, first = run({"n": 4})
assert result == {"ok": True, "result": 8}
[declaration] = [tool for tool in first.tools if tool["name"] == "double"]
assert declaration["description"] == "Double a number. Returns `int` instance."
assert declaration["parameters"]["properties"]["n"]["type"] == "integer"
assert declaration["parameters"]["required"] == ["n"]

result, _first = run({"n": "four"})
assert result["ok"] is False
assert result["error"].startswith("Tool double failed: ToolArgumentError"), result

A valid call ran the procedure. An argument of the wrong type did not end the run: the model received Kedi's correction and could call the tool again.

items.title: Models and Integrations
items.text: Adapters translate Kedi's uniform prompt contract into a model framework or an agent harness. Selection is explicit because those backends have materially different capabilities.

items.title: Agent Framework Adapters
items.text:
Use > adapter: or Python adapter=:

Shortname Backend pydantic Pydantic AI langchain LangChain agents

Framework adapters accept Kedi-defined tools and structured output directly.

items.title: Agent Harness Adapters
items.text:
Use > agent: or Python agent=:

Shortname Backend claude Claude Agent SDK codex Codex App Server acp Generic stdio ACP agent a2a Remote Agent2Agent agent

Harnesses are full agent processes with their own tools, sessions, sandboxing, and permission models. Kedi maps what each protocol actually supports.

items.title: Shared Adapter Contract
items.text:
Every adapter provides async and sync paths for:

  • produce(...): a template plus structured output schema;
  • invoke(...): a raw prompt returning text.

It also declares kind, shortname, and AdapterCapabilities. Optional protocols add profile overrides, tool registration, approvals, subagents, compact artifacts, and stateful conversation handoff.

items.title: Capability Negotiation
items.text:
The capability matrix is generated from the built-in adapters' declared metadata and is the canonical support table. Kedi checks required capabilities rather than silently emulating a missing surface. For example, >> ... [field] requires structured output; a text-only adapter must use raw capture instead:

[answer] << Answer the question in plain text.

Transport modes, provider restrictions, native harness tools, and lifecycle details are adapter-specific and remain documented on each adapter page.

items.title: Choose a Backend
items.text:
• Choose Pydantic for the broadest typed Python integration.
  • Choose LangChain for LangChain models, middleware, and tool ecosystems.
  • Choose Claude or Codex when a coding-agent harness and its native tools are part of the task.
  • Choose ACP when driving an existing stdio ACP agent as a text harness.
  • Choose A2A when orchestration stays local but an independently deployed agent owns execution, tools, and sandboxing.

items.title: A2A Cloud Agents
items.text:
Kedi can serve an exported agent profile as a remote A2A agent and can use any compatible A2A agent as an agent-harness. The coordinator may stay local while repository work, browser automation, or other expensive execution runs in a remote sandbox.

Install the optional protocol and server dependencies:

uv add 'kedi[a2a]'

For persistent task and session state, install kedi[a2a-persistence] instead.

Kedi uses the official a2a-sdk Python package. A2A is a transport boundary, not a model provider: the serving process owns its model, tools, sandbox, and approval policy.

items.title: Serve a Kedi Profile
items.text:
Only an explicitly exported profile can become the server entry:

> profile: researcher:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > model: openai:gpt-6-luna
    > instructions:
        Inspect the available evidence before answering.
        State uncertainty instead of inventing missing facts.

> export:
    researcher

The entry must resolve to a local framework or harness capable of executing a Kedi child profile. It cannot use a2a as its own primary backend. A model must be selected by the profile, --model, or KEDI_A2A_MODEL; startup fails before binding a socket when the executable configuration is incomplete.

Serve it with authentication:

export RESEARCH_AGENT_TOKEN='replace-with-a-secret'

kedi a2a serve research-agent.kedi \
  --entry researcher \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8000 \
  --public-url https://agents.example.com \
  --auth bearer \
  --secret-env RESEARCH_AGENT_TOKEN

--public-url is required when binding beyond loopback. Terminate TLS at the service or a trusted reverse proxy, and ensure the public URL reaches the same process. The default JSON-RPC route is /a2a; the protected Agent Card is published through the official SDK routes.

Supported server authentication modes are Basic, Bearer, and header API key:

kedi a2a serve research-agent.kedi \
  --entry researcher \
  --auth api-key \
  --api-key-header X-Research-Key \
  --secret-file /run/secrets/research-agent

Credentials may come from --secret-env, --secret-file, or KEDI_A2A_SECRET. An interactive terminal may prompt for the secret. Literal secrets should not be placed in source, shell history, or process arguments. Use --allow-unauthenticated only for an explicitly loopback-bound development server.

items.title: Persist Tasks and Sessions
items.text:
Persistence is opt-in. Give one server process a dedicated local directory on a persistent volume:

uv add 'kedi[a2a-persistence]'

kedi a2a serve research-agent.kedi \
  --entry researcher \
  --auth bearer \
  --secret-env RESEARCH_AGENT_TOKEN \
  --state-dir /var/lib/kedi/research-agent

KEDI_A2A_STATE_DIR is the environment equivalent of --state-dir. The directory must be private to the serving user; Kedi will create it with restricted permissions when it does not exist. A process lock prevents a second server from opening the same directory. The directory is bound to the served program, its Kedi imports, entry, adapter, model, and history configuration. Changing these requires a new state directory; Kedi will not silently discard or reinterpret existing state.

Completed A2A tasks, owner-scoped results, conversation checkpoints, and referenced artifact payloads survive a process restart. Pydantic AI and LangChain profiles with history enabled restore their native message history, not a reconstructed text transcript. Other adapters can persist stateless task results, but history-enabled serving with an unsupported adapter fails at startup. Without --state-dir, the existing in-memory behavior remains.

Artifact-producing tools and read_artifact/query_artifact use the same session-owned store. Tools are rebound to that store after restoration. They do not share the compiled program's artifact storage with other remote sessions.

A task that was submitted or working when the server stopped becomes failed with server_interrupted metadata on the next startup. It is not replayed automatically: a model call or tool may already have had external effects. A previously canceled task remains canceled. The last committed session turn is the recovery point; uncommitted turns are not added to history. Use GetTask to inspect the old task, then start a new attempt deliberately.

Terminal task records cannot be overwritten by late completion, failure, or cancellation events. Task completion and the session checkpoint are committed in one database transaction. Cancellation and shutdown wait for in-flight storage work before releasing session resources or the directory lock; this does not make external tool effects transactional.

Failed checkpoint writes also restore the SDK's in-memory task view. A transient storage error can then be recorded as failed instead of leaving the client polling a stale working task. If storage remains unwritable, Kedi cannot promise a durable failure update: the operation errors, and the last committed task is reconciled as interrupted after storage recovers and the server restarts. Neither case automatically repeats model calls or external tool effects.

This mode is single-process and requires a local filesystem with OS file locks. It does not preserve provider sockets, runtime globals, tool-created files, remote sandbox filesystems, or effects in external services. Back up the state directory and its artifact files together. Persistent artifact payloads must use Kedi's safe file codecs; an unsupported value cannot be checkpointed as a usable reference. Each session checkpoint is limited to 64 MiB; session, retained-task, and artifact quotas still apply. Released and expired artifact payloads are compacted after a successful commit while their unavailable status is retained. Artifact expiry and idle deadlines survive restart; reopening the server does not extend an artifact's lifetime. Retention evicts only terminal tasks, including tasks marked interrupted during restart, and never running tasks. The state directory has no global byte quota, so place it on a volume with an explicit capacity limit and free-space monitoring. Disk-full or corrupt referenced payloads fail closed rather than reporting a successful task. Basic-auth password rotation retains the username's state, while rotating a Bearer/API key changes the principal and does not transfer old records.

items.title: Connect from Kedi
items.text:
The connection belongs to the selected agent profile, so lexical profile scoping also scopes the endpoint and credential reference:

> profile: cloud_researcher:
    > agent: a2a:
        endpoint: https://agents.example.com
        auth:
            scheme: bearer
            token_env: RESEARCH_AGENT_TOKEN
        request_timeout: 30
        task_timeout: 21600
        poll_interval: 0.5

@research(question: str) -> str:
    > use: cloud_researcher
    [answer] << Investigate <question> and return a concise evidence-based answer.
    = `answer`

Pass the discovery base URL as endpoint, not the JSON-RPC route from the Agent Card. Non-loopback endpoints require HTTPS. Embedded credentials, query strings, and fragments are rejected.

Client authentication fields are:

Scheme Required fields Optional fields basic username, password_env or password_file none bearer token_env or token_file none api_key api_key_env or api_key_file header (default X-API-Key)

The generic aliases credential_env and credential_file are accepted for all three schemes. Exactly one environment, file, or Python provider source is required; combining an alias with a scheme-specific source is rejected. Kedi snapshots the reference, never the resolved credential value.

items.title: Structured Results
items.text:
A generic A2A peer is a text agent, so it supports raw invocation such as [answer] << .... Typed template filling is available only when the Agent Card advertises Kedi's versioned structured-output extension:

> profile: cloud_researcher:
    > agent: a2a:
        endpoint: https://agents.example.com
        auth:
            scheme: api_key
            api_key_env: RESEARCH_AGENT_KEY

@inspect(topic: str) -> tuple[str, list[str]]:
    > use: cloud_researcher
    >> The evidence about <topic> supports [summary: str].
    >> The material risks are [risks: list[str]].
    = `(summary, risks)`

Kedi sends the JSON Schema through the negotiated extension and validates the returned data before assigning any capture. It does not ask a second model to repair a generic text response. See the structured-output v1 contract.

items.title: Remote Subagents
items.text:
An A2A profile can be a child of a local Pydantic AI, LangChain, Codex, or other subagent-capable coordinator:

> profile: cloud_worker:
    > agent: a2a:
        endpoint: https://agents.example.com
        auth:
            scheme: bearer
            token_env: RESEARCH_AGENT_TOKEN

> profile: coordinator:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > model: openai:gpt-6-luna
    > subagent: cloud_worker

@coordinate(question: str) -> str:
    > use: coordinator
    [answer] << Delegate repository inspection when useful, then answer <question>.
    = `answer`

Kedi sends only the task text and, when requested, the final JSON Schema. Local tools, MCP servers, model settings, effort, CodeMode, approval handlers, and replayable model history are not projected into the remote process. Configure those concerns in the served agent.

items.title: Python API
items.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel

from kedi.agent_adapter import A2AAdapter
from kedi.agent_profile import A2AAuthConfig, A2AConnection


class Finding(BaseModel):
    summary: str
    risks: list[str]


connection = A2AConnection(
    endpoint="https://agents.example.com",
    auth=A2AAuthConfig(
        scheme="bearer",
        secret_env="RESEARCH_AGENT_TOKEN",
    ),
    task_timeout=21_600,
)
agent = A2AAdapter(connection=connection)

text = agent.invoke_sync(prompt="Inspect the release candidate.")
finding = agent.produce_sync(
    "The release evidence supports [summary], with risks [risks].",
    output_type=Finding,
)

get_task() reads a known task without resending it, cancel_task() requests cancellation, and continue_task() resumes an input_required or auth_required task. Synchronous variants use the _sync suffix. Lifecycle errors retain known task_id, context_id, and state coordinates.

items.title: Recovery and Timeouts
items.text:
• Stream failure after Kedi learns the task ID falls back to status polling.
  • An ambiguous send with no task ID is never resent automatically; duplication would be less safe than surfacing A2AAmbiguousSendError.
  • task_timeout bounds local observation. It raises A2ATaskTimeoutError but does not cancel remote work. Use the task ID to inspect or cancel it later.
  • Conversation continuation stores only remote task/context coordinates. A2A does not provide full replayable model history to Kedi.

items.title: Security and Deployment Limits
items.text:
• A remote endpoint must use HTTPS; plain HTTP is limited to loopback hosts.
  • Agent Card authentication requirements must match the configured client credential, and advertised JSON-RPC interfaces must remain same-origin.
  • Request body, input, schema, result, pending-task, session, concurrency, and retained-task counts are bounded. Tune the corresponding kedi a2a serve options for the deployment.
  • Tasks and sessions are scoped by authenticated principal. Queued and running calls keep their in-memory sessions alive; only idle sessions can be evicted. Calls sharing a context run sequentially without consuming concurrency slots while waiting for that context. Without --state-dir, restart loses that state. With it, completed state is restored, but live execution is not. Neither mode supports multiple workers sharing one state directory.
  • Shutdown stops SDK tasks and drains active and queued invocations before closing session and runtime resources.
  • A2A is not a sandbox. Run the server with filesystem, process, network, and secret permissions appropriate for the exported profile.
  • OAuth/OIDC, mTLS identity, push notifications, remote file transfer, webhooks, and cross-process task ownership are not implemented by this release.

Use an external gateway for rate limiting and production identity controls. The built-in server provides bounded capacity and credential authentication, not a complete public-edge security product.

items.title: Stdio Agent Commands
items.text:
The generic ACP adapter launches an Agent Client Protocol process and speaks newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdio:

> agent: acp:
    command: npx @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp

Command strings are shell-split without invoking a shell. Python may pass a sequence to avoid quoting ambiguity.

items.title: Explicit Commands
items.text: ACP does not have an implicit command source. Every runnable ACP configuration must bind the command in a typed > agent: acp: body or construct ACPAdapter(command=...) in Python. Plain > agent: acp, CLI command options, and environment command fallbacks are intentionally unsupported.

items.title: Working Directory and Environment
items.text:
> settings:
    cwd: /workspace/project
    env: `{"MODE": "review"}`
    timeout: 300

Clients are reused by (command, cwd, env) and each prompt opens a fresh ACP session. Stdio process cwd and session/new.cwd receive the configured cwd.

items.title: Timeouts
items.text:
timeout is the prompt request timeout and must be a positive number. request_timeout on ACPAdapter governs protocol requests by default. Disconnect errors include the last 40 stderr lines for diagnosis.

When a prompt times out or its async caller is cancelled, Kedi sends session/cancel for that prompt's session and waits for the agent to stop. Other sessions are not cancelled. If the agent does not acknowledge within five seconds, Kedi closes the connection; other calls sharing that unresponsive process then fail as disconnected. Cancellation during session setup does not submit a prompt after the setup finishes.

Closing an adapter first closes its input stream so the agent can stop its own children. On POSIX systems Kedi also cleans up the process group it created, then joins the reader threads. This does not terminate unrelated agent processes.

Only an end_turn response is a completed answer. Token/request exhaustion, refusal, cancellation, and invalid stop reasons raise an error rather than returning partial text as success. Unsupported inbound client requests receive a protocol error; permission requests are denied with the ACP cancelled outcome. Kedi does not silently approve remote tools.

items.title: Model Selection
items.text: Generic ACP model selection is not currently mapped. > model: and > effort: are unsupported capability overrides. Configure the child ACP agent's own default model through its command/environment.

items.title: Prompt and Structured Results
items.text:
ACP supports raw text only:

> agent: acp:
    command: npx @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp
[answer] << Inspect the repository and summarize the risk.
= `answer`

Kedi concatenates agent_message_chunk text updates. Structured >> output raises NotImplementedError; no prompting shim fabricates a schema.

items.title: ACP Capability Mapping
items.text:
Kedi sends protocol initialization, session/new with cwd and an empty mcpServers list, session/prompt, streamed updates, then session/close. Each call is independent.

Unsupported model/effort overrides and local tool or MCP registration are rejected rather than ignored. Remote tools configured inside the child agent are separate from Kedi's local tool registry.

items.title: Current Limits
items.text:
• no structured output;
  • no Kedi tool registration;
  • no Kedi MCP projection;
  • no model or effort override;
  • no Kedi subagents;
  • only text agent_message_chunk updates are collected.

items.title: Claude Agent SDK
items.text:
Install the optional SDK:

uv add "kedi[claude]"

In a source checkout use uv sync --extra claude.

items.title: Authentication
items.text: The Claude Agent SDK owns authentication. Configure the SDK-supported credentials before running Kedi; ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is the common non-interactive path. Authentication and other non-retryable 4xx SDK events fail immediately with actionable context; transient retry events may continue.

items.title: Model and Effort
items.text:
> agent: claude
> effort: high

With no model override, the Claude Agent SDK selects its default Claude model. Effort is normalized through the shared Kedi effort mapping.

Luna is an OpenAI model, not a Claude model. To use Luna, select a compatible backend instead:

> adapter: pydantic
> model: openai/gpt-6-luna
> effort: high

items.title: System Presets
items.text: Claude Code's system prompt preset remains active. > instructions: is appended to that preset rather than replacing it, preserving coding/file-tool behavior.

items.title: Working Directory
items.text:
> settings:
    cwd: `str(project_root)`

Other supported settings are allowed_tools, disallowed_tools, env, fallback_model, max_budget_usd, max_turns, permission_mode, and tools.

items.title: Permission Mode
items.text: Non-interactive runs default to permission_mode: acceptEdits. Override it explicitly when a narrower Claude SDK mode is required. Kedi still installs its approval hook; SDK permission mode and Kedi approval are separate layers.

items.title: Built-In File Tools
items.text:
Claude Code tools are enabled through the SDK preset by default. Kedi-projected tools are exposed through an in-process SDK MCP server and added to allowed_tools. External stdio/SSE/HTTP MCP servers are also mapped.

Native Read, Glob, Grep, WebFetch, and WebSearch are classified read-only. Other native/MCP operations require policy.

items.title: CodeMode
items.text:
> codemode: enabled exposes the three shared CodeMode controls through Kedi's in-process Claude SDK MCP server. Kedi procedures and declared stdio/SSE/HTTP MCP tools are materialized into the run-scoped catalog and are callable only from execute_code. Claude's built-in filesystem, search, web, and shell tools remain native control-plane tools.

The SDK approval hook skips the three controls; the nested application call is the single approval owner. Kedi closes the local MCP clients and Monty session on completion, error, or cancellation.

items.title: Subagent Lifecycle
items.text: Claude supports foreground/background children and native resume using the SDK session ID. Child options preserve model, tools, system, MCP, approval ceiling, and usage constraints.

items.title: Capability Limits
items.text: The SDK must be installed for this adapter. Exact built-in tool availability and model names follow the installed Claude Agent SDK. Kedi validates its own setting keys but does not emulate missing SDK capabilities.

items.title: Codex-Authenticated Models
items.text: Codex Responses provides model access inside a framework adapter. This is different from Codex App Server, which runs an agent harness. Choosing a model route does not switch the surrounding agent framework.

items.title: Codex Responses Connections
items.text:
The factory signature is codex_responses_model(model_id, adapter, *, connection="http", fallback="error", transport_observer=None). adapter must be "pydantic" or "langchain". The identifier may include the codex/ prefix. fallback="http" is valid only with WebSocket. transport_observer receives content-free transport events. The helper reads existing Codex login credentials; KEDI_CODEX_AUTH_FILE selects an explicit auth file. Do not include that file in source, logs, or published examples.

codex_responses_model() builds a Codex-authenticated Pydantic model. HTTP is the default. Install kedi[codex-model] on Python 3.11 or newer for the pinned codex-auth-helper[websocket]==1.13.0. Select WebSocket explicitly; it is not enabled just by installing the extra.

from kedi import codex_responses_model
from kedi.agent_adapter import PydanticAdapter

model = codex_responses_model(
    "gpt-6-luna",
    adapter="pydantic",
    connection="websocket",
    fallback="error",
)
adapter = PydanticAdapter(model)

async def review():
    async with adapter.responses_session():
        first = await adapter.run("The current release is amber. Acknowledge it.")
        second = await adapter.run(
            "Which release is current?",
            message_history=first.all_messages(),
        )
    return second.output

An ordinary adapter run keeps its connection across model/tool turns. The explicit session above also retains it across sequential adapter calls. It owns the connection, not the history: supply native message history as shown or use Kedi's normal stateful-history surface. Concurrent child tasks remain isolated, and exit, errors, and cancellation clean up the connection.

Updated helper builds scope a separate routing turn to every adapter run. HTTP and WebSocket echo the first server-provided x-codex-turn-state within its tool loop, but discard it before the next run, even on a shared connection. Kedi does not put this opaque value in history or transport metrics. Prompt-cache keys and native history remain unchanged; provider cache hits are not guaranteed.

Auth recovery reloads same-account credentials after an explicit 401, then allows one refresh if necessary. Account changes require a new client; permanent auth failures and exhausted 401s do not trigger HTTP fallback. Same-file refresh locking is in-process only. Older helper builds work without the new turn-state feature.

Append-only requests can transmit only their new suffix. History edits or changed request settings reset continuation. If the socket is already known to be closed before the next request, a new connection receives full history. Changing handshake headers also replaces the connection.

With helper 1.8.0, non-streaming model requests recover transient WebSocket send/receive failures by discarding incomplete output and rebuilding full history on a new connection. Completed local tools are not rerun by recovery. The client max_retries controls reconnects (default two), with bounded backoff. fallback="http" permits HTTP after retries are exhausted, as well as initial-handshake fallback. The model can still choose another tool call, and lost provider work may incur unreported cost.

Raw client calls and exposed streams are not replayed; cancellation, permanent auth/permission failures and provider-hosted tools also prevent response replay. Install the pinned helper with uv add 'kedi[codex-model]'. Stream consumers can stop on response.completed without discarding the completed response; stopping before completion abandons it. The closing handshake has a 250 ms timeout, separate from generation and tool execution.

Connection reuse can improve provider cache reads, but does not guarantee a particular hit rate or lower latency. Cached input is part of total input, not an additional token count.

items.title: Codex App Server
items.text:
The Codex adapter starts:

codex app-server --stdio

It communicates directly over App Server JSON-RPC. The default thread is ephemeral, so ordinary Kedi calls do not become persistent Codex threads.

items.title: Authentication
items.text: Install the Codex CLI, ensure codex is on PATH, and authenticate it before running Kedi. The App Server uses the CLI's existing authentication and configuration; Kedi does not accept or persist Codex credentials.

items.title: Model and Reasoning Settings
items.text:
> agent: codex
> model: gpt-6.1-sol
> effort: high

Supported settings are approval_policy, config, cwd, model_provider, personality, sandbox, service_tier, summary, and timeout.

items.title: Working Directory
items.text:
cwd defaults to the Kedi process working directory:

> settings:
    cwd: /workspace/project

The directory governs Codex built-in filesystem and shell behavior.

items.title: Sandbox Policy
items.text: Kedi defaults Codex to workspace-write. Accepted aliases normalize to Codex App Server sandbox values. Use read-only for analysis-only tasks or a broader mode only when the environment and approval policy justify it.

items.title: Approval Policy
items.text:
Kedi leaves the App Server in approval-requesting mode by default and resolves native shell/file approval methods through Kedi policy. A static/dynamic Kedi policy also guards projected dynamic tools.

App Server native approvals cannot apply Kedi's edited arguments. An edit decision for such a native request is declined rather than silently treated as allow.

items.title: Built-In Tools
items.text:
Codex retains its harness-native shell and filesystem tools. Kedi procedures and Python tools become App Server dynamic tools for the active run.
