Kedi MCP declarations are currently unsupported by CodexAdapter and raise; this does not mean the Codex installation itself has no MCP configuration.

items.title: CodeMode
items.text:
> codemode: enabled publishes only search_tools, get_tool_schema, and execute_code as App Server dynamic tools. Kedi procedures and Python tools move behind the run-scoped catalog, while Codex's native filesystem, shell, and search tools remain available as harness controls. CodeMode settings and the catalog participate in thread reuse identity.

Nested calls use Kedi inline approval exactly once. CodeMode does not add MCP support to this adapter; Kedi MCP declarations still fail explicitly.

items.title: Structured Output
items.text:
Kedi passes JSON Schema through turn/start.outputSchema, parses the returned JSON, and validates Pydantic models. Object schemas are closed with additionalProperties: false.

Supported string formats are date, date-time, duration, email, and time. Other JSON Schema string formats fail before the turn; use a plain or Annotated string when semantic guidance is sufficient.

items.title: Subagent Lifecycle
items.text:
Codex supports foreground/background children. Dynamic tools, sandbox, cwd, model, instructions, and approval ceilings are rebuilt per child scope.

Each native turn owns its active Kedi tools and approval callbacks. Turn timeout or cancellation stops async callbacks and waits for their cleanup before the call returns. Repeated cancellation does not interrupt that cleanup a second time, and sibling turns retain their own bindings. Closing an event consumer alone does not cancel the underlying run.

Cancellation does not undo committed effects or forcibly stop arbitrary synchronous Python code. Cleanup that cannot finish within its bounded deadline raises an error instead of claiming the work stopped. An interrupted native turn may end without a final token-usage notification; missing usage is not evidence that no inference occurred.

items.title: Capability Limits
items.text:
• Kedi MCP server declarations are unsupported.
  • Native approval handlers support allow/deny, not argument editing.
  • The codex executable and compatible App Server are required.

items.title: Custom Adapters
items.text:
A custom adapter connects Kedi to a model framework or agent harness that Kedi does not ship. The complete contract, with tested code for every part, is the Adapter Development section. Start with the Reference Adapter: a working adapter that every page of the section extends.

Pass an adapter instance when compiling a program:

from kedi.lang import compile_program, parse_program

runtime = compile_program(parse_program(source), adapter=MyAdapter())

items.title: The Adapter Contract
items.text: An adapter declares kind, shortname, and capabilities, and implements invoke, invoke_sync, produce, and produce_sync. Kedi renders the prompt and instructions; the adapter sends them unchanged and returns text or the decoded value. See Call Lifecycle and Prompts and Instructions.

items.title: Framework and Harness Kinds
items.text: "agent-framework" adapters are selected with adapter= / > adapter:, "agent-harness" adapters with agent= / > agent:. See the overview.

items.title: Shortnames
items.text: shortname names the adapter in diagnostics, telemetry, approvals, and conversation state. Keep it stable.

items.title: Text Invocation
items.text: invoke_sync(prompt=..., instructions=...) returns the response text. See Call Lifecycle.

items.title: Structured Outputs
items.text: produce_sync receives output_schema for template captures and output_type for claims and typed raw invokes, and returns the decoded value. See Structured Output.

items.title: Tool Registration
items.text: tool_scope and register_tool receive the call's tools; executing a call goes through the tool's wrapped fn. See Tools.

items.title: MCP Support
items.text: See MCP, Skills, and Capability Tools.

items.title: Capability Metadata
items.text: See the Capability Reference.

items.title: Parallel Thread Safety
items.text: See Concurrency and Event Loops.

items.title: Error Translation
items.text: See Errors, Retries, and Cancellation.

items.title: Archived DSPy Runtime Adapter
items.text:
The DSPy runtime adapter is no longer built into Kedi. Its implementation and adapter-specific tests are preserved in the unmaintained kedi-lang/dspy-adapter repository.

Use Pydantic AI or LangChain for maintained framework integration. The dspy runtime shortname is no longer accepted by > adapter:, Python adapter=, or the CLI.

items.title: Existing DSPy Applications
items.text:
The external package is installed from GitHub and imported separately:

python -m pip install "git+https://github.com/kedi-lang/dspy-adapter.git"

It exports kedi_dspy_adapter.DSPyAdapter. Pass an adapter object through kedi.context(adapter=...) or compile_program(..., adapter=...) rather than using the removed built-in shortname. See the external repository for its tested Python example, compatibility requirements, and original limitations.

DSPy-only > settings: keys such as model_type, cache, num_retries, and provider are no longer accepted in Kedi source. Shared settings such as temperature and max_tokens remain available on the backends that support them.

items.title: GEPA Is Unchanged
items.text: kedi[dspy] still installs DSPy for GEPA optimization. GEPA's DSPy modules, optimizer LM, and reflection LM remain in Kedi and do not depend on the external runtime adapter. Calls outside an optimized span use the selected runtime --adapter and --adapter-model.

items.title: Jev Claims and Thresholds
items.text: A claim asks for a decision, not generated prose. Its acceptance threshold is application policy, not a proof that the claim is true.

items.title: Claims and Thresholds
items.text:
> adapter: pydantic
> model: typesafe/jev-latest
> settings:
  decision_boolean_threshold: 0.9

> if: Ankara is the capital of Turkey
  = established
> else:
  = not established

Replace pydantic with langchain to use the other adapter. The default decision rule is probability > 0.85; equality is false. Explicit request/profile settings override the model constructor threshold without changing the shared model. Thresholds must be finite numbers in [0, 1], not strings or booleans.

This threshold applies to boolean outputs and individual multi-label memberships. It does not threshold raw probabilities, categorical choices, or rubric scores. A provider probability is not a guarantee of empirical accuracy.

items.title: Migration from 0.1
items.text:
The extended integration defaults to strict > 0.85, rather than the old 0.5 threshold. Set an explicit threshold when migrating an existing decision policy. Do not assume an unwrapped upstream model enforces this policy: Kedi rejects that model for claims when the policy cannot be enforced.

The package pins the upstream integration versions because it extends schema and decision behavior at tested framework boundaries. Upgrade those pins together with the compatibility tests, not independently.

items.title: Jev Criteria and Output Types
items.text:
Describe finite choices, binary evidence, probabilities, and ordered score levels. Import the primitives directly with > import: decisions, or select only the names you need. The types come from the optional kedi-decisions package and also work with Laya. Importing them does not select a model, load weights, or require a provider SDK. Python callers use kedi.decisions; standalone callers without Kedi can import from kedi_decisions.

The shared package is currently available from the decision-model monorepo. It is included in Kedi's source development environment. For other environments, install that checkout with uv pip install -e /path/to/kedi-decisions.

> import: decisions:
  Probability
  Rubric

~Assessment(
  correctness: Probability,
  quality: Annotated[
    float,
    "Assess the answer against the reference",
    `Rubric(["Incorrect", "Partly correct", "Fully correct"])`
  ]
)

Native metadata calls use backticks; arbitrary bare function calls are not added to the type grammar. Python aliases remain an alternative:

items.title: Typed Criteria
items.text:
```
from typing import Annotated
from kedi.decisions import Probability, Rubric

Correctness = Annotated[
    Probability,
    "Does the answer agree with the reference?",
]
Quality = Annotated[
    float,
    "Assess the answer against the reference",
    Rubric(["Incorrect", "Partly correct", "Fully correct"]),
]
```
> adapter: pydantic
> model: typesafe/jev-latest

~Assessment(
  correctness: `Correctness`,
  quality: `Quality`
)
>> The reference is Ankara and the answer is Ankara. The assessment is [assessment: Assessment].
= `assessment`

Probability is a finite float between 0 and 1. A rubric with N ordered levels produces a score between 0 and N-1; float scores retain their fractional part. Integer rubric outputs round to the nearest level, with ties rounded upward. Rubric bounds are automatically included and validated; no separate range is needed.

ChoiceCriteria supplies descriptions for each exact Literal/enum option. BooleanCriteria(true=..., false=...) supplies descriptions for positive and negative evidence. Import them with > import: decisions for Kedi, or from kedi.decisions in Python. They can be used in native backtick metadata or Python Annotated aliases. Importing criteria without the optional package fails with installation advice. Ordinary import kedi and decision-evidence inspection remain available without it. The former provider-specific Kedi type-import modules are removed; provider model IDs, settings, and standalone model package APIs are unchanged.

items.title: Outputs and Limitations
items.text:
• Nested required objects are reconstructed after evaluation.
  • Lists of finite string choices are multi-label decisions, in declaration order.
  • Nullable finite choices include an explicit no-match option.
  • Email, phone, regex, and custom extractors produce finite candidates locally; Jev chooses among them. These are extraction, not arbitrary text generation.
  • Nullable extraction without candidates returns None without a provider request.
  • General unconstrained strings, free-form invokes, arbitrary numeric extraction, multimodal input, recursive schemas, and arbitrary arrays are unsupported.
  • Independent fields share one request. Dependent decisions need separate calls.
  • Unsupported schemas and malformed provider output raise errors; they are not silently converted to false, repaired, or sent to another model.

items.title: Jev Decision Evidence
items.text: Inspect the evaluation that produced a binding without changing the binding's native type or making another provider call. For a field-by-field API reference, see Decision Evidence.

items.title: Decision Evidence in Kedi
items.text:
Jev-backed output bindings retain their decision evidence without changing the normal output type:

```
from kedi import decision_info
```
> adapter: pydantic
> model: typesafe/jev-latest

[ticket] = I was charged twice for the same invoice.
>> It is [duplicate_charge: bool] that <ticket> describes a duplicate charge.

`print(decision_info("duplicate_charge").probability)`
`print(decision_info("duplicate_charge").threshold)`

[ticket] := I was charged only once.
`print(decision_info("duplicate_charge").matches_inputs(ticket=ticket))`

The helper resolves the nearest lexical binding. For an interactive session, session.decision_info("duplicate_charge") inspects a top-level binding without executing another fragment. Unknown names raise NameError; values without Jev evidence return None.

Evidence includes the provider/model, source location, Noul probability, the threshold used for boolean conversion, and Choice/Score confidence and distributions when the provider supplied them. Noul does not gain an invented confidence value. Multiple fields produced by one template share one call record while retaining field-specific evidence. For a nested or multilabel output, answers contains each matching child path separately; Kedi never merges several Noul answers into one probability.

state_fingerprint, criteria_fingerprint, config_fingerprint, and request_fingerprint identify the evaluated provider state, resolved criteria, decision configuration, and their combined request. These are one-way identities, not recoverable prompt copies.

matches_inputs(**values) performs a local fingerprint comparison over the explicit <name> inputs. It makes no model or tool call and does not claim that history or external state is unchanged. Reassigning an input leaves the historical record intact, so this check can report False. Reassigning the output removes the record from that current binding. Kedi does not automatically re-evaluate a decision or apply a new threshold.

Decision records participate in strict interactive-session dump/load. They contain versioned fingerprints, not recoverable copies of the original input text. A fingerprint is an identity check, not anonymization; do not publish snapshots that may contain sensitive provider evidence.

items.title: Capture Decisions from Python Calls
items.text:
kedi.capture_decisions() collects the completed template decisions produced by @kedi.query and @kedi.bind calls without changing their return types:

import kedi

@kedi.query(adapter="pydantic", model="typesafe/jev-latest")
def review(ticket: str) -> bool:
    """kedi
    >> It is [duplicate: bool] that <ticket> describes a duplicate charge.
    = `duplicate`
    """

with kedi.capture_decisions() as run:
    duplicate = review("I was charged twice for the same invoice.")

for decision in run.decisions:
    print(decision.field_path, decision.probability, decision.threshold)

decisions is a tuple of immutable DecisionInfo views, one per output binding, in call completion order. Multiple fields share their call_id. These historical snapshots remain accessible after the function returns. Nested capture scopes also contribute to their enclosing scope; separate concurrent scopes are isolated. Use regular with around await calls and await desired work before exiting. Exit does not wait for pending work; the capture stops accepting records.

Capturing makes no additional model calls. Response-cache hits, failed calls, and outputs without provider evidence do not create decision records. Successfully completed decisions remain available if a later call raises. This captures typed template outputs, not implicit control-flow claims or arbitrary SDK calls.

items.title: Finite Extraction with Jev
items.text:
Extraction enumerates candidate text locally and asks Jev to select among those candidates. It is not unconstrained string generation and cannot produce a missing address or identifier by inference.

```
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import EmailStr

CurrentEmail = Annotated[
    EmailStr | None,
    "The current support email, not the retired address",
]
```

> adapter: pydantic
> model: typesafe/jev-latest

[notice] = Old support: archive@example.org. Current support: help@example.org.
>> From <notice>, the current contact is [email: `CurrentEmail`].
= `email`

This live example requires the TypeSafe extra and email validation dependencies. Native EmailStr, supported phone-number schemas, regex patterns, and explicitly configured extractors can supply finite candidates. Nullable extraction with no candidates can return None without a provider request. Required extraction with no suitable candidates cannot invent a valid answer.

items.title: Custom Identifiers
items.text:
For a custom candidate policy, configure the model in Python with text_extractors={"ticket_id": RegexExtractor(pattern=r"CASE-\d+")} from kedi_typesafe, then pass that model to the framework adapter. The dictionary key selects the output field path expected by the integration. A regex finds candidates; the field description guides Jev's choice. Test the candidate recall separately from the selection decision.

Kedi validates the selected typed result. It does not interpret a probability as a guarantee that an extractor found every relevant candidate.

items.title: Jev Tool Selection
items.text: Tool selection is a finite decision. Argument generation and execution remain separate operations with their own validation and approval boundaries.

items.title: Explicit Tool Routing
items.text:
Both framework integrations support opt-in selection of registered tools. Jev may select a zero-argument tool for framework execution. A tool requiring arguments produces a ToolCallProposed exception for an explicit argument-producing handler; it does not invent arguments or silently delegate to an LLM.

Tool selection has its own decision_tool_call_threshold (default 0.6, inclusive). It is not the claim threshold. Selection is not authorization: retain Kedi hooks, approval policy, and framework execution limits. Review or fallback behavior must be explicitly written by the application.

items.title: Generate, Evaluate, Route
items.text:
A generative model writes a draft; Jev evaluates it against explicit evidence; Kedi selects the next operation. Neither the draft nor a high probability is permission to send a message or perform a financial action.

This example requires kedi[typesafe] and credentials for both providers. It prints a review result; it does not send email. Model availability is a provider prerequisite, not a compiler guarantee.

> adapter: pydantic

@draft_reply(ticket: str, policy: str) -> str:
  > model: openai:gpt-6-luna
  >> Customer request: <ticket>.
  Policy: <policy>.
  A brief reply that does not invent completed actions is [reply].
  = `reply`

@check_reply(reply: str, policy: str) -> bool:
  > model: typesafe/jev-latest
  > settings:
    decision_boolean_threshold: 0.9
  >> Given policy <policy>, does reply <reply> avoid unsupported commitments?
  It is [supported: bool] that the reply is supported by the policy.
  = `supported`

[ticket] = Please refund my duplicate payment today.
[policy] = A reviewer must verify duplicate charges before approving refunds.
[reply] = `draft_reply(ticket, policy)`
[supported: bool] = `check_reply(reply, policy)`

> if: `supported`:
  = Draft for human review: <reply>
> else:
  = Manual review required; do not send the draft.

items.title: Boundaries
items.text:
The first procedure can generate arbitrary prose. The second produces a boolean using Jev's strict threshold policy, not a generative text fallback. Unsupported schemas and provider failures remain errors rather than becoming a negative decision. The final branch is deterministic because it reads an existing bool.

The program deliberately does not retry until acceptance. A revision loop needs an explicit attempt budget, fresh evaluation of each revision, and a terminal manual-review outcome. Such a policy belongs to the application, not to hidden adapter behavior.

Use decision capture around an embedding call to retain the check_reply output's evidence after its procedure frame ends. The caller's deterministic supported initialization is not itself a new Jev evaluation record.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
Install the optional LangChain integrations:

uv add 'kedi[langchain]'

Other providers may require their own LangChain integration package.

items.title: Chat Models
items.text:
> adapter: langchain
> model: openai:gpt-6-luna

String models are passed through langchain.chat_models.init_chat_model. An existing chat model object may be supplied directly to LangChainAdapter. A missing model fails when the adapter first runs.

items.title: Model Fallback and Request Retries
items.text:
Use ordered fallback models through > fallback: or the adapter constructor:

from kedi.agent_adapter import LangChainAdapter

adapter = LangChainAdapter(
    "openai:gpt-6-luna",
    fallback_models=["openai:gpt-6.1-sol"],
    request_retries=2,
)

fallback_models accepts an ordered sequence of strings or native chat models. A scoped AgentProfile.fallback_models list of IDs replaces this default; () clears it and None inherits. Selection is invocation-local, not a mutation of the original chat model or its clients.

Each candidate gets the bounded request retry policy for HTTP 408, 429, and 5xx errors before advancing. An active settings.request_retries overrides the constructor default; 0 disables same-model retries, not explicit fallback. Output/tool validation, tool-body failures, authentication, refusals, and control signals do not trigger fallback. Every attempt reenters admission and accounting, using the same usage limits and deadline without replaying completed tools or approvals. Only stream-opening failures before exposed content can recover.

SDK retries may compound with Kedi retries. Use ChatOpenAI(max_retries=0) or the provider's equivalent when Kedi should own attempts. Strict request budgets reject enabled or uninspectable SDK retries rather than undercounting. Portable history is retained across models, while stale response IDs and incompatible server state are not reused; history-processor continuation resets remain active.

items.title: Model Settings
items.text:
The full list of supported > settings: keys comes from Kedi's agent_profile.settings:

Setting Meaning api_key Provider API key used when constructing the chat model. base_url Base URL for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. callbacks LangChain callbacks attached to model calls. configurable_fields Fields exposed as LangChain configurable fields. configurable_prefix Prefix applied to configurable field names. context_limit Model context window in tokens for Kedi's request ceiling; default 200,000. decision_boolean_threshold Probability above which a boolean decision counts as true. decision_tool_call_threshold Probability above which a hand-off tool is selected. disable_streaming Disable streaming globally or during tool calls. extra_body Extra fields merged into the provider request body. extra_headers Extra HTTP headers sent with provider requests. frequency_penalty Penalty scaled by how often a token already appeared. logit_bias Per-token logit adjustments. max_retries Maximum retries for failed model calls. max_tokens Maximum tokens in the model response. media_limit Largest media value, in bytes, a request may attach; default 20 MB cap. metadata Metadata attached to model calls. model_kwargs Extra keyword arguments passed to the chat model. organization Provider organization identifier. parallel_tool_calls Whether the model may call several tools in one turn. presence_penalty Penalty for repeating tokens already present. rate_limiter Rate limiter applied to model calls. reasoning Reasoning configuration mapping (for example {"effort": "high"}). reasoning_effort Reasoning effort level for models without a reasoning mapping. request_retries Retries for transient provider request failures; does not replay tools or entire runs. response_cache Enable provider response caching for identical requests. response_cache_ttl Cache time-to-live in seconds for cached responses. seed Seed for deterministic sampling where the provider supports it. stop Stop strings for the chat model. stop_sequences Sequences that stop generation. stream_usage Include token usage in streamed responses. streaming Enable streaming responses. tags Tags attached to model calls. temperature Sampling temperature; higher values are more random. timeout Request timeout in seconds. tool_choice Tool selection policy (none, auto, required). tool_reason Opts into an optional reason string on tool calls. top_p Nucleus sampling cutoff. voice Voice of [x: Audio] << speech: OpenAI's audio voice or the chat model's voice field; LangChain's Gemini models take none.

For openrouter: model names, or models with an existing reasoning mapping, effort is written to reasoning={"effort": ...} while retaining the other reasoning options. Other models receive reasoning_effort.

The Python constructor's model_settings accepts native options without the DSL settings filter. An existing model is copied for each run: request fields such as reasoning are applied, and its model_kwargs are merged with constructor kwargs, constructor model_settings, then active profile settings. Original objects are not mutated. Explicit cache keys override generated history keys.

Configure endpoint, credentials, timeout and retries when constructing a native model. Changing those fields on an already initialized model would leave its existing clients unchanged, so Kedi rejects that combination. String models can receive those construction settings through the adapter.

items.title: Codex Responses Sessions
items.text:
from kedi import codex_responses_model
from kedi.agent_adapter import LangChainAdapter
from kedi.agent_adapter.conversation import ConversationState

model = codex_responses_model(
    "gpt-6-luna", adapter="langchain", connection="websocket",
)
adapter = LangChainAdapter(model, model_settings={"reasoning": {"effort": "high"}})
conversation = ConversationState(session_id="release-review")
try:
    async with adapter.responses_session():
        for prompt in ("Review release amber.", "Recheck the selected release."):
            async with conversation.adapter_turn_async("langchain") as context:
                with adapter.conversation_scope(context):
                    answer = await adapter.invoke(prompt=prompt, instructions="Review the evidence.")
                context.record_exchange(prompt, answer)
finally:
    conversation.close()

Install kedi[codex-model,langchain] on Python 3.11 or newer. This selects codex-auth-helper[websocket]==1.13.0. Authentication uses the existing Codex login. See Codex Models for factory parameters and the distinction from the Codex App Server harness.

HTTP remains the default. Kedi owns one transport session for the complete agent run, including tool turns. An explicit responses_session() shares the connection across sequential calls, but does not manage message history itself. Child Kedi runs use isolated sessions. Exceptions, cancellation and early stream close release resources. Changes to history, instructions, schemas, tools or settings invalidate response-ID continuation and send full input.

Updated helpers give each adapter run its own routing turn, matching Pydantic. HTTP and WebSocket echo server-provided x-codex-turn-state within the run's tool loop and clear it for the next run, without closing a shared connection. It is not stored in history or metrics and does not guarantee a provider cache hit. Older helpers remain compatible without this feature.

Explicit HTTP and handshake 401s have bounded same-account reload/refresh recovery. Account changes require a new client, and permanent auth failures or exhausted 401s do not trigger HTTP fallback. Same-file refresh locking is in-process; accepted requests and uncertain sends are not replayed by auth recovery.

The helper maps active system messages to Codex instructions and retains the factory instruction when no active system message exists. Native LangChain tool, structured-output and stream-event conversion remain in use. HTTP invocation also consumes streaming responses internally.

Do not set use_previous_response_id or supply response IDs manually. WebSocket requires async native model calls or Kedi's sync wrappers; HTTP response-header capture is unavailable in this mode. With helper 1.8.0, ordinary ainvoke buffers each model response and retries transient WebSocket failures with full history. Completed local tools are not rerun by recovery. The client max_retries controls reconnects (default two), with bounded backoff; fallback="http" permits HTTP after retries are exhausted or the initial handshake fails. Lost provider work can still incur unreported cost.

The WebSocket factory uses automatic streaming selection. astream, explicit streaming=True, or streaming callbacks use the exposed-stream path, which does not replay partial output. Cancellation, permanent auth/permission failures and provider-hosted tools also prevent response replay. HTTP defaults are unchanged. The model can independently request a tool again; recovery is not an exactly-once tool guarantee. Install the pinned helper with uv add 'kedi[codex-model]'. transport_observer= receives content-free transport metrics, including receive failures and retry/fallback events.

Connection reuse supports cache reuse, but does not guarantee cache hits or a fixed hit percentage. Measure actual provider usage.

items.title: Structured Outputs
items.text:
Kedi builds a Pydantic output model and calls create_agent with a response format. It reads LangChain's structured_response field and fails if the agent does not provide one.

Subagent JSON Schema uses LangChain ToolStrategy, preserving the child schema rather than inventing a Kedi output format.

items.title: Tool Binding
items.text:
LangChain supports eager capability bundles through its tool and middleware surfaces. > use: registers their tools, guidance, and owned policies without a loading call. Deferred capabilities are rejected before inference; supports_deferred_tools remains false.

Kedi tools become StructuredTool instances with JSON argument schemas. Sync and async functions retain the correct invocation path. Kedi's approval middleware guards projected tools and preserves tool metadata.

items.title: MCP Tools
items.text:
MultiServerMCPClient maps:

  • Kedi stdio to LangChain stdio;
  • Kedi SSE to sse;
  • Kedi HTTP to streamable_http.

MCP tools are added to each agent run. External MCP tools are treated as mutating by default and upgraded to sensitive when arguments target dotenv secret files.

items.title: Native Tool Artifacts
items.text:
When artifacts are enabled, LangChain-native and MCP tool results cross Kedi's artifact-admission middleware before their ToolMessage is committed to history. Large successful content is replaced by the same compact ArtifactRef representation used by Kedi-defined tools.

The original tool_call_id and message metadata remain attached to the result. Error ToolMessage values remain native errors, approval and hook ordering are unchanged, and tools already wrapped by Kedi are not admitted twice. Request-time cache markers are projected only for the provider call and are not persisted in canonical conversation history.

items.title: CodeMode
items.text:
> codemode: enabled replaces LangChain's model-facing application tools with search_tools, get_tool_schema, and execute_code. Scoped Kedi tools and MultiServerMCPClient tools enter one run-scoped catalog. Nested calls retain Kedi argument validation and inline approval; the direct-call approval middleware does not approve the three controls a second time.

LangChain receives Monty and boundary failures as failed tool results, allowing the model to correct a snippet without terminating the complete agent run. See CodeMode for the shared contract.

items.title: Subagent Lifecycle
items.text: LangChain supports foreground/background child runs. Request, tool-call and token limits apply to the native child loop. Graph recursion is an additional guard, not a substitute for a request limit. Usage is collected per model response, independently of messages retained in history, and reported to Kedi's budget observer.

items.title: Run Limits and Tool Corrections
items.text:
LangChainAdapter(default_usage_limits=UsageLimits(...)) uses the same limit object as PydanticAdapter. A call's usage_limits overrides that default; explicit None uses normal run defaults. Import UsageLimits from pydantic_ai.

Request and successful tool-call limits are checked before dispatch, including reservations for parallel tools. Input, output, total and per-request input token limits use provider-reported usage. These input limits include cached tokens; Kedi's separate model-request budget uses uncached input. Provider-exact preflight token counting and USD cost_limit are unsupported here and fail before sending a model request rather than silently going unenforced.

Use config={...} for native LangGraph configuration. A recursion_limit keyword is also forwarded into config; neither is inserted into the model's message state. Caller callbacks are preserved when Kedi streaming callbacks are added.

Filesystem, terminal, dynamic-workflow, subagent and artifact errors use the same Kedi correction messages as Pydantic AI. The model may correct a failed tool call up to tool_retries=3 times per tool per run by default. The adapter does not automatically execute the same command again. Unclassified application exceptions and cancellation still propagate.

Structured output that fails parsing or validation, including a subagent result's JSON Schema, gets a correction turn like Pydantic AI's output retry: the failed response and its validation feedback go back to the model, output_retries=1 times by default. Each correction is a counted model request. A truncated response is reported as incomplete rather than corrected. When the rejected response also called business tools, those calls run first and the correction follows with their results, as on Pydantic AI. An empty list tool result is sent as the text [], because an empty content-parts array is rejected by some gateways; the program and hooks still see the native value.

items.title: Exact History Archives
items.text:
Both framework adapters accept the same opt-in policy:

from kedi.agent_adapter import LangChainAdapter
from kedi.agent_adapter.compaction import HistoryArchiveSettings

adapter = LangChainAdapter(
    history_archive=HistoryArchiveSettings(
        threshold_tokens=32_000,
        preserve_recent_tokens=12_000,
        minimum_reduction_tokens=8_000,
    ),
)

Supply the model normally and enable Kedi artifacts for the run. Without an active artifact manager and enabled policy, archival does nothing.

Old completed tool exchanges are stored losslessly as native message records and replaced by a checkpoint containing an artifact reference and tool-outcome counts. This is not LLM summarization and does not introduce a DSL compaction mode. The original user request, protected messages, unresolved tool-call pairs, earlier checkpoints and recent tail remain intact. Provider input growth triggers the policy when available; otherwise a conservative local estimate is used.

Graph history is persistently replaced, so archived messages do not return on the next tool turn. Each checkpoint changes the cache epoch once. Token and cache-read usage remain counted even after the corresponding messages leave history. Storage or quota failures leave history unchanged. Exact archives can contain sensitive tool output; apply the artifact store's retention/access policy accordingly.

For direct message processing, LangChainArtifactHistoryProcessor is exported from kedi.agent_adapter.compaction; using it alone does not manage graph state.

For application-defined retention or summarization, pass a native history_processor= callback. Kedi commits its accepted result through LangGraph Overwrite, so removed history cannot reappear on a later tool step. See User-Defined History Processing.

items.title: Capability Limits
items.text: Backend-specific settings still depend on the selected chat model. Native approval middleware covers tools represented in the LangChain agent; it cannot grant capabilities the provider itself does not expose.

items.title: Local Laya
items.text: Laya evaluates typed decisions locally. It supports boolean judgments, finite choices, probabilities, described rubrics, and constrained extraction. It does not generate free-form text or replace a general-purpose coding agent.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
The development packages live in the separate kedi-decisions monorepo. They are not published to PyPI yet. From your Kedi checkout, clone it into decisions/ if that directory does not already exist, then install into the active Kedi environment:

git clone https://github.com/kedi-lang/kedi-decisions.git decisions
uv pip install -e decisions -e 'decisions/packages/kedi-laya[mlx,pydantic]'

Use [torch,pydantic] for the upstream PyTorch runtime, or include langchain for that adapter. Neither installation requires TypeSafe or a Jev API key. Installation does not download weights; the first inference loads the selected checkpoint. An existing local checkpoint directory avoids network downloads.

items.title: Images, Audio and Video
items.text:
laya/vega loads Laya's engine (laya 0.5+, PyTorch). It reads one image, audio or video per decision as data; the prompt text reaches each question as context. Other checkpoints read text only, and Kedi rejects media for them before the call.

> adapter: pydantic
> model: laya/vega
> import: media

[photo: Image] = `image("ticket.png")`
[team: Literal["billing", "technical"]] << The team for the ticket in <<photo>> is?
= `team`

Install the PyTorch extra (kedi-laya[torch] includes Laya's vision and audio extras); video also needs the ffmpeg binary.

items.title: A Kedi Program
items.text:
> import: decisions
> adapter: pydantic
> model: laya/aac6fef/laya-multilingual-mlx

> settings:
  decision_boolean_threshold: 0.85

>> A customer reports a duplicate charge and asks for a refund.
The responsible team is [team: Literal["billing", "technical"]].
The probability that a refund is requested is [refund: Probability].

= <team> receives the request, with refund probability <refund>.

Change the adapter directive to > adapter: langchain to use the same program through LangChain. > import: decisions exposes Probability, Rubric, BooleanCriteria, and ChoiceCriteria; importing these types does not select a model or start inference. Python code can import them from kedi.decisions. The same import works for Jev; only the model and its provider settings change.

items.title: Provider and Backend
items.text:
laya/<checkpoint> always identifies the laya provider. Its automatic backend selection prefers installed MLX on Apple Silicon and otherwise selects PyTorch. The laya-mlx/<checkpoint> compatibility alias forces MLX. Python callers can choose explicitly:

from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from kedi_laya import LayaClient

class Route(BaseModel):
    team: Literal["billing", "technical"]

with LayaClient("path/to/checkpoint", backend="mlx") as client:
    agent = Agent(client.as_pydantic_model(), output_type=Route)
    result = agent.run_sync("Please refund my duplicate charge.")
    print(result.output.team)

For LangChain, use client.as_langchain_model().with_structured_output(Route). The direct client.as_evaluator() API returns values, usage, and decision evidence without either framework. Framework integrations are optional dependencies.

items.title: Decision Policy and Evidence
items.text:
Booleans use the strict rule probability > decision_boolean_threshold, default 0.85. decision_tool_call_threshold, default 0.6, controls finite tool selection. Parameterized tool selections require an explicit argument-producing handler; the model does not fabricate arbitrary tool arguments. Kedi's implicit artifact toolset is disabled for decision models.

decision_info("team") exposes the provider, checkpoint, confidence, and probabilities through the normal decision evidence API. Laya uses the decisions metadata envelope; Jev retains typesafe. Their confidence values are not interchangeable calibrated probabilities.

items.title: Operational Limits
items.text:
• One client loads weights once and serializes its predictions. Async inference runs off the event loop; cancelling the waiter does not stop a native kernel.
  • Closing a model wrapper does not close a borrowed client. The owner should close the client when its session ends. No hosted fallback is used.
  • Owned MLX predictors reject input exceeding the checkpoint's actual token budget instead of silently truncating it. Injected predictors and PyTorch retain their own context handling.
  • Real inference has been verified with the multilingual MLX checkpoint. PyTorch loader contract tests do not establish correctness for every checkpoint.

items.title: Local Models
items.text:
Kedi programs can run on small models on your own machine, offline, with no API key. Kedi needs no special support for this. A local model joins through an adapter Kedi already has:

  • A LangChain chat model. Its profile declares what it reads and produces: image_inputs, audio_inputs or audio_outputs.
  • A Pydantic AI model. It receives Kedi's typed output as an output tool, separate from Kedi's own tools.
  • A JSON-RPC bridge. Use this for a runtime outside Python.

The program is the same as for a cloud model. Only the adapter's model changes.

items.title: Tested Setups
items.text:
Each row was measured end to end through Kedi on 2026-11-26, on an Apple M1 with 8 GB of RAM and Python 3.12, with outbound networking denied. Every example has a README with setup, commands, evaluation sets and results.

Task Model Kedi surface Joins as Download Measured Typed fields from text Cactus Needle 3 [refund: Refund] << ... Pydantic AI model 34 MB schema-valid 24/24, every field right 15/24 or 12/24 depending on the process, 0.16 s, 193 MB peak Typed records from images Qwen3-VL-2B on llama.cpp's llama-server [receipt: Receipt] << Read the receipt in <<photo>>. Pydantic AI's OpenAI chat model on the local server 1.5 GB every field right 18/18, the same as gemini-3.5-flash-lite on the same program; 3.8 s, 2.4 GiB server peak Reading text in images Cactus Mirage [writing] << Read the writing in <<photo>>. LangChain, image_inputs 21 MB character error rate 0.002, 0.15 s, 267 MB peak Turkish speech EMA Lightning [speech: Audio] << <sentence> LangChain, audio_outputs 34 MB, plus PyTorch real-time factor 0.064, 481 MB peak English speech Phonon 31m [speech: Audio] << <sentence> LangChain, audio_outputs 65 MB real-time factor 0.081, 347 MB peak English transcription Cactus Whistle [text] << Transcribe <<clip>>. LangChain, audio_inputs 16 MB word error rate 0.067 on Phonon's speech, 0.06–0.11 s per clip Turkish transcription Whisper small [text] << Transcribe <<clip>>. LangChain, audio_inputs 484 MB 2 real errors in 43 words on EMA's speech, real-time factor about 0.3

The examples are local_extraction, local_vision and local_speech.

Typed decisions are covered separately. For booleans, choices, probabilities, rubrics and constrained extraction, with decision evidence, use Local Laya. The setups above cover what Laya does not: open fields such as names and amounts, text in images, and speech.

items.title: Capabilities
items.text:
Each cell comes from a run through Kedi. "Refused" means the wrapper or server fails with a clear error. "Not tested" makes no claim either way.

Model Text answer Typed output Program tools Image input Audio input Speech output Cactus Needle 3 refused yes refused not tested not tested not tested Qwen3-VL-2B, llama-server not tested yes not tested yes not tested not tested Cactus Mirage yes, the text it reads refused refused yes not tested not tested EMA Lightning not tested not tested not tested not tested not tested yes, Turkish Phonon 31m not tested not tested not tested not tested not tested yes, English Cactus Whistle yes, the transcript refused refused not tested yes, English not tested Whisper small yes, the transcript refused refused not tested yes, Turkish not tested

For decisions (booleans, choices, probabilities and rubrics), see Local Laya.

items.title: What These Models Do Not Do
items.text:
Each wrapper does only what its model does and refuses the rest with a clear error:

  • Needle 3 answers only with structured output. An untyped << prompt or a program tool from > use: fails. Kedi's artifact tools, offered to every model, go unused.
  • Mirage and the transcribers answer with text. Their LangChain profiles declare tool_calling: False, so Kedi offers them no tools, and a typed capture or a program tool fails. Mirage is used only to read text, in Latin script, and its form fields did not read receipts.
  • The speech models produce audio only. EMA Lightning has a single voice, so a voice setting for it is an error.

items.title: Writing for a Small Model
items.text:
Small models are sensitive to the program's shape. These rules come from the measurements:

  • Use a typed raw invoke. [x: T] << message sends the message alone. A >> template capture adds template instructions written for capable models. On the refund set, the raw invoke scored 25/32 fields and the template capture 16/32.
  • Describe the allowed values. A Literal whose description explains each value raised the reason field from 10/24 to 15/24.
  • Send the model only Kedi's request. A wrapper that passes text to a small model should take it from current_request().render() (see Rendered Request), not from the framework's messages. Pydantic AI's messages also carry a transport note from Kedi's Pydantic adapter. With that note, Needle read "1,299.00 euros" as 1.299 on every run; without it, Needle read it correctly in all 16 processes we ran.
  • Drop the artifact tools when nothing is large. Kedi offers its artifact tools to every model by default. Qwen3-VL-2B called read_artifact until its retries ran out, on every receipt. With > artifacts: and enabled: false, it read 18 of 18.
  • Let the program decide. The model reads; Kedi or Python code checks and routes. In the examples, a refund goes to a person when its amount is not one the message states in euros, and a receipt fails when its items do not add up. Schema validation alone cannot catch these misreads.
  • Measure before relying on it. A consistent answer can still be wrong: Needle gave the same wrong reason on every run.
  • Repeat across processes, not only within one. Within a process, Needle's answers never changed. Across 16 processes, it read one request's amount as 75.00 in 6 and as the shoe size, 42, in 10.

items.title: Offline Runs
items.text:
• Download once, then run offline. Provisioning needs the network; running does not. Set HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 for models from Hugging Face.
  • Turn off Cactus telemetry. Cactus sends a usage event on each call unless CACTUS_TELEMETRY=0 or DO_NOT_TRACK is set. The example wrappers set both before Cactus loads.
  • Check it with the network denied. On macOS: sandbox-exec -p '(version 1)(allow default)(deny network*)' python ....
  • Turn off cloud handoff. Some local runtimes forward requests to a cloud. cactus serve, from Cactus Engine, hands low-confidence completions to Cactus's cloud unless it gets --no-cloud-handoff. llama.cpp's llama-server, run from local model files, worked with outbound networking denied.
  • Keep model packages out of Kedi. The model packages are not Kedi dependencies. Each example pins its own in requirements.txt, for a separate environment.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
Pydantic AI is a core Kedi dependency:

uv add kedi

Provider credentials and optional provider packages follow Pydantic AI's model requirements.

items.title: Model Names
items.text:
Select the adapter and a Pydantic-style or LiteLLM-style model:

> adapter: pydantic
> model: openai:gpt-6-luna

Strings using vendor/model are normalized to Pydantic's model naming form. An existing Pydantic AI Model may be passed to PydanticAdapter directly.

CLI and Python API lazy adapter selection defer native provider-name validation until the model is selected for a call. A program with its own > model: does not require credentials for an unused default provider. This does not waive credentials for the selected model. Direct PydanticAdapter(...) construction keeps Pydantic AI's eager-validation default; pass defer_model_check=True to opt in. Python API adapter options can explicitly set defer_model_check=False to retain eager validation when the lazy adapter is constructed.

items.title: Model Fallback and Request Retries
items.text:
Use ordered fallback models through > fallback: or the adapter constructor:

from kedi.agent_adapter import PydanticAdapter

adapter = PydanticAdapter(
    "openai:gpt-6-luna",
    fallback_models=["openai:gpt-6.1-sol"],
    request_retries=2,
)

fallback_models accepts an ordered sequence of strings or native Pydantic AI Model objects. A scoped AgentProfile.fallback_models list of IDs replaces this default; () clears it and None inherits. Selection is local to a run and does not mutate the caller's models or SDK clients.

Each candidate gets the bounded request retry policy for HTTP 408, 429, and 5xx errors before advancing. An active settings.request_retries overrides the constructor default; 0 disables same-model retries, not explicit fallback. Output/tool validation, tool-body failures, authentication, refusals, and control signals do not trigger fallback. Attempts share admission, usage limits and deadlines; completed tools and approvals are not replayed. Streaming recovery stops once response content reaches the caller.

SDK retries may compound with Kedi retries. Disable them explicitly, for example with AsyncOpenAI(max_retries=0), when Kedi should own attempts. Strict request budgets reject enabled or uninspectable SDK retries rather than undercounting.

Native pydantic_ai.capabilities.ModelFallback backups and ordinary FallbackModel chains both pass through Kedi's per-attempt admission guard, including when request_retries=0. A spent request budget prevents the backup from starting; refused admission adds no provider attempt or token usage.

items.title: Model Settings
items.text:
The full list of supported > settings: keys comes from Kedi's agent_profile.settings:

Setting Meaning context_limit Model context window in tokens for Kedi's request ceiling; default 200,000. decision_boolean_threshold Probability above which a boolean decision counts as true. decision_tool_call_threshold Probability above which a hand-off tool is selected. extra_body Extra fields merged into the provider request body. extra_headers Extra HTTP headers sent with provider requests. frequency_penalty Penalty scaled by how often a token already appeared. logit_bias Per-token logit adjustments. max_tokens Maximum tokens in the model response. media_limit Largest media value, in bytes, a request may attach; default 20 MB cap. parallel_tool_calls Whether the model may call several tools in one turn. presence_penalty Penalty for repeating tokens already present. request_retries Retries for transient provider request failures; does not replay tools or entire runs. response_cache Enable provider response caching for identical requests. response_cache_ttl Cache time-to-live in seconds for cached responses. seed Seed for deterministic sampling where the provider supports it. service_tier Provider service tier (auto, default, flex, priority). stop_sequences Sequences that stop generation. temperature Sampling temperature; higher values are more random. thinking Thinking budget (minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh) or boolean. timeout Request timeout in seconds. tool_choice Tool selection policy (none, auto, required). tool_reason Opts into an optional reason string on tool calls. top_p Nucleus sampling cutoff. voice Voice of [x: Audio] << speech: OpenAI's audio voice or the chat model's voice field; LangChain's Gemini models take none. 
> settings:
    timeout: 120
    max_tokens: 2048
    parallel_tool_calls: true

max reasoning effort maps to Pydantic AI's xhigh.

items.title: Capability Bundles
items.text:
Capabilities compose tools, instructions, and owned tool policies through > use:. Eager use needs no loading call. > defer: true uses Pydantic AI's native load_capability path and withholds the bundle's callable tools until activation. Activation is run-local; model retries do not reevaluate a Kedi defer expression.

An instruction reset suppresses current Kedi guidance without erasing an older load result from history. A deferred parent reveals its nested catalog only after activation; nested deferred bundles and their subagent tools require their own load. See the capability guide for explicit reuse, history, MCP connection lifetime, and cache limitations.

items.title: CodeMode
items.text:
Use > codemode: enabled to replace application tool schemas with Kedi's search_tools, get_tool_schema, and execute_code controls:

> adapter: pydantic
> codemode: enabled

The outer capability wraps constructor, caller, scoped Kedi, and local MCP toolsets together. Nested calls retain validation, approval, required-tool, telemetry, cancellation, and artifact behavior. Provider-native MCP and external deferred approval are rejected while CodeMode is active. See CodeMode for the complete contract.

items.title: Structured Outputs
items.text:
Kedi builds a dynamic Pydantic model from each output field:

~Finding(severity: str, message: str)

>> The findings from inspecting <code> are [findings: list[Finding]].

Field descriptions from Annotated[T, "description"] are preserved. Pydantic AI produces and validates the result before Kedi publishes captured fields. For completion templates, the generated output schema reinforces that captures contain replacement values rather than the completed template. This preserves the provider's output mode and does not trim or otherwise rewrite returned strings. Raw invokes and decision-model templates do not receive this rule.

items.title: Python and Procedure Tools
items.text: Python @kedi.tool functions and Kedi procedures selected by > use: become native Pydantic AI tools for one lexical run. Registration is context-local, so tools do not leak between concurrent calls.

items.title: MCP Toolsets
items.text:
All Kedi MCP transports are mapped to Pydantic AI toolsets:

  • stdio with command, args, and env;
  • SSE with URL and headers;
  • streamable HTTP with URL and headers.

Application and MCP toolsets are approval-required before execution.

items.title: Native Tool Artifacts
items.text:
When artifacts are enabled, constructor tools, caller-provided tools, and local MCP toolsets cross Kedi's artifact-admission boundary before Pydantic AI commits their successful results to message history. Large values therefore become the same compact ArtifactRef objects used by Kedi-defined tools.

Admission preserves Pydantic AI's native tool_call_id, validation, retries, approval flow, and streaming result handling. Failed tool results remain native errors, and a tool already wrapped by Kedi is not admitted twice. The exact returned ref ID must be used with read_artifact; IDs must not be predicted.

items.title: Approval Integration
items.text:
Pydantic's deferred-tool capability is used to resolve Kedi approval requests. Read-only calls pass automatically; mutating and sensitive calls flow through the active static/dynamic policy. Edited arguments are supplied as Pydantic tool overrides after validation.

Nested subagent policies form a ceiling: a child cannot widen a parent's restriction.

items.title: Foreground and Background Subagents
items.text: Pydantic supports both modes and native conversation resume. Usage limits are translated to Pydantic AI request, tool-call, and token limits. Child tool, MCP, skills, model, and instruction scopes remain isolated.

items.title: Usage and Retry Behavior
items.text:
Pydantic run usage is reported to Kedi's subagent budget observer. The adapter tracks requests, tool calls, and input/output/total tokens.

Unless retries is supplied explicitly, PydanticAdapter allows three bounded retries for correctable tool-call failures. The output-validation retry budget remains Pydantic AI's default. An explicit integer or AgentRetries value overrides Kedi's tool retry default.

subagent_failure_policy="fail_closed" is the default. "recover" exposes a sanitized child error to the parent instead of failing the parent run.

items.title: Codex Responses Connections
items.text:
See Codex Responses Connections.

On Codex WebSocket models, Kedi reveals activated capability tools through Pydantic AI's ordinary tool list instead of native tool-addition/deferral parameters that the gateway rejects. load_capability and run-local activation still apply. The compatibility profile is scoped to the call: the caller's model is not mutated, the WebSocket client is retained, and request budgets remain enforced. HTTP models and other providers keep their original profiles. Changing the visible tool list is not a prefix-cache preservation guarantee.

items.title: Native History Policy
items.text: For application-defined retention or summarization, pass a native history_processor= callback. Pydantic AI's processed history is written back to the active graph before dispatch, including tool-loop requests. Kedi validates tool lifecycles and continuation safety around that callback. See User-Defined History Processing.

items.title: TypeSafe Jev
items.text: Jev evaluates claims, selects finite options, and scores described rubrics. It is not a free-form text generator. Kedi exposes it through the Pydantic AI and LangChain adapters using the optional kedi-typesafe package.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
For a published compatible release:

uv add 'kedi[typesafe]'
# For LangChain, also install the classifier integration:
uv add 'kedi[langchain,typesafe]' 'kedi-typesafe[langchain]'

The current typesafe and codex-model/terminal-bench extras pin incompatible Pydantic AI release lines. Install them in separate environments; uv rejects the unsupported combined selections explicitly.

Set TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the environment. The extended API described here requires kedi-typesafe 0.2.1 or later, which includes the decision evidence used by Kedi bindings. The 0.3.5 package lives in the kedi-decisions monorepo and reuses its shared schema implementation without changing these imports. Local Laya inference is provided by a separate Laya extension, not TypeSafe.

items.title: Claims and Thresholds
items.text: See Claims and Thresholds.

items.title: Custom Endpoint
items.text:
The development SDK integration accepts TYPESAFE_BASE_URL for both adapters. Set it to the HTTPS service origin; the SDK appends /v1/systemone. Keep the key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY. An explicit base_url= on TypeSafeModel or TypeSafeChatModel overrides the environment value.

import os
from kedi_typesafe import TypeSafeModel

model = TypeSafeModel(
    "jev-latest",
    api_key=os.environ["TYPESAFE_API_KEY"],
    base_url=os.environ["TYPESAFE_BASE_URL"],
)

A failed custom-endpoint request does not fall back to the public service. This integration targets TypeSafe SDK 0.7.2 and Pydantic AI 2.54.0; it is not available in the previously published kedi-typesafe package. Use the reviewed development checkout until its compatible release is published.

items.title: Typed Criteria
items.text: See Typed Criteria.

items.title: Outputs and Limitations
items.text: See Outputs and Limitations.

items.title: Decision Evidence in Kedi
items.text: See Decision Evidence in Kedi.

items.title: Python API
items.text:
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic_ai import Agent
from kedi_typesafe import Probability, TypeSafeModel

class Assessment(BaseModel):
    supported: bool
    probability: Probability

async def assess():
    async with TypeSafeModel(threshold=0.9) as model:
        result = await Agent(model, output_type=Assessment).run(
            "Reference: Ankara is Turkey's capital. Claim: Turkey's capital is Ankara."
        )
        return result.output

LangChain uses kedi_typesafe.integrations.langchain.TypeSafeChatModel and with_structured_output(Assessment, include_raw=True). Raw results expose decision evidence, provider probabilities/confidence when available, and usage. Evidence is metadata, not an additional generated output field. Streaming exposes the completed assessment; it does not simulate token-by-token Jev generation.

Reuse model instances for warm connections. Close owned models using their context manager or aclose; caller-supplied clients remain caller-owned. Configure transport timeout on the constructor. Unsupported generation settings are rejected.

items.title: Agents and Orchestration
items.text:
Kedi treats model execution as scoped agent configuration rather than a global string. A scope can select a framework or harness, model, reasoning effort, instructions, settings, tools, MCP servers, skills, approvals, and child agents.

Choose the language construct by who controls the next step:

Construct Who selects the next step? What it provides Procedure The Kedi program Explicit statements, arguments, return types, and captured configuration. Profile No execution by itself Reusable configuration applied to later calls or used by a child agent. Tool-using model call The model, within the exposed tool surface A request that may call tools before returning its result. Subagent The parent requests work; the child owns its conversation An isolated task with its own profile and a bounded lifecycle. Dynamic workflow The parent writes orchestration code Sandboxed composition of the permitted child agents.

Start with a procedure when the sequence is known. Add a tool-using call where the model needs to choose an action. Use a child agent when a task needs a separate conversation and capability boundary, not merely a different prompt.

items.title: Framework Adapters and Agent Harnesses
items.text:
Framework adapters embed Kedi's prompt and tool contracts in an agent framework:

  • pydantic
  • langchain

Agent harnesses drive a complete external coding/agent runtime:

  • claude
  • codex
  • acp

Select the first group with > adapter: and the second with > agent:. These are mutually exclusive backend kinds, not interchangeable aliases.

items.title: Active Agent State
items.text:
Directives update immutable agent state for following calls in the lexical scope:

> adapter: pydantic
> model: openai:gpt-6-luna
> effort: low
> instructions: Use tools only when they improve factual accuracy.

Top-level state is captured by following procedures. A procedure-body override applies only to later calls in that invocation. When the scope exits, Kedi restores the previous state.

items.title: Profiles
items.text:
Profiles name reusable state:

> profile: reviewer:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > model: openai:gpt-6-luna
    > instructions: Review evidence before making a claim.

> use: reviewer

Profiles can be exported, imported, merged with later directives, and exposed as direct child subagents.

items.title: Capability Surfaces
items.text:
• Procedures become typed tools through > use:.
  • > mcp: attaches external MCP tools.
  • > skills: exposes scoped registry, project, and user skill discovery.
  • > codemode: enabled progressively discloses tools and executes hydrated calls in bounded code.
  • > approval: controls risky tool calls.
  • > hooks: observes, edits, or denies agent lifecycle boundaries.
  • > subagent: adds bounded delegation tools to a profile.
  • semantic stream events expose completed commentary and final messages to terminals, UIs, and orchestration code without changing adapter results.

Each surface is capability-checked against the selected backend. Unsupported structured output is an execution error. Tools and MCP currently produce forward-compatible editor warnings where an adapter may gain support later.

items.title: Design Rule
items.text: Define the narrowest agent surface that can perform the task. Give profiles specific instructions, only required tools, bounded child agents, and the least permissive approval and sandbox settings. A broader model is not a substitute for a clear contract.

items.title: Approvals and Sensitive Operations
items.text: Approvals mediate individual tool calls after arguments are produced and before the tool executes. They are not model-output validation and do not sandbox ordinary embedded Python.

items.title: Risk Classes
items.text:
Kedi uses three ordered risk classes:

  • read_only: observes non-sensitive state;
  • mutating: changes state or performs an effect;
  • sensitive: accesses secrets or otherwise requires stronger review.

Custom Kedi and Python tools default to mutating. A Python @kedi.tool can declare a different risk:

import kedi


@kedi.tool(risk="read_only")
def list_public_files() -> list[str]:
    return ["README.md", "CHANGELOG.md"]

An argument-aware risk resolver may elevate a call, but cannot downgrade a tool's static risk.

items.title: Default Policy
items.text:
Without an explicit policy, read_only calls are allowed and mutating or sensitive calls are denied. This is the Python/runtime fail-closed default.

The interactive kedi CLI installs a prompt policy for risky calls. It offers Allow once, Deny, and Allow always for this run. “Always” is scoped to the current process, tool, and risk level; it is never persisted.

In non-interactive execution, an unanswered prompt is denied.

items.title: Static Policies
items.text:
> approval: allow

allow permits registered mutating and sensitive tools in that scope. Use it only when the complete tool surface and arguments are already trusted.

> approval: deny

deny refuses risky calls. Read-only calls remain automatically allowed. edit is not a static mode.

items.title: Dynamic Policy
items.text:
Define a sync or async handler in Python and select it:

```
from pathlib import Path
from kedi import ApprovalDecision

def review_tool(request):
    if request.tool_name != "write_report":
        return ApprovalDecision.deny(reason="tool is outside this workflow")

    path = Path(request.arguments["path"])
    safe_path = Path("reports") / path.name
    return ApprovalDecision.edit(
        {**request.arguments, "path": str(safe_path)},
        reason="redirected to the reports directory",
    )
```

> approval: `review_tool`

The handler must return ApprovalDecision.allow(), ApprovalDecision.deny(), or ApprovalDecision.edit(arguments). Returning a string or arbitrary mapping is an error.

items.title: LLM-backed approval helper
items.text: llm_approval requires enabled tool reasons. Its judgment is fallible and does not replace a deterministic authorization boundary. See Tool Reasons and LLM Approval.

items.title: Optional Tool Reasons
items.text: Enable tool_reason in settings or the supported adapter constructor to collect an optional justification for approval-applicable tools. Kedi removes the synthetic argument before the real callable or MCP server receives the call. See configuration and failure rules.

items.title: Approval Request
items.text:
The immutable request contains:

Field Meaning tool_name Registered tool name arguments Deep-copied, read-only argument mapping risk Effective risk after argument-aware elevation adapter_shortname Active adapter when known description Tool description when available metadata Deep-copied tool metadata when available reason Optional model-provided action justification, separate from tool arguments tool_reason_enabled Whether the calling adapter enabled justification collection

The handler cannot mutate the request in place. It must return edit with a new complete argument mapping.

items.title: Edited Arguments
items.text:
Edited arguments are reclassified and revalidated against the tool signature, custom Kedi models, and schema before invocation. An edit that redirects a normal path to .env can therefore become sensitive and face subsequent policy checks. Invalid edited types fail before the tool runs.

Only an edit decision may carry replacement arguments. Allow and deny cannot smuggle an edit payload.

items.title: Sensitive Files
items.text:
The bundled filesystem tools classify .env and .env.* as secrets. Normal read_text_file(path) refuses them. The caller must set secret_files=True, which elevates the call to sensitive, and approval must then permit it.

Writes and patches targeting secret filenames are likewise elevated before mutation. The opt-in flag requests review; it does not itself authorize access.

items.title: Scope and Descendants
items.text:
Approval is lexical and restored when a scope exits. A procedure directive applies to its following tool calls; a profile carries its policy when used.

Subagents have their own policy, but an ancestor's approval ceiling remains in force. A child cannot replace a parent deny with allow. Parent edits are reclassified and checked by child policy. This makes delegation monotonically restrictive rather than a route around approval.

items.title: Limits of Approval
items.text: Approval wraps registered tool calls. It does not intercept arbitrary I/O in a Python block, a package prelude, or third-party code. Treat embedded Python as trusted executable code and use host isolation when that boundary matters.

items.title: Backend Selection
items.text: Kedi separates framework adapters from agent harnesses because they expose different execution and capability contracts.

items.title: Frameworks with > adapter:
items.text:
> adapter: pydantic
> model: openai:gpt-6-luna

>> A summary of <document> is [summary: str].

Built-in framework shortnames are pydantic and langchain. Frameworks are appropriate when Kedi owns structured prompting and registers typed tools through the framework's model interface.

items.title: Harnesses with > agent:
items.text:
> agent: codex
> model: gpt-6-luna
> settings:
    cwd: .
    sandbox: workspace-write

>> The repository evidence suggests that [answer: str].
= <answer>

Built-in harness shortnames are claude, codex, acp, a2a, and rpc. Harnesses are appropriate when the underlying agent owns its tool loop, repository context, or protocol session.

items.title: Literal and Dynamic Selection
items.text:
Literal names are validated by the parser/LSP and runtime:

> adapter: langchain

Use a backtick expression only when selection is genuinely dynamic:

```
selected_backend = "pydantic"
```

> adapter: `selected_backend`

Dynamic selection postpones validation and reduces static diagnostics. Prefer a literal or profile in production source.

items.title: Required Capabilities
items.text:
Make nonnegotiable backend behavior explicit with > requires::

> adapter: langchain
> requires:
    structured_output
    tool_registration
    history_replay

Literal selections receive source-located LSP errors when the adapter cannot meet the contract. Dynamic selections are checked at runtime before model I/O. Requirements accumulate through lexical scope and applied profiles; an inner scope cannot erase an outer obligation. See Scoping and Capabilities.

items.title: ACP Commands
items.text:
Select ACP using an explicit command:

> agent: acp:
    command: `["uv", "run", "my-acp-agent"]`

The command can be plain text or a Python expression evaluating to a string or sequence of strings. The connection body binds the command to the acp harness.

ACP commands are always explicit. Use > agent: acp: syntax or construct ACPAdapter(command=...) in Python. Plain > agent: acp, CLI command options, and environment command fallbacks are unsupported.

items.title: JSON-RPC Bridges
items.text:
A backend in any language that speaks Kedi's JSON-RPC protocol is selected the same way:

> agent: rpc:
    command: node my_bridge.mjs

Kedi launches one bridge for each distinct command, completes its handshake before the first call, and stops it when the runtime closes. The bridge negotiates its capabilities, so > requires: is checked against the launched bridge. > agent: rpc: accepts bridges that negotiate agent-harness; select an agent-framework bridge from Python with compile_program(adapter=JsonRpcAdapter(...)).

items.title: Package Adapters
items.text:
An installed package can expose adapters of its own (see Package Manifests). Importing it makes them selectable in the importing module:

> import: pi
> agent: pi

A package adapter takes no connection body: the package says how to launch it. Its kind is the one the package declares, so a package can also offer an agent-framework bridge through > adapter:.

items.title: A2A Endpoints
items.text:
Bind a remote A2A harness to its endpoint and credential reference:

> agent: a2a:
    endpoint: https://agents.example.com
    auth:
        scheme: bearer
        token_env: RESEARCH_AGENT_TOKEN

The remote process owns its model and tool loop, so local > model:, > effort:, > settings:, > mcp:, and tool registration are not forwarded. Generic peers support raw text; Kedi-served peers can negotiate typed captures. See A2A Cloud Agents.

items.title: CLI and Environment Defaults
items.text:
If source does not select a backend, Python configuration or CLI defaults can provide one. The Python API loads .env and recognizes:

Variable Meaning KEDI_ADAPTER Framework adapter shortname KEDI_AGENT Harness shortname KEDI_ADAPTER_MODEL Model for either selected backend

KEDI_ADAPTER and KEDI_AGENT are mutually exclusive.

items.title: Selection Precedence
items.text:
For a model call, selection priority is:

  1. a direct directive in the current lexical scope;
  2. a profile applied in that scope;
  3. Python/CLI default agent profile;
  4. environment-based default selection.

Nested scopes may choose another backend and restore the outer selection when they exit. Sequential directives can also change backend kinds in the same scope: the most recent selection applies to following calls. Python/CLI and environment defaults do not prevent this. Procedures retain the selection captured where they were defined.

When switching frameworks, Kedi preserves the explicit > model: or the initial framework's string model ID if no model directive was given. The destination must support that ID. Framework-specific Python model objects, credentials, and provider clients are not converted to another framework.

An implicit framework model is not transferred to a harness. Explicit model directives remain in scope; select a compatible model when switching kinds:

> adapter: pydantic
> model: openai:gpt-6-luna
>> Summarize the repository requirements.

> agent: codex
> model: gpt-6-luna
>> Inspect the repository and summarize its test coverage.

Changing backends does not itself transfer conversation history. Configure history explicitly when calls should share context.

items.title: Invalid Combinations
items.text:
A declarative > profile: cannot contain both > adapter: and > agent: members. Unlike executable directives, these describe one backend, not a sequence. Kedi also rejects a framework name in > agent:, a harness name in > adapter:, conflicting environment defaults, a dynamic value with the wrong type, and an adapter instance whose declared kind does not match the selected API.

Define separate profiles when you need reusable configurations for both kinds.

items.title: Capabilities
items.text:
Unreleased

This page describes the next Kedi release. Eager composition is supported by Pydantic AI and LangChain; deferred loading is supported by Pydantic AI only.

A profile selects agent configuration. A capability contributes reusable instructions, tools, and tool-local policies without replacing the host model or base instructions. Both are applied with > use:. Neither starts a model call.

Use a subagent when the contribution needs a separate model, conversation, or execution loop.

items.title: Compose Instructions
items.text:
> capability: evidence:
    ###
    Separate observed facts from assumptions when assessing readiness.
    ###
    > instructions: Use the supplied evidence and identify unfinished checks.

> capability: concise:
    > instructions: Keep the explanation to one sentence.

> profile: release_reviewer:
    > instructions: Assess whether the release can proceed.
    > use: evidence
    > use: concise

> use: release_reviewer
>> Unit tests passed, but staging verification is still running.
The release readiness is [readiness: Literal["ready", "pending"]],
because [reason: str].
= `{"readiness": readiness, "reason": reason}`

The request receives the profile's release-assessment instruction followed by the evidence and concise contributions. The docstring describes the capability in the editor and, when deferred, in its discovery catalog. The example needs a configured model, just like any other template program.

Use > use: inside a profile to compose capabilities. There is no separate > capabilities: directive. A capability may itself use another capability or a tool, but cannot use a profile to import host-wide configuration indirectly.

items.title: Reset, Then Reuse
items.text:
Using the definitions above:

> use: release_reviewer
> instructions: Report only the observed deployment state.
>> Staging verification is still running, so its status is [status: str].

> use: concise
>> The current status of <status> means [explanation: str].

The first request has only the new user instruction. The second also has the concise contribution. An explicit instruction assignment clears prior user guidance even when the new base text equals the old text.

Resetting instructions does not remove tools, capability approval, hooks, history, or runtime instructions such as the template-filling contract. Reusing a capability restores its guidance once; repeated use does not duplicate it. Deduplication uses capability identity, not matching instruction text.

Profiles still override. A profile with explicit instructions replaces the current user instruction composition; a model-only profile does not. Profile members follow source order: instructions after capability use clear earlier guidance; capability use after instructions appends to the new base.

items.title: Contribute Tools
items.text:
This exportable review module is a small building block for a harness. It reads a caller-supplied source file and returns a typed finding, not a complete coding agent or a sandbox.

```
from pathlib import Path
```

@read_source(path: str) -> str:
    ###
    Read a UTF-8 source file for inspection.
    ###
    = ```
    source = Path(path)
    return source.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    ```

> capability: source_reader:
    > instructions: Read the named file before describing its implementation.
    > approval: allow
    > use: read_source

> instructions: Review code without changing files.
> use: source_reader

@review_file(path: str) -> str:
    >> The most significant concrete issue in <path> is [finding: str].
    = <finding>

> export:
    source_reader
    review_file

The local allow policy belongs only to read_source; it does not allow unrelated host tools. An explicit policy on the exposed tool takes precedence, then the capability policy, then the calling agent's default. Independent mandatory enforcement still applies. A procedure's internal > approval: governs its internal agent calls, not whether the outer caller may invoke that procedure.

Tools retain their concrete definition-site bindings when imported. Exporting the capability does not export its private procedures separately. Incompatible ownership or policy for the same tool name is an error, not last-writer-wins.

The example reads paths allowed by the process. Instruction text and capability names do not impose filesystem restrictions; enforce those in the tool or its execution boundary when needed.

items.title: Local Procedure Instructions
items.text:
Procedures capture the configuration visible at their definition site. A local > instructions: replaces that invocation's inherited user guidance, while captured tools remain available. A later local capability use appends there. Returning, failing, or cancelling the procedure does not alter its caller.
