This is not a fresh conversation and does not erase history. A procedure declared before a later base instruction does not acquire that later instruction, even when it had no base instruction at its definition site. The same rule applies across notebook and IDLE cells.

A procedure with no model binding still falls back to the invoking agent's model, as before. That inference fallback does not import the caller's later instructions or tools; an explicitly captured model continues to win.

items.title: Deferred Loading
items.text:
Using the source tool defined above:

> capability: source_reader_on_demand:
    ###
    Read source files when implementation evidence is required.
    ###
    > defer: true
    > instructions: Read the requested source file before answering.
    > use: read_source

> use: source_reader_on_demand

Without defer, use is eager: tools and guidance are available for the next request without a discovery call. With defer: true, the native Pydantic AI loader exposes a catalog entry first. Tools cannot execute until activation, even if the model guesses their names. Repeated loads are idempotent. This means registrations and activation are not duplicated; the native loader may return a retry response for an already-active capability.

defer also accepts an inline Python expression returning an actual boolean. Kedi evaluates it once per use context, not on every model retry. Strings and numbers are not accepted as truthy substitutes.

The initial adapter contract is Pydantic AI eager/deferred and LangChain eager only. Unsupported adapter combinations fail before inference. Nested deferred capabilities and deferred subagent targets are supported on Pydantic AI.

Deferred instructions can remain in historical load results after a reset. Reset suppresses their automatic reinjection; it does not make the model forget history. Explicit reuse restores guidance only after native activation. Native MCP setup/catalog discovery may occur before loading, so deferral is not a promise of lazy connections or zero resource cost.

items.title: Nested Capabilities
items.text:
Using read_source from the earlier example:

> capability: implementation_evidence:
    > defer: true
    > instructions: Read the named source before making implementation claims.
    > use: read_source

> capability: code_review:
    > defer: true
    > instructions: Distinguish observed defects from suggestions.
    > use: implementation_evidence

> use: code_review

Initially only code_review is discoverable. After the native loader confirms its activation, implementation_evidence becomes discoverable. Loading that second capability makes read_source callable. Loading the parent does not automatically load its deferred child; parent and child load calls in one model response do not skip that boundary. Eager child contributions become available with their deferred parent.

A shared child has one stable registration even when multiple parents include it. Any activated parent makes it discoverable. Explicit direct use also makes that child discoverable independently of its parents. These are contribution and loading relationships, not a sequence of tasks or separate agents.

items.title: Deferred Subagent Targets
items.text:
> profile: evidence_reviewer:
    > instructions: Review supplied evidence and identify unsupported conclusions.

> capability: specialist_review:
    > defer: true
    > subagent: evidence_reviewer

> use: specialist_review

The child profile is captured when the capability is used. Its target becomes available to the shared delegation or dynamic-workflow tools only after loading specialist_review. Guessing the target before activation does not start a child or invoke its capability-owned hooks. If the host already has other subagents, their shared controls remain available, with only those active targets exposed.

Background work, waiting, continuation, and messaging keep the captured binding and ownership checks. The subagent's own model and instructions remain those of its profile. CodeMode catalogs and schema results obey the same target visibility and activation rules as native calls.

Reset suppresses guidance throughout the nested contribution graph while retaining registrations. Reuse restores guidance once, still gated on native activation. If two deferred parents share a child and only one parent is reused after a reset, the child's guidance returns only after that parent and the child are loaded. Loading the other parent alone does not restore the child's guidance; the order of the parent declarations does not change this behavior. Each run owns its activation; sharing an adapter or descriptor does not share loaded state. Revealing a nested catalog changes its instruction prefix, so this path does not guarantee prefix-cache preservation.

items.title: Conditional Contributions
items.text:
Use deterministic guards to choose an instruction/tool bundle or its loading policy. The capability still contributes resources, not agent-wide overrides:

[needs_citations: bool] = `True`

> capability: evidence_policy:
    > if: `needs_citations`:
        > instructions: Support factual conclusions with supplied sources.
    > else:
        > instructions: Clearly distinguish suggestions from observed facts.

> use: evidence_policy

The Python expression must return an exact bool and is evaluated once per application. Only the selected branch's computed values and uses run. Nested guards and optional > else: follow the same rules as conditional profile configuration. Selected instructions remain additive to the host's base instructions. Selected approval and hooks remain limited to this capability's owned tools. A selected > defer: true makes the resulting capability load on demand; it does not defer the guard itself. Unselected tools are not registered.

All branches must respect the configuration boundary below, including branches whose guard is false. A condition is not a way to add model selection or other caller-owned settings to a capability.

items.title: Configuration Boundary
items.text:
Capability member Effect instructions Owned instruction contribution; local replacements affect only its bundle use, mcp, subagent Contribute tools, MCP sources, or child-profile bindings approval Override the default for owned concrete tools only hooks Owned tool lifecycle events, retaining mandatory enforcement requires Declare adapter requirements, not permissions defer Choose immediate contribution or native on-demand loading

Host model, fallback, effort, settings, agent, adapter, output, history, budgets, skills discovery, CodeMode policy, and artifacts are rejected at the capability root. user_prompt_submit hooks and tool_reason remain agent-wide.

Use the calling agent's artifact exclude_tools for exact-name exceptions. Exclusion does not disable approval, reason, output limits, or tracing. See Artifact Policy and Hooks.

items.title: Inspect Behavior
items.text:
Telemetry records application/reuse, instruction replacement, request snapshots, native load attempts and activation, tool ownership and approval source, and artifact admission decisions. CodeMode retains the actual inner tool span. Capability IDs are stable hashes; source locations require source-path capture. Instruction content follows the existing content capture policy.

Deferred loading can change request prefixes. Cache reuse depends on the provider and transport; it is not guaranteed. Capability loading does not require schema search or CodeMode, and is not automatically more efficient than a small eager tool set.

See Python Capability Definitions for the same composition contract through kedi.Capability, and the adapter capability matrix for support checks.

items.title: CodeMode Sandbox and Recovery
items.text: CodeMode is bounded execution over hydrated tools, not general host Python. The model must discover a tool and request its schema before using it unless the application explicitly lists that exact exposed name in preload_tools. See Discovery and Execution for that protocol.

items.title: Supported Sandbox Subset
items.text:
The shared CodeMode instruction teaches the verified Monty subset:

  • scalar, list, tuple, dictionary, and string literals;
  • indexing and read-only slicing;
  • arithmetic, comparisons, boolean expressions, and f-strings;
  • if/elif/else, for, while, break, and continue;
  • range, enumerate, zip, comprehensions, sorting, filtering, grouping, joining, and aggregation;
  • small helper functions;
  • asyncio.gather for independent hydrated tool calls.

The pinned Monty 1.2 runtime supports both mapping[key] and mapping methods such as mapping.get(...).

CodeMode does not provide host filesystem, environment, process, unrestricted network, or third-party package access. Monty's eval and exec remain inside the same sandbox; they do not grant host access. Prefer direct expressions. Generators are not supported. This is not general CPython execution.

items.title: Lifecycle and Limits
items.text:
Every agent run receives an isolated catalog, hydration set, Monty process checkout, and variable state. Kedi closes the session and cancels active host callbacks on normal completion, errors, cancellation, and early close. After a worker crash or watchdog timeout, its session is discarded. A subsequent cell starts with empty variables. Cancellation also discards the interrupted session; it must not reuse partially executed state or automatically replay tools. Preloaded schemas count toward the same hydration set. Restarting Monty clears variables but preserves that run's hydrated allowlist; it never carries the allowlist into another run. Concurrent cells execute in order of lock acquisition. A cell with restart=True waits for the active cell to finish before discarding its sandbox variables.

The runtime bounds search pages, discovery payload bytes, hydrated tools, code characters, nested call count, nested concurrency, individual result bytes, aggregate result bytes, captured output, and execution time. Invalid cursors, unhydrated calls, non-JSON nested values, denials, and budget failures are model-correctable errors rather than silent fallbacks.

Setting Default Meaning default_search_limit 10 Tool names returned when search_tools omits limit. max_search_limit 50 Maximum accepted search page size. max_hydrated_tools 64 Exact schemas that may be hydrated in one run. max_discovery_result_bytes 256000 Serialized bound for search and schema results. max_code_chars 20000 Maximum source length for one snippet. max_nested_calls 64 Host tool calls allowed in one execution. max_concurrent_calls 8 Concurrent host tool calls allowed in one execution. max_tool_result_bytes 256000 Serialized bound for one nested result. max_total_tool_result_bytes 1000000 Aggregate nested-result bound per execution. max_print_bytes 256000 Captured standard-output bound. request_timeout 60 Worker-response watchdog in seconds; expiry discards the session. Host tool execution has separate application/run limits.

CodeMode telemetry records payload-free search tools, get tool schema, and execute code spans. It records counts, byte totals, restart state, duration, and outcome without recording query text, code, arguments, or tool results.

items.title: Recover Without Repeating Effects
items.text:
A Monty-language error returns captured output and an error separately. Variables assigned before the failure remain available for the next execute_code call. Inspect that checkpoint before repeating host calls; a write that completed before a later expression failed is still a real write.

restart=True resets sandbox variables, not external effects. Application-tool failures, policy denials, and execution-limit errors remain failed tool calls. Do not treat an empty printed output as evidence that nothing ran.

items.title: Different From an Artifact Query
items.text: execute_code consumes hydrated tools. run_artifact_code consumes values already stored as artifacts. Dynamic workflows consume child-agent functions. These contracts share a sandbox implementation but not the same capabilities.

items.title: CodeMode
items.text:
CodeMode lets a model discover tools and process intermediate results without putting each intermediate result in its conversation. Instead of sending every application tool schema to the model, Kedi exposes three stable control tools and keeps selected tool execution inside a bounded Monty sandbox.

This can reduce context traffic for large catalogs or multi-tool computations. It is not a universal cost or latency improvement: discovery adds calls, and a small shell-centric toolset may gain little. Choose it for the dataflow, not as a promise that every task becomes cheaper.

CodeMode is disabled by default and implemented for Pydantic AI, LangChain, Claude Agent SDK, and Codex App Server. All four adapters expose the same three controls and use the same catalog, Monty subset, limits, approval composition, and artifact boundary.

On a JSON-RPC bridge whose backend has a code mode of its own, such as fast-agent or pi, > codemode: enabled turns the backend's code mode on instead. Every tool call from its code still goes through Kedi's hooks, approval and budgets. CodeMode settings do not apply there.

items.title: Enable CodeMode
items.text:
Enable it in the current lexical scope:

> adapter: pydantic
> codemode: enabled

The directive is valid at top level, in a profile, and in a procedure. Disable an inherited or adapter-constructor policy with > codemode: disabled.

The expanded form enables CodeMode and configures its limits. enabled defaults to true when omitted:

> codemode:
    preload_tools:
        lookup_release
        list_versions
    default_search_limit: 10
    max_search_limit: 50
    max_hydrated_tools: 64
    max_nested_calls: 64
    max_concurrent_calls: 8
    max_tool_result_bytes: 256000
    max_total_tool_result_bytes: 1000000
    max_memory_bytes: 268435456
    max_feed_seconds: 60
    request_timeout: 60

> codemode: is Kedi-owned and is never forwarded as provider model configuration. > settings: does not accept a codemode field.

Every sandbox session has a 256 MiB memory ceiling and a 60-second execution ceiling per cell by default. max_memory_bytes and max_feed_seconds configure those limits; request_timeout independently bounds the sandbox request. Hitting a sandbox resource limit returns a script error; resetting the session starts with fresh state. Catching a host-side budget, Kedi execution, or result delivery error inside generated code cannot suppress that fatal error.

The equivalent Python API is available on every supported adapter:

from kedi.agent_adapter import PydanticAdapter

adapter = PydanticAdapter("openai:gpt-6-luna", codemode=True)

Use CodeModeSettings when Python should preload known tools:

from kedi import CodeModeSettings
from kedi.agent_adapter import PydanticAdapter

adapter = PydanticAdapter(
    "openai:gpt-6-luna",
    codemode=CodeModeSettings(preload_tools=("lookup_release",)),
)

items.title: Preload Known Tools
items.text:
preload_tools accepts one exact exposed tool name or an indented list. Kedi resolves the names and hydrates their schemas before the first model request, so generated code may call those tools without search_tools or get_tool_schema. Their schemas are included in the first CodeMode instruction. Preloading does not execute a tool or expose a result.

Resolution is atomic and run-local. Unknown or ambiguous names, duplicate catalog names, and max_hydrated_tools overflow fail before model I/O and leave no partial hydration. Aliased tools must be named by the alias exposed to the model. Preloaded tools count toward max_hydrated_tools and remain hydrated after execute_code(restart=True) resets sandbox variables.

Static lists with more than five unique names produce an LSP warning by default. VS Code users may change the lint-only kedi.codemode.preloadWarningThreshold setting; it does not change the runtime hydration limit.

items.title: Model-Facing Tools
items.text:
The model sees three CodeMode controls instead of the ordinary application tool schemas.

For a small executable fixture, configure a model through the CLI or embedding application and expose one read-only tool:

```
from kedi import tool

@tool(risk="read_only")
def load_counts() -> list[int]:
    """Return the counts from the local test fixture."""
    return [2, 3, 5]
```

> use: load_counts
> codemode: enabled
[answer] << Sum load_counts through CodeMode. Return only the total.
= <answer>

The expected total is 10. The controls below describe how a model reaches that result; enabling CodeMode does not itself execute the tool.

items.title: search_tools
items.text:
search_tools(
    *,
    query: str | None = None,
    limit: int | None = None,
    cursor: str | None = None,
)

The result contains only tool_names and next_cursor. Omitting query returns the next deterministic alphabetical page. Supplying a query performs a bounded name search; it does not return descriptions or schemas. The cursor is opaque and bound to the current catalog snapshot, query, page size, and offset. A changed tool catalog makes old cursors stale.

items.title: get_tool_schema
items.text:
get_tool_schema(*, tool_names: list[str])

Names must exactly match values returned by search_tools. The result includes the description, input JSON Schema, output schema when available, sequential constraint, and the callable name used by Monty. Successfully resolved tools are added to the current run's hydrated allowlist. Unknown, duplicate, or ambiguous names fail explicitly.

The callable name is the tool name made into a Python identifier: invalid characters become _, a leading digit gets a _ prefix, and a Python keyword or builtin name, or asyncio, gets a _ suffix. A tool named type is called as type_(...), and type(...) stays Python's builtin. Two tools that resolve to the same callable name are rejected when the catalog is built.

items.title: execute_code
items.text:
execute_code(*, code: str, restart: bool = False)

Only hydrated tools exist in the sandbox. Tool functions are async and accept keyword arguments. The following snippets illustrate code generated after the named tools have been registered, discovered, and hydrated; they are not host Python programs with built-in list_records or list_users functions:

records = await list_records(project="kedi")
active = [record for record in records if record["active"]]
len(active)

Independent calls may run concurrently:

import asyncio

users, projects = await asyncio.gather(
    list_users(team="runtime"),
    list_projects(owner="kedi-lang"),
)
{"users": len(users), "projects": len(projects)}

A tool call must be awaited, directly or through asyncio.gather. Kedi checks the snippet before running it: a call whose result is discarded or used without await (a bare statement, subscripted, iterated, tested, formatted, or passed to a builtin such as print) fails before any tool runs, with the corrected form:

Tool functions are async, and these calls are used without await: list_users on line 1. Write `result = await list_users(...)`, or pass the calls to `asyncio.gather(...)`. Nothing was executed.

Assigning a call, pending = list_users(team="runtime"), is allowed and is awaited later. If such a coroutine is then used without await, the sandbox error adds the same hint and names the tools that already ran in that snippet, so the model does not repeat them.

A sequential tool runs exclusively relative to the other nested calls in that snippet. Merely hydrating it does not serialize unrelated independent calls. restart=True resets variables in the current run's sandbox without affecting another run. Variables and successful tool results persist between execute_code calls in the same run; reuse them instead of repeating completed host calls.

When Monty code fails, execute_code returns the captured standard output and traceback message separately:

{
  "output": "loaded 3 rows",
  "error": "AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'"
}

output contains only text printed before the failure, while error contains only the sandbox error. For ordinary interpreter errors, variables assigned before the failure remain available to the next cell, so the model can inspect the checkpoint and continue without repeating successful host calls. Application-tool failures, approval denials, and Kedi execution limits remain failed tool calls rather than successful sandbox results.

A worker crash or watchdog timeout is different: Monty has lost that session. Kedi discards it, and the next cell starts with empty variables. Cancellation also discards the interrupted session. No completed host tool is automatically replayed.

items.title: Supported Sandbox Subset
items.text: CodeMode runs restricted Python in Monty, not CPython. See Sandbox and Recovery for supported constructs, unavailable host capabilities, and recovery rules.

items.title: Tool Semantics
items.text:
Nested calls use the adapter's fully assembled application tools through one Kedi-owned invocation bridge. Kedi therefore retains:

  • schema and callable validation;
  • argument_validator canonicalization;
  • static and dynamic risk resolution;
  • approval allow, deny, and edit behavior;
  • edit revalidation;
  • required_before_output tracking;
  • nested tool telemetry and cancellation;
  • sequential constraints and local MCP session ownership.

CodeMode requires Kedi-owned inline approval. A deferred decision cannot safely suspend and replay half of a snippet. Pydantic therefore rejects approval_resolution="external" while CodeMode is active; other adapters apply the same inline policy ownership to nested calls.

items.title: MCP Tools
items.text:
MCP support follows the adapter's interceptable local tool path:

Adapter CodeMode MCP behavior Pydantic AI Local MCPToolset tools join the catalog; provider-native MCP is rejected. LangChain MultiServerMCPClient tools join the catalog. Claude Agent SDK Kedi-declared stdio, SSE, and HTTP MCP tools are materialized locally and join the catalog. Codex App Server Kedi MCP declarations remain unsupported by the adapter.

Kedi preserves each exact exposed MCP tool name and schema. Duplicate names from multiple sources are configuration errors. A provider-native path is not accepted when it would let the model call an application tool outside execute_code.

Claude and Codex keep their harness-native filesystem, search, shell, and other control-plane tools available. Those controls are not application tools and do not enter the CodeMode catalog.

items.title: Artifact Boundary
items.text:
Tool results called inside Monty are not admitted to model history one by one. They remain bounded, JSON-compatible sandbox values while code filters, joins, or aggregates them. Only the final execute_code result passes through Kedi's normal artifact policy:

  • a compact derived result remains inline;
  • a large final result becomes an ArtifactRef;
  • oversized individual or aggregate nested results fail explicitly;
  • artifact-store read helpers are not exposed inside execute_code.

Use run_artifact_code when the source values are already artifact references. CodeMode and artifact code have separate responsibilities.

items.title: Lifecycle and Limits
items.text: Catalogs, hydration, and variable state are isolated per run. See Lifecycle and Limits for defaults, cleanup, and bounded resource behavior.

items.title: Native Pydantic Capability
items.text:
Use the public capability directly for a single native Pydantic run:

from kedi.agent_adapter import PydanticAdapter, PydanticCodeModeCapability

adapter = PydanticAdapter("openai:gpt-6-luna")
result = adapter.run_sync(
    "Use CodeMode for this task.",
    capabilities=[PydanticCodeModeCapability()],
)

The capability is outermost around the fully assembled Pydantic application toolset. It is a native Pydantic convenience; LangChain, Claude Agent SDK, and Codex use adapter projections over the same Kedi CodeMode core.

items.title: Dynamic Workflows
items.text:
run_workflow accepts only code. A child's optional final_schema belongs inside the generated code, on that child call. Missing code or extra outer arguments produce a correctable tool error before any child starts; they do not grant a new delegation attempt or bypass the existing run budgets.

Delegate mode lets the parent choose one child call at a time. Dynamic mode lets it write a bounded orchestration program over its declared children. This is useful for dependency graphs, concurrent independent work, and typed result composition; it does not grant access to arbitrary profiles.

items.title: Enable the Mode
items.text:
> profile: evidence:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > instructions: Assess the supplied evidence and return an integer count of failures.
    > output: int

> profile: explanation:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > instructions: Explain the supplied findings concisely.

> profile: coordinator:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > subagent: evidence
    > subagent: explanation
    > max_agents: 4
    > workflow: dynamic

Apply coordinator before a model invocation. It receives run_workflow(code) instead of the delegation/lifecycle tool set. At least one direct child is required. Each exposed child is an async, keyword-only function accepting task and optional final_schema.

A direct child may also come from a capability applied with > use:. With a deferred capability, the model loads that capability before the child becomes available to run_workflow; nested capabilities retain their individual load boundaries. A profile whose resolved contributions contain no child is rejected before inference.

items.title: Dependent Work
items.text:
This is model-generated Monty code, not a host Python script:

evidence_result = await evidence(task="Tests: parser passed; compiler failed.")
count = evidence_result["final_result"]
explanation_result = await explanation(
    task=f"Explain what {count} failing test suite means for release readiness."
)
{"failures": count, "explanation": explanation_result["task_summary"]}

Each child returns the same run_id, subagent, task_summary, and final_result envelope as delegate mode. A declared profile output type supplies the default schema. The workflow's last expression becomes its result; printed text is bounded diagnostic output, not an alternate structured return value.

items.title: Independent Work
items.text:
import asyncio

parser, compiler = await asyncio.gather(
    evidence(task="Parser tests: 12 passed, 0 failed."),
    evidence(task="Compiler tests: 10 passed, 2 failed."),
)
{"failures": parser["final_result"] + compiler["final_result"]}

asyncio.gather expresses concurrency, not unlimited capacity. All child starts still consume ancestor budgets and active slots. A plain await chain preserves dependencies. The outer run_workflow tool is sequential so separate workflow executions do not race the same parent orchestration state.

items.title: Sandbox and Recovery
items.text:
Monty is a restricted Python environment. It has no host filesystem, network, environment variables, credentials, runtime objects, processes, clocks, or arbitrary imports. Read returned dictionaries using result["key"]; do not assume the entire CPython standard library or mapping API is available.

Syntax and type checking happen before children start. Child failures become sanitized RuntimeError values that generated code may catch. Successful identical child calls can be reused from a bounded retry-salvage table when a workflow is corrected. This is recovery within the workflow machinery, not a global cache for every task with similar wording.

Budget exhaustion is terminal. Cancellation cancels and joins the workflow's owned children. Output is bounded and only JSON-safe values cross the boundary. Dynamic workflows cannot nest, although a child can use ordinary delegation within the existing limits.

items.title: Not CodeMode
items.text:
Dynamic workflow CodeMode Functions represent permitted child agents. Functions represent hydrated application tools. Each child has a conversation and profile. Each tool retains its schema, risk, and approval contract. Composes child results and dependencies. Filters/joins tool data before returning it to the model. Enabled with > workflow: dynamic in a profile. Enabled with > codemode: enabled.

Both use Monty; neither grants unrestricted host Python execution. See CodeMode and the reviewed workflow.

items.title: Agent Lifecycle Hooks
items.text: Hooks let application code observe or govern agent boundaries without moving that policy into model instructions. They are synchronous with the boundary: the run waits for each handler before it continues.

items.title: Events
items.text:
Event Boundary May edit May deny user_prompt_submit Immediately before the prompt enters the adapter yes yes pre_tool_use After argument canonicalization and before approval/execution yes yes post_tool_use After one successful tool execution no no post_tool_use_failure After one failed tool execution no no post_tool_result_failure After a returned body encounters result preparation or handoff failure no no

A denied prompt is never transported to the model. A denied tool call does not execute and does not produce a post-failure event. Denial is policy behavior, not a tool execution failure.

post_tool_use and post_tool_use_failure describe the body lifecycle. post_tool_result_failure is a separate result lifecycle event: a body that returned successfully is not relabeled as a failed execution when artifact admission, a post-success hook, or delivery subsequently fails.

items.title: Kedi Configuration
items.text:
Handlers are ordinary Python callables available to the Kedi environment:

```
from pathlib import Path

from kedi import PreToolUseDecision, UserPromptSubmitDecision

audit_events = []

def redact_prompt(event):
    return UserPromptSubmitDecision.edit(
        event.content.replace("customer@example.com", "[email]")
    )

def constrain_report_path(event):
    if event.tool_name != "write_report":
        return None
    path = Path(event.arguments["path"])
    return PreToolUseDecision.edit(
        {**event.arguments, "path": str(Path("reports") / path.name)}
    )

def observe_tool(event):
    audit_events.append((event.event, event.tool_name, event.tool_call_id))
```

> hooks:
    user_prompt_submit: `redact_prompt`
    pre_tool_use: `constrain_report_path`
    post_tool_use: `observe_tool`
    post_tool_use_failure: `observe_tool`
    post_tool_result_failure: `observe_tool`

A field may evaluate to one callable or a sequence of callables. Use the short form to control inherited lexical/profile handlers:

> hooks: disabled

disabled does not unregister handlers attached directly to an adapter instance. The expanded form enables the handlers it declares.

The directive is valid at top level, inside a procedure, and inside a profile. Top-level hooks are captured by following procedures according to normal source order.

items.title: Decisions
items.text:
Prompt handlers return None or UserPromptSubmitDecision:

from kedi import UserPromptSubmitDecision

UserPromptSubmitDecision.continue_()
UserPromptSubmitDecision.edit("replacement prompt")
UserPromptSubmitDecision.deny("prompt violates application policy")

Pre-tool handlers return None or PreToolUseDecision:

from kedi import PreToolUseDecision

PreToolUseDecision.continue_()
PreToolUseDecision.edit({"path": "reports/output.md"})
PreToolUseDecision.deny("writes are disabled in this run")

None means continue. Only edit may carry replacement content or arguments, and only deny may carry a denial reason. Invalid combinations fail before the boundary continues. Post-success and post-failure handlers are observers and must return None.

Edited tool arguments are revalidated before approval and execution. A handler cannot bypass a tool signature, argument validator, risk resolver, secret-file classification, or approval policy by editing the request.

items.title: Event Data
items.text:
Every event contains:

Field Meaning event Stable event name run_id Identity of the current agent run sequence Monotonic event sequence within that run adapter_shortname Active adapter parent_run_id Parent run for delegated work, when present agent_name Active agent identity, when present profile_name Active profile identity, when present

Tool events additionally contain tool_call_id, logical tool_name, optional native_tool_name, origin, immutable arguments, optional description, and immutable metadata. origin is one of kedi, mcp, adapter_native, or provider_builtin.

PostToolUseEvent.result contains the native successful result. PostToolUseFailureEvent contains error_type, error_message, the original exception when the adapter exposes it, duration_seconds when the execution boundary can measure it, and an interrupted flag for cancellation or process interruption. It is emitted only after tool execution starts; hook and approval denials are not tool-execution failures. Payload values are available to the handler but omitted from event representations and default telemetry.

PostToolResultFailureEvent.tool_call is a ToolCallRecord with tool_call_id, 1-based attempt, execution_state, result_state, failure_stage, and output_available. If the body returned, output retains the native body value, including a valid None. The record's representation does not print that payload. A result-stage failure does not automatically retry the body, even when the tool has retries configured. Kedi-managed tools provide this evidence; opaque provider-built-in tools may not.

items.title: Ordering and Errors
items.text:
Handlers execute serially in this order:

  1. adapter constructor hook_handler=;
  2. adapter event-specific handlers registered with adapter.on(...);
  3. lexical/profile handlers in merge and source order.

An edit becomes the input seen by the next handler. A denial short-circuits the remaining chain. A raised exception becomes HookExecutionError; cancellation propagates and drains the active handler. Sync boundaries accept sync handlers. Use an adapter's async API when a handler itself is async.

Hook dispatch is suspended while a handler runs. Agent work started by a hook does not recursively invoke the same active chain.

items.title: Python API
items.text:
Register one handler for one or several events:

import kedi

audit_events = []

@kedi.on(("post_tool_use", "post_tool_use_failure"))
def audit_terminal_event(event):
    audit_events.append((event.run_id, event.tool_call_id, event.event))

kedi.configure(), kedi.context(), @kedi.query, and @kedi.bind accept a hooks= mapping. Adapter instances expose @adapter.on(...), and supported adapter constructors accept one catch-all hook_handler= callable.

items.title: Profiles and Subagents
items.text:
Profile-local hooks belong to that profile. A child profile runs its own local handlers. Direct top-level/procedure hook directives and Python API registrations are enforcement policy and propagate to descendants. A parent's profile-local handler is not copied into an unrelated child profile.

Child events use the child run_id and identify the child agent/profile. parent_run_id links to a parent when a parent run context is available; it may be None without that context. Do not use its absence alone to classify a tool as a top-level call. Stream observation provides run lifecycle context for UIs that need a complete parent/child activity tree.

items.title: Persistence
items.text: Interactive session dumps never pickle hook handlers. Kedi records only an importable module and qualified name. A top-level function from an importable module can be restored; lambdas, local functions, closures, bound methods, and __main__ handlers make the dump fail explicitly. Nothing is silently omitted.

items.title: Adapter Support
items.text:
A handler execution failure is terminal, not a recoverable tool error asking the model to try again. Approval cancellation and run-budget exhaustion also stop the run. This differs from an intentional pre-tool denial, which can be returned to the model for recovery. On Claude, fatal hook failures request a native SDK stop and are re-raised with their original error when control returns to Kedi; they are not reduced to a tool-denial message.

Adapter Prompt Pre tool Post tool Tool failure Result failure Tool origins Pydantic AI yes yes yes yes yes Kedi, MCP, adapter-native LangChain yes yes yes yes yes Kedi, MCP, adapter-native Claude Agent SDK yes yes yes yes yes Kedi, MCP, provider built-ins Codex App Server yes yes yes yes yes Kedi projected tools WebGPU yes yes yes yes yes Kedi, MCP ACP yes no no no no none A2A yes no no no no none

"Tool failure" is post_tool_use_failure (a tool body that raised after execution started); "Result failure" is post_tool_result_failure (a failure after the tool body returned, for example artifact admission or a post-success hook). Both are declared in every full adapter's HookCapabilities; ACP and A2A declare prompt-only capabilities.

Kedi validates support per event. A configuration that requests an unsupported event fails before model transport and is reported by the LSP. Dynamic adapter selection defers that check to runtime.

items.title: Security and Telemetry
items.text:
For CodeMode, a result record's destination is sandbox. handed_off is recorded only after the sandbox execution accepts the result. If execution fails and individual receipt cannot be established, delivery remains unknown. A successful tool body whose output fails serialization or size validation produces a post_tool_result_failure event and a terminal error retaining the native output; it is not converted into a model request to repeat that tool.

Hooks execute trusted Python and can inspect prompt, argument, result, and error payloads. Keep audit sinks bounded and redact before forwarding data to another system. A post hook cannot undo an effect that already succeeded.

The in-memory lists above are small examples, not durable audit logs. A failing post hook may make the run fail after the tool has already performed its effect; re-running that tool can duplicate the effect. Keep policy in pre-hooks and approval, and use Stream Events for non-blocking UI progress.

Kedi emits one telemetry span for a nonempty hook chain and records event name, handler count, adapter, origin, outcome, edit/deny status, duration, failures, and timeouts. Prompt text, arguments, tool result, error message, metadata, and handler return values are not captured by default.

items.title: Instructions and Settings
items.text:
Use > instructions: for scoped agent instructions. The old spelling > system: is no longer accepted and produces a parse error. Replace the name without changing the body; lexical scope and override rules stay the same. Python's system= configuration parameter is unchanged.

Instructions define agent behavior; settings define adapter/model mechanics. Both are lexical and apply to following calls.

Instructions express desired behavior; they are not permissions or enforced invariants. Use typed captures for output validation, tool schemas for argument contracts, and approvals for effectful operations. Asking a model to "never write outside reports" does not replace a path check.

items.title: Single-Line Instructions
items.text:
> instructions: Answer with evidence from available tools.

Use a single line for one stable rule. It is rendered when active state is materialized.

items.title: Multiline Instructions
items.text:
[audience] = maintainers

> instructions:
    Act as a release engineer for <audience>.
    Inspect evidence before reaching a conclusion.
    Report uncertainty explicitly.

Continuation lines are newline-joined. Multiline instruction bodies are read-only templates: literal text, <name> substitutions, and inline Python substitutions are allowed. Output fields and procedure calls are not.

A later > instructions: replaces the previous instruction value; it does not append another paragraph. Compute one combined instruction explicitly when both parts must survive. Profile composition uses the same rule.

For named reusable instruction contributions, use capabilities. They append without changing profile override semantics. A later explicit > instructions: clears those contributions as well, including when the replacement text is identical. Runtime-owned instruction sections are not removed.

> instructions:
    Current audience: <audience>.

An instruction cannot declare [output] or call <helper()>; compute that value before the directive and substitute the resulting variable. Use <``> when the instruction itself must mention a literal triple-backtick fence.

items.title: Runtime Instruction Sections
items.text:
Kedi keeps scoped user instructions separate from its runtime rules. For an LLM template with output captures, the runtime adds a <TemplateInstructions> section to the request's instructions. The user message contains the field list and the rendered template, without repeating the completion rules in its prefix or in conversation history.

Profiles with tools, MCP, or enabled skills also receive a separate <ToolCallInstructions> section. It covers evidence, explicit tool requirements, permissions, and untrusted retrieved content. It does not prescribe a tool-use strategy or require a lookup for every answer. The two sections are siblings, not nested, and neither replaces the active > instructions: value.

When enabled, artifact and skill guidance use sibling <ArtifactInstructions> and <SkillInstructions> sections. Built-in instruction XML tags, including their internal headings, consistently use PascalCase. These headings do not rename tool parameters, output fields, or serialized protocol data.

Raw invokes and claims do not receive template-completion rules. Jev and Laya keep their decision-specific prompt semantics rather than sentence-completion instructions. Runtime sections are assembled for the current call, not appended to the stored user conversation on each turn.

These section names are internal prompt formatting, not Kedi syntax or security boundaries. Typed validation and approval policies remain responsible for enforcing contracts; provider caching still depends on the model and transport.

items.title: Settings Blocks
items.text:
> settings:
    temperature: 0.2
    max_tokens: 1024
    parallel_tool_calls: false

Each setting has a value contract: booleans use lowercase true/false, numeric fields accept numeric values, and option fields use their documented choices. There is no generic null/none reset literal. Omitted settings retain their default or inherited value; tool_choice: none is a documented string option, not Python None. Containers and computed values require backticks.

Use backticks for explicit Python objects:

> settings:
    stop_sequences: `["END", "DONE"]`
    extra_body: `{"mode": "json"}`
    parallel_tool_calls: `False`

Backticks are necessary for computed values and remove ambiguity about list, dict, or object identity.

items.title: Merge and Filtering
items.text:
Settings merge by key. A later value replaces the same earlier key while unmentioned keys remain:

> settings:
    temperature: 0.2
    timeout: 30

@patient_call() -> str:
  > settings:
      timeout: 120
  >> The completed task's result is [answer: str].
  = <answer>

The inner call retains temperature: 0.2 and uses timeout: 120.

Kedi validates setting names against its known public setting inventory, then filters the merged mapping at the adapter boundary. Pydantic receives supported ModelSettings; LangChain receives its chat-model fields; harnesses receive their own process/runtime settings.

items.title: Common Framework Settings
items.text:
Common fields include temperature, max_tokens, timeout, top_p, parallel_tool_calls, tool_choice, retry controls, stop sequences, and provider extension bodies. Exact support still depends on the active adapter and model provider.

Do not copy a provider-specific setting into every profile. Keep it in the profile that owns that backend.

Pydantic AI and LangChain also support request_retries (a non-negative integer, default 2) for transient HTTP 408, 429, and 5xx model-request failures. It is a Kedi policy, not a provider model parameter:

> settings:
    request_retries: 1

Retries preserve history and completed tool results, remain inside the same budget and deadline, and are independent of output/tool corrections. With fallback models, each candidate gets this bounded retry policy. 0 disables same-model retries, not explicit fallback. Provider SDK retries are separate and must be disabled for strict request budgets; Kedi does not mutate user SDK clients to do so.

items.title: Harness Settings
items.text:
ACP accepts cwd, env, and timeout. Codex accepts fields including cwd, sandbox, approval_policy, config, model_provider, service_tier, and timeout. Claude accepts fields including cwd, env, tools, allowed_tools, disallowed_tools, permission_mode, max_turns, and max_budget_usd.

> agent: acp:
    command: npx @zed-industries/codex-acp
> settings:
    cwd: /workspace/project
    env: `{"LOG_LEVEL": "INFO"}`
    timeout: 120

cwd is passed to ACP, Codex, and Claude where supported. Relative child-agent working directories are constrained by their parent safety boundary.

Claude appends > instructions: content to its Claude Code preset, preserving built-in file behavior. Non-interactive Claude defaults to permission_mode: acceptEdits; set tool and permission fields explicitly to narrow it. Codex defaults to workspace-write unless settings narrow or replace its sandbox.

items.title: Settings Inventory
items.text:
Kedi knows the keys below in > settings: (see MODEL_SETTING_KEYS in src/kedi/agent_profile/settings.py). Any other name belongs to the adapter: one that declares it takes it (a package adapter in capabilities.settings, a JSON-RPC bridge in its handshake's settings), and any other adapter refuses it before the first model request. Where no package adapter or bridge can be selected (the module imports no package and has no > agent: rpc:), the parser warns about such a name with K-SETTING-KEY. "Accepted by" names the adapters whose boundary forwards the key; a key can still be filtered out for a given provider or model. Value contracts come from the shared directive-value registry (src/kedi/directive_values.py) where one exists.

Key Value contract Accepted by allowed_tools Backtick Python list or mapping Claude api_key Text value LangChain approval_policy No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter Codex base_url Text value LangChain callbacks Backtick Python object LangChain config Backtick Python list or mapping Codex configurable_fields No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter LangChain configurable_prefix No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter LangChain context_limit Model context window in tokens for Kedi's request ceiling Kedi runtime cwd Path string Claude, Codex, ACP decision_boolean_threshold Numeric value Pydantic AI, LangChain decision_tool_call_threshold Numeric value Pydantic AI, LangChain disable_streaming Disable streaming globally or during tool calls: true/false or tool_calling LangChain disallowed_tools Backtick Python list or mapping Claude env Backtick Python list or mapping Claude, ACP extra_body Backtick Python list or mapping Pydantic AI, LangChain extra_headers Backtick Python list or mapping Pydantic AI, LangChain fallback_model Text value Claude frequency_penalty Numeric value Pydantic AI, LangChain logit_bias Backtick Python list or mapping Pydantic AI, LangChain max_budget_usd No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter Claude max_retries Nonnegative integer LangChain max_tokens Integer value Pydantic AI, LangChain max_turns Integer value Claude media_limit Largest media value sent to the model (byte size, e.g. 100kb) Kedi runtime metadata Backtick Python list or mapping LangChain model_kwargs Backtick Python list or mapping LangChain model_provider Text value Codex organization Text value LangChain parallel_tool_calls Boolean: true/false Pydantic AI, LangChain permission_mode Text value Claude personality Text value Codex presence_penalty Numeric value Pydantic AI, LangChain rate_limiter Backtick Python object LangChain reasoning No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter LangChain reasoning_effort Text value LangChain request_retries Additional attempts for transient model request errors Kedi runtime response_cache Boolean: true/false Pydantic AI, LangChain response_cache_ttl Positive integer Pydantic AI, LangChain sandbox Filesystem sandbox policy: read-only, workspace-write, danger-full-access Codex seed Integer value Pydantic AI, LangChain service_tier Provider service tier: auto, default, flex, priority Pydantic AI, Codex stop No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter LangChain stop_sequences Backtick Python list or mapping Pydantic AI, LangChain stream_usage Boolean: true/false LangChain streaming Boolean: true/false LangChain summary Text value Codex tags Backtick Python list or mapping LangChain temperature Numeric value Pydantic AI, LangChain thinking Thinking budget: true/false or minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh Pydantic AI timeout No DSL value rule; validated by the selected adapter Pydantic AI, LangChain, Codex, ACP tool_choice Tool selection policy: none, auto, required Pydantic AI, LangChain tool_reason Activation: enabled/disabled, or a backtick expression returning bool Kedi runtime tools Backtick Python list or mapping Claude top_p Numeric value Pydantic AI, LangChain voice Voice name for speech output ([x: Audio] <<) Kedi runtime

items.title: Unknown and Inapplicable Settings
items.text:
Unknown setting names are parser/LSP errors. A known union-level key can still be irrelevant to a selected backend and is filtered rather than passed blindly. Adapter docs list the exact mapping.

Prefer a minimal settings block. Every additional provider knob is part of the profile's operational contract and should have a tested reason.

Conversation history and compaction are intentionally not model settings. Use > history: enabled for stateful calls or the expanded history policy described in Caching and Conversation History.

items.title: MCP Servers
items.text:
> mcp: attaches one Model Context Protocol server to the active agent state. The selected adapter translates the normalized specification into its MCP client/toolset surface.

MCP supplies tools, not a new model or a child-agent conversation. A connected server's tools still need an adapter that can expose them and an approval policy that permits their effects. The commands and example.com URLs below illustrate configuration shapes; they are not bundled Kedi services.

items.title: Stdio Transport
items.text:
> mcp:
    transport: stdio
    command: uv
    args: `["run", "project-mcp"]`
    env: `{"LOG_LEVEL": "WARNING"}`

stdio requires command. args must be a list or tuple of strings; env must be a dictionary whose keys and values are strings.

When command is present and transport is omitted, Kedi infers stdio:

> mcp:
    command: project-mcp

The process inherits adapter/runtime environment according to that adapter; the directive's env supplies explicit server variables.

items.title: Streamable HTTP
items.text:
```
import os
token = os.environ["PROJECT_MCP_TOKEN"]
```

> mcp:
    transport: streamable-http
    url: https://tools.example.com/mcp
    headers: `{"Authorization": "Bearer " + token}`

http is an alias for streamable-http. Both normalize to the same transport contract and require url. headers must be a string dictionary.

Do not hard-code production tokens in .kedi source. Read them from a trusted runtime environment and avoid rendering them into prompts or logs.

items.title: SSE
items.text:
> mcp:
    transport: sse
    url: https://tools.example.com/events
    headers: `{"X-Tenant": "example-team"}`

SSE also requires url and supports string headers. It remains a separate transport from streamable HTTP.

items.title: Dynamic Fields
items.text:
String fields can be plain Kedi strings or Python expressions:

```
import os
```

> mcp:
    transport: `os.getenv("MCP_TRANSPORT", "stdio")`
    command: `os.getenv("MCP_COMMAND", "project-mcp")`
    url: `os.getenv("MCP_URL")`

Use dynamic transport only when deployment configuration truly selects among valid shapes. Kedi validates the evaluated specification: stdio cannot omit a command, HTTP/SSE cannot omit a URL, and collection element types must be strings.

Transport normalization removes irrelevant fields. A stdio spec does not carry URL/headers; a remote spec does not carry command/args/env.

items.title: Scoping and Profiles
items.text:
MCP follows agent-state scope:

  • a top-level server is captured by following procedures;
  • a profile member is attached when that profile is applied;
  • a procedure-body directive affects following calls in that invocation;
  • leaving an inner scope restores the outer server list.

MCP server lists append in declaration/merge order. Applying another profile does not erase existing servers unless a separate API creates a new outer configuration.

items.title: Adapter Support
items.text:
Pydantic and LangChain map specs through their MCP integrations. Harness and provider support varies.

The LSP emits capability diagnostics when the selected adapter cannot attach MCP tools. Treat that as an unmet profile contract. Kedi does not emulate an MCP server by inserting tool descriptions into prompt text.

items.title: Failure Behavior
items.text: Invalid transport names, wrong collection types, missing required fields, connection failures, protocol errors, and missing optional adapter packages surface explicitly. Server lifecycle is adapter-owned; consult the adapter page for startup, cleanup, and concurrency behavior.

items.title: Permission Boundary
items.text:
Do not assume a remote server's self-description makes its tools harmless. Kedi's local MCP integration uses its approval boundary; the optional tool reason is projected locally and removed before the server call. CodeMode can include MCP only where the adapter can materialize and intercept the local tool path. Provider-hosted MCP that bypasses this path has a different contract; see CodeMode MCP.

Keep server credentials in configuration, not in the task text. Tool output from a server is data, not authorization to enable additional capabilities.

items.title: Models and Reasoning
items.text: Model, fallback, and reasoning directives refine the active backend. They do not select a framework or harness by themselves.

items.title: Select a Model
items.text:
> adapter: pydantic
> model: openai:gpt-6-luna

The model identifier is passed to the selected adapter. Its accepted syntax, availability, credentials, and provider prefix therefore depend on that adapter.

A model directive applies to following calls in the current lexical scope:

> model: fast-model

@draft(topic: str) -> str:
  >> A draft about <topic> is [text: str].
  = <text>

> model: quality-model

@review(text: str) -> str:
  >> Review feedback for <text> is [feedback: str].
  = <feedback>

Each procedure captures the top-level state present when it is defined.

items.title: Dynamic Model Expressions
items.text:
```
selected_model = "openai:gpt-6-luna"
```

> model: `selected_model`

The expression must return a string. Prefer literal models or profiles so the LSP can reason about adapter capability and configuration.

items.title: Ordered Fallback Models
items.text:
Pydantic AI and LangChain support alternatives to the effective primary model:

> adapter: pydantic
> model: openai:gpt-6-luna
> fallback: openai:gpt-6.1-sol

>> The capital of Turkey is [capital: str].
= <capital>

Replace the inline declaration with a block for ordered alternatives:

> fallback:
    openai:gpt-6.1-sol
    openai:gpt-6-luna

Entries are model IDs, not profiles or adapters. Whole backtick expressions may return a nonempty model ID or a list/tuple of nonempty IDs, including within a block. Values are validated before model I/O, not coerced from arbitrary objects. The same forms work with > adapter: langchain; harness adapters reject them. Fallback is caller-owned model selection, so it is not a capability member.

items.title: Scope and Inheritance
items.text:
> fallback: is independent of > model:. The primary can come from an enclosing scope, an applied profile, Python, or the environment; a model directive need not immediately precede it. A fallback-only profile is valid:

> adapter: pydantic
> model: openai:gpt-6-luna

> profile: resilient:
    > fallback: openai:gpt-6.1-sol

> use: resilient

@capital() -> str:
    >> The capital of Turkey is [city: str].
    = <city>

> fallback: `[]`
= <capital()>

capital keeps the chain captured at its definition site even though the caller clears its own list. A local declaration likewise leaves the caller unchanged. Each declaration replaces the list, never appends; changing > model: replaces only the primary. Conditional profile members and subagent profiles follow the same rules. Omission inherits; > fallback: `[]` explicitly clears the chain. none is not a reset literal. A primary must resolve before invocation: the first backup is never an implicit primary.

items.title: Recovery Boundaries
items.text:
Each candidate first uses request_retries for HTTP 408, 429, and 5xx failures (two additional attempts by default), then advances to the next eligible candidate. request_retries: 0 disables same-model retries, not explicit fallback. Retry-After is honored; a delay beyond the bounded retry policy can skip further requests to that candidate without preventing another configured candidate. Authentication errors, refusals, argument/output validation failures, tool-body errors, budget exhaustion, cancellation, and deadline expiry never trigger fallback. Exhaustion raises a terminal failure with attempt context.

All attempts share admission, request and usage limits, and the enclosing deadline. Selecting a backup does not restart the template, agent, or child, consume another child-start slot, or replay completed tools and approvals. Only stream-opening failures before any response content reaches the caller can recover; partially delivered output is never replayed or combined across models.

Model changes preserve portable history and tool results, not incompatible response IDs, server conversation IDs, or cache settings. History-processor continuation resets stay in effect. Incompatible required server state or output/tool/media/settings contracts fail instead of being silently discarded. One invocation's selection does not change another's primary.

For Python constructor and SDK retry controls, see Pydantic AI and LangChain.

items.title: Reasoning Effort
items.text:
Accepted values are:

  • minimal
  • low
  • medium
  • high
  • xhigh
  • max
> effort: high

A backtick expression may choose the value dynamically:

> effort: `"high" if args.deep else "low"`

Not every provider implements every effort level. Pydantic maps max to xhigh; harness adapters map or validate according to their runtime.

items.title: Inheritance and Overrides
items.text:
An inner scope inherits the outer model and effort until it replaces either:

> model: default-model
> effort: low

@deep_review(text: str) -> str:
  > effort: high
  >> A detailed review of <text> is [result: str].
  = <result>

The effort override does not discard the inherited model, tools, MCP servers, or instructions. Applying a profile merges its specified members; omitted members continue to inherit.

items.title: Choosing Effort
items.text: Use low effort for extraction, formatting, classification, and routine tool selection. Use higher effort for ambiguous planning, multi-source synthesis, or code reasoning where additional latency and cost are justified. Do not use effort as compensation for vague instructions or an oversized tool surface.

items.title: Errors
items.text: Kedi reports an invalid effort value before execution. Unknown or unavailable model identifiers, missing credentials, and unsupported model settings are reported by the selected adapter/provider. A profile that requires a model override fails if its adapter cannot construct one.

items.title: Profiles
items.text:
Profiles can also select a lexical native history processor through > history: with enabled: true and processor: `callback`. This overrides the adapter constructor default only for the scoped invocation. See History Processing for callback types, explicit disable, safe group retention, and lineage.

Profiles are named, reusable agent configuration. A profile describes how a model call should run: its backend, instructions, tools, permissions, and optional children. Defining or applying a profile does not start a model call, create a conversation, or run its tools.

A procedure describes executable steps; a profile supplies configuration to those steps. A child profile describes a separate agent invocation that a parent may request. These are different roles even when they share the same tools.

Capabilities are the separate additive surface for reusable tool and instruction bundles. A profile may use them with > use: without changing its own override semantics.

items.title: Define a Profile
items.text:
> profile: reviewer:
    ###
    Reviews one change against repository evidence.
    ###
    > adapter: pydantic
    > model: openai:gpt-6-luna
    > effort: medium
    > instructions: Cite the evidence used for every finding.
    > settings:
        timeout: 120

A profile body contains directives, not an executable procedure body:

Concern Members Meaning Backend adapter, agent, model, fallback, effort Select execution backend, primary model, ordered alternatives, and reasoning behavior. Instructions instructions, settings Supply instructions and supported runtime/model settings. Tools use, mcp, skills Expose procedures, external tools, and skill discovery. Permissions and lifecycle approval, hooks Mediate sensitive calls and lifecycle boundaries. Context history, artifacts Configure conversation retention and artifact handling. Tool execution codemode Enable the code-based tool interface. Child agents subagent, max_agents, workflow, output Define delegation, its budget, orchestration mode, and a default child result type.

Choose either adapter or agent on one selected profile path, not both. Profiles are top-level declarations. Tools referenced by the profile must exist; declaring their names does not implement them.

items.title: Conditional Configuration
items.text:
Group related settings under a deterministic condition instead of repeating the same expression in each field:

[detailed_review: bool] = `True`

> profile: reviewer:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > if: `detailed_review`:
        > model: openai:gpt-6.1-sol
        > effort: high
        > instructions: Explain each finding using repository evidence.
    > else:
        > model: openai:gpt-6-luna
        > effort: medium
        > instructions: Return only actionable findings supported by evidence.

> use: reviewer

The guard must return an exact Python bool. It runs once when the profile is applied, in the same environment as its computed fields. Unselected expressions and uses do not run. The selected members contribute to the profile in source order; later members can override them. Without > else:, a false condition adds nothing. Guards can nest and selected branches may contain > use:.

This is configuration selection, not an executable body: templates, calls, returns, and model-evaluated claims are not allowed as members or guards. The closing colon after the Python expression is required. Both branches are checked for valid members. A selected path cannot contain both agent and adapter, or multiple output or workflow members in one profile. A dynamic workflow must have a child after its selected configuration has merged.

When applied before a procedure definition, the selected configuration is captured there; changing the guard's inputs later does not rewrite the captured profile. Editor analysis does not execute guards. Runtime validates selections it cannot prove statically.

items.title: Profile Documentation
items.text:
When a ### block is the first profile member, it becomes the profile docstring. The LSP shows it in hover and subagent tool descriptions. A later block remains an ordinary comment.

Document what task the profile owns, what evidence it should return, and any important limitation. Child-agent descriptions depend on this text.

items.title: Apply a Profile
items.text:
Single-line > use: applies a profile when no procedure with that name exists:

> use: reviewer

>> A review of the current change is [review: str].
= <review>

If a procedure and profile share a name, the procedure wins and is registered as a tool. Avoid such collisions.

items.title: Merge Rules
items.text:
Applying a profile merges it into the state already active at that location. It is not a reset to an empty configuration:

Member Composition rule Backend, model, effort, instructions, approval, output type, maximum starts, workflow mode A specified value replaces the earlier value. Instructions are replaced, not concatenated. Fallback models Replace the entire ordered list; omission inherits, and > fallback: `[]` clears it. A model override alone does not clear it. Settings Merge by key; later values replace the same key. Nested dictionaries are not recursively merged. Tools and children Merge by name. Later bindings win, and reintroduced names move to the end of the ordered list. MCP servers Append in declaration/application order. Hooks Compose per event; a supplied empty handler list clears that event's local handlers. Inherited enforcement is a separate boundary. Skills, CodeMode, history/compaction Supplied configuration replaces the corresponding earlier configuration. Artifacts Overlay the explicitly supplied policy fields. Omitted members Keep their earlier values.

These are ordinary profile merge rules. Capability-owned resources are stricter: conflicting concrete bindings or approval policies fail instead of transferring ownership to a later same-named tool. An explicit instruction replacement also clears preceding capability guidance, without removing its tools or policies.

An empty tools list is not a request to revoke tools inherited through profile composition. For a separate restricted agent, define a child with its own tool surface and use delegation. See Hooks for inherited handlers that child code cannot disable.

Direct directives after profile application can override profile members:

> use: reviewer
> effort: high

The result retains the reviewer's configuration and changes effort to high. The selected provider must support that effort value.

Profile application and direct directives follow source order. A direct directive does not have unconditional priority: a profile applied after it can replace it. Procedures capture the configuration at their definition site; see Scoping and Capabilities.

> fallback: may be the only model-selection member in a profile. It uses the effective inherited primary and needs no adjacent > model:. The primary must resolve before invocation; a backup is never promoted implicitly. Procedures, conditional members, and subagent profiles retain normal lexical capture rules; local list replacement leaves the caller unchanged. Fallback is supported by Pydantic AI and LangChain, not harness adapters or capability bundles. See Ordered Fallback Models.

items.title: Default Child Result Type
items.text:
~Finding(path: str, explanation: str)

> profile: reviewer:
    ###
    Reviews supplied evidence and returns actionable findings.
    ###
    > adapter: pydantic
    > model: openai:gpt-6-luna
    > instructions: Base findings only on the evidence supplied in the task.
    > output: list[Finding]

When a parent delegates to reviewer without supplying final_schema, this output type supplies the child's result schema. The returned envelope contains run_id, subagent, task_summary, and the validated final_result. An explicit final_schema on the child call takes precedence over > output:. Without either schema, the child returns its text in task_summary and has no structured result.

This is a child-result contract, not a way to change the types of unrelated template captures. A template's [finding: Finding] still declares its own output type. The profile type must be representable as JSON Schema; declaring two output members is an error.

items.title: Export and Import Profiles
items.text:
Profiles are module values and can be explicitly exported:

> profile: reviewer:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > model: openai:gpt-6-luna

> export:
  reviewer

Imported profiles retain private tool and child-profile bindings needed by their contract without flattening those dependencies into the importer's procedure namespace. This lets a package expose a profile facade while keeping helpers private.

items.title: Forward References and Validation
items.text:
A profile can name a child profile declared later. Kedi resolves the complete profile graph and rejects unknown children and cycles.

On one selected profile path, framework and harness selection remain mutually exclusive. Invalid backend kinds, unknown members, duplicate output/workflow declarations, invalid settings, nonpositive max_agents, missing tools, and unsupported required capabilities produce diagnostics or compile-time errors.

items.title: Child Profiles
items.text:
> profile: coordinator:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > subagent: researcher
    > max_agents: 3
    > workflow: dynamic

> profile: researcher:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > instructions: Investigate one self-contained question.

Only directly listed children can be delegated to. max_agents bounds the descendant work started by one parent invocation. Workflow mode defaults to delegate; dynamic exposes one sandboxed Python orchestration tool. See Subagents for lifecycle and safety rules.

items.title: Choosing Profile Boundaries
items.text: Create a profile when a task needs a stable combination of behavior and capabilities. Do not create one merely to alias a model string. Profiles should be narrow enough that their tools, approvals, and child relationships can be reviewed as a coherent security boundary.

items.title: Reviewed Evidence Workflow
items.text:
This example connects the whole boundary: a parent delegates, a child reads a local fixture, the child returns a typed result, and the parent writes a report through an approval handler. The parent cannot read the fixture directly; the child cannot write the report.

Download both files into one directory: reviewed_evidence.kedi and reviewed_evidence.py.

items.title: The Kedi Program
items.text:
~Review(failures: list[str], may_release: bool)

> profile: reviewer:
    ###
    Read the named test suite and report failures without inventing results.
    ###
    > adapter: pydantic
    > use: read_evidence
    > output: Review
    > instructions:
        Read evidence for the requested suite.
        Release only if no tests failed.

> profile: coordinator:
    > adapter: pydantic
    > subagent: reviewer
    > max_agents: 2
    > use: write_report
    > approval: `approve_report`
    > instructions:
        Delegate the review and use its validated result.
        Write failure names and the release decision to requested.txt.
        Use write_report and return the actual saved path.
        Never treat missing evidence as success.

> use: coordinator
[receipt] << Review suite parser and save its report.
= <receipt>

The Python companion supplies all three referenced callables through runtime_globals. There are no hidden network tools: read_evidence returns 12 passing tests and one failure named unicode_identifier from a local fixture.

items.title: Host Responsibilities
items.text:
run_review(adapter, output_dir) builds the runtime and closes it in finally. Its child tool calls current_subagent_execution() to record the child run, profile, and conversation identity. It raises if invoked outside a child.

The report approval handler accepts only write_report and replaces its path with the application's fixed output_dir/review.txt. The writer independently checks that destination before performing I/O. Kedi revalidates edited arguments before calling it. The original model-provided path is never the write target.

The function returns the model's receipt plus native observations, approval requests, and actual writes. These make the effect inspectable without treating the final model sentence as proof that it happened.

items.title: Run With a Provider
items.text:
Install Kedi with its Pydantic provider support and configure the provider's credentials. From the directory containing the two downloaded files:

from kedi.agent_adapter import PydanticAdapter
from reviewed_evidence import run_review

result = run_review(
    PydanticAdapter("openai:gpt-6-luna"),
    output_dir="reports",
)
print(result["receipt"])
print(result["writes"])

This makes real model calls. Tool selection and prose can vary. Expected behavior is a report that names unicode_identifier and does not approve release. An empty writes list is not success, regardless of what the model claims.

items.title: Deterministic Verification
items.text:
The documentation tests run these exact files with a local Pydantic FunctionModel. They assert the parent delegates, the child's tools exclude the writer, the parent's tools exclude the reader, the returned child schema is used, run IDs agree with the child tool's context, and the parent consumes that result before writing. They also check that approval changes the destination without changing the report text.

This establishes the program/runtime contract, not a model-accuracy result. Separate negative tests exercise unavailable children, invalid results, denied writes, and lifecycle failures. No external model or credentials are needed for the deterministic test suite.

items.title: Adapter Boundary
items.text: The downloadable program selects Pydantic explicitly. To use LangChain, change both profile declarations to > adapter: langchain and supply a configured LangChainAdapter to the same embedding function. The tools, approval handler, child result envelope, and limits remain Kedi contracts; do not retain an explicit Pydantic profile and assume that injecting a different adapter changes its backend selection. The deterministic tutorial checks use Pydantic, while the shared adapter regression suite covers the corresponding LangChain surfaces.

items.title: Dynamic Variant
items.text:
Add > workflow: dynamic to the coordinator. Its child call then happens inside run_workflow, for example:

review = await reviewer(task="Inspect suite parser using read_evidence.")
review["final_result"]

The parent receives this structured workflow result and still calls its approved writer afterward. Do not move writing into the Monty snippet: only declared child functions exist there. The test suite runs both variants.

items.title: Agent Scope and Adapter Requirements
items.text:
Agent state follows lexical source scope. Capability metadata determines whether the selected adapter can honor the resulting contract.

Adapter capability metadata describes backend support. It is distinct from composable capabilities, the > capability: language surface for reusable instructions and owned tools.

items.title: Lexical Agent State
items.text:
> adapter: pydantic
> model: default-model

@quick(text: str) -> str:
  > effort: low
  >> A summary of <text> is [summary: str].
  = <summary>

The effort override exists only inside quick; the outer adapter and model are inherited. On return, the prior state is restored.

items.title: Top-Level Capture
items.text:
Top-level directives are captured by procedures declared after them. A later top-level change does not retroactively change a previously declared procedure:

> model: first-model

@first() -> str:
  >> A brief answer is [answer: str].
  = <answer>

> model: second-model

@second() -> str:
  >> A brief answer is [answer: str].
  = <answer>

This source-order rule also applies to tools, MCP, instructions, and profiles.

items.title: Precedence
items.text:
Start with the configured defaults and the captured lexical state. Then apply profile applications and direct directives in source order in the current scope. They are not separate priority tiers:

> profile: concise:
    > instructions: Return one sentence.

> instructions: Return a paragraph.
> use: concise

Here the profile's one-sentence instruction wins because the profile is applied last. Reversing those last two statements makes the paragraph instruction win. Collection members follow the profile merge rules.

Calling a previously defined procedure does not recapture the caller's model or tools. To make a procedure use different configuration, declare the override in its body or define it under that configuration.

items.title: Tool Frames
items.text:
Tool registration is block-scoped. Inner registrations can shadow an outer tool with the same name; leaving the block restores the previous binding. A procedure tool receives its schema from that procedure's signature and docstring.

The same profile used in two scopes does not make mutable tool state global. Each invocation materializes its active tool surface.

items.title: Configuration Scope and Value Scope
items.text:
Agent configuration and variable bindings are related but separate. An if or loop body has its own scope: newly initialized local values do not leak to the outer environment. Mutation of an existing outer binding follows the language's assignment rules; changing a model directive does not change those rules.

Likewise, a procedure captures agent configuration at definition time, not a promise that all referenced mutable Python objects are deep-copied. Child-agent conversation isolation does not sandbox arbitrary shared host objects. See Outputs and Assignment for binding semantics and Subagent Isolation for the child boundary.

items.title: Capability Metadata
items.text:
Adapters advertise kind and capabilities such as:

  • structured outputs;
  • dynamic Kedi/Python tools;
  • MCP servers;
  • skills;
  • subagent foreground or background execution;
  • approval mediation.
  • event-specific lifecycle hooks.

The parser and LSP combine literal backend selection with this metadata. Dynamic backend expressions defer some checks to runtime.

items.title: Explicit Requirements
items.text:
Use > requires: when a capability is a hard contract rather than an inferred feature warning:

> adapter: pydantic
> requires:
    structured_output
    tool_registration
    stream_events

The scalar form accepts one name: > requires: stream_events. Requirements are additive across lexical scopes and applied profiles, with stable deduplication. They may appear at top level, inside a procedure, or inside a profile.

Literal adapter selections are checked by the LSP. Dynamic selections defer the decision until runtime, but Kedi still validates the contract before the first model request. A missing or unadvertised capability is an error, not a fallback. Python query and bind accept the same callable-boundary contract through requires=(...).
