  [result] := failed

= <result>

The condition is evaluated exactly once. Its result must have exact Python type bool; values that are merely truthy or falsey are rejected. The closing : after the embedded Python expression is required. Kedi runs only the selected body, so Python statements, procedure definitions, and model calls in the other body have no effect.

> else: is optional. Kedi has no elif form; nest another > if: when a second condition is needed:

[grade] = unknown

> if: `score >= 90`:
  [grade] := A
> else:
  > if: `score >= 75`:
    [grade] := B
  > else:
    [grade] := C

Each selected body owns a child value scope. A Kedi = initialization remains inside that branch, while := or embedded Python may update a binding already owned by a containing scope. New Python-only names never become Kedi bindings. Agent-profile directives inside the body are also lexical. The first evaluated return ends the enclosing procedure or regular program; later conditions and statements do not execute. Use > show: to display a value and continue.

items.title: Template Conditions
items.text:
[city] = Ankara
[minimum_population: int] = `5_000_000`
[result] = unknown

> if: <city> has more than <`minimum_population`> residents
  [result] := major city
> else:
  [result] := smaller city

= <result>

A template condition has no trailing :. Plain text, <name> substitutions, procedure calls, and Python substitutions such as <`minimum_population`> use normal Kedi rendering semantics. Bare backtick expressions are rejected during parsing; angle brackets make their place in the rendered claim explicit. [output] fields are rejected because a condition does not create a binding.

Kedi evaluates the rendered claim using the current agent profile and its available context. A claim that cannot be established is treated as false. The evaluation does not create a Kedi binding.

The trailing colon distinguishes a deterministic condition from a claim even when both contain one inline Python segment:

> if: `is_ready`:
  [kind] = deterministic

> if: <`is_ready`>
  [kind] = model-classified

items.title: Conditional Loops
items.text: See Conditional Loops.

items.title: Sequential Loops
items.text: See Sequential Loops.

items.title: Map Continuations
items.text: See Map Continuations.

items.title: Loops and Map Continuations
items.text: Conditional loops repeat a condition; iterable loops visit values; map adds a continuation per retained iteration. None creates an implicit result collection.

items.title: Conditional Loops
items.text:
[remaining: int] = `3`

> loop: `remaining > 0`:
  `remaining -= 1`

= `remaining`

The exact-bool condition is evaluated before every iteration. A false first result executes no body. Every body execution receives a fresh child scope. State needed by the next condition must update an existing outer binding with := or owner-aware Python write-back; new body-local declarations disappear after that iteration.

Template conditional loops use the same claim syntax and re-render the claim before every iteration:

> loop: <work> remains unfinished
  >> Continue the unfinished work.

Conditional loops allow 10,000 completed iterations by default. If their condition is still true, Kedi raises LoopIterationLimitError before starting the next body. Nested loops have independent counters. Python callers can set a positive loop_iteration_limit through compile_program(), configure(), context(), or interactive().

items.title: Sequential Loops
items.text:
[items: list[int]] = `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`
[total: int] = `0`

> loop [n]: `items`:
  `total += n`

= `total`

The expression is evaluated once and must return an Iterable. Kedi traverses it sequentially in its native order without materializing it or adding implicit parallelism. Lists, tuples, dictionaries, strings, generators, ranges, and custom iterables therefore retain their normal iteration behavior. If the iterator exposes close(), Kedi calls it after normal traversal and on an early exit caused by a loop-body failure.

The binder receives each yielded value without coercion and is visible to every statement and nested block in the current iteration. Every iteration owns a fresh child scope, so its binder and local declarations cannot leak into or overwrite another iteration. The binder's lifetime is restricted to the loop:

[n: int] = `99`
[values: list[int]] = `[]`

> loop [n]: `range(3)`:
  `values.append(n)`

= `(values, n)`

This returns ([0, 1, 2], 99). Each iteration binder belongs to a fresh child scope, so the outer n is never overwritten and the iteration binding is discarded when that scope ends. Nested loops may shadow the same binder safely. Outer values change only through :=, owner-aware Python write-back, or mutation of an outer object.

items.title: Map Continuations
items.text:
One sibling > map: clause may immediately follow an iterable loop:

[selected: list[str]] = `[]`
[candidates: list[str]] = `["Ada <ada@example.org>", "Missing address"]`

> loop [candidate]: `candidates`:
  >> Eligible candidates have a named contact and a usable email address.
  It is [qualified: bool] that <candidate> meets these criteria.
  Their contact email, if present, is [email: str | None].
> map:
  > if: `qualified and email is not None`:
    `selected.append(email)`

= `selected`

This is a deferred continuation stage, not Python's collection-producing map(). Kedi first traverses the iterable and starts every loop-body job. It then schedules one continuation for each retained iteration scope. Each map execution sees only its own binder, declarations, and model outputs plus the containing scopes.

The configured execution engine controls concurrency. Sequential execution preserves source order; a parallel engine may finish independent records out of order. Kedi joins and drains the entire stage before continuing after the loop, then surfaces the first failure.

Parallel map continuations may overlap. Source-order side effects and atomic read-modify-write operations are not implied: shared aggregates must use operations or synchronization appropriate for the active execution engine.

A map body that defines a procedure or Kedi type executes its continuations in source order, even with a parallel engine. The same applies to declarations inside nested branches, loops, and active forms: these names belong to the enclosing invocation and cannot be published concurrently. Define reusable procedures and types before the map to retain parallel continuations. Failures still drain the remaining iterations before being raised.

Kedi accepts one map stage on an immediately preceding binder-based loop. It has no binder and creates no implicit output collection. Orphan maps, maps attached to conditional loops, and chained maps are parse errors.

items.title: Nested Stages
items.text:
Nested loops and map stages retain their own binders. This deterministic example uses indexed writes so its result does not depend on completion order:

[rows: list[list[int]]] = `[[1, 2], [3, 4]]`
[squares: list[list[int]]] = `[[0, 0], [0, 0]]`

> loop [row_index]: `range(len(rows))`:
  > loop [column_index]: `range(len(rows[row_index]))`:
    [square: int] = `rows[row_index][column_index] ** 2`
  > map:
    `squares[row_index][column_index] = square`

= `squares`

The result is [[1, 4], [9, 16]]. The inner stage completes before that outer iteration finishes. Independent map callbacks can overlap; use disjoint destinations as above or explicit synchronization. A shared increment such as total += square is not an implicit atomic reduction.

items.title: Multiline Syntax and Escaping
items.text: Kedi has separate multiline rules for model prompts, rendered returns, Python, comments, and directives. Do not transfer one construct's continuation syntax to another.

items.title: Multiline Templates
items.text:
Same-indentation lines following >> form one model request:

>> The deployment risk is [risk: Literal["low", "medium", "high"]].
The reason for that decision is [reason: str].
= <risk>: <reason>

The two prompt lines are newline-joined and share one structured schema. Another >> starts another model call:

>> The affected service is [service: str].
>> The recommended owner for <service> is [owner: str].

Use one block when outputs belong to one judgement. Use separate blocks when a later prompt depends on an earlier output or represents an independent call.

A plain >> block without output fields still runs the model but discards the response. Use [answer] << ... to keep unstructured response text.

items.title: Multiline Instructions and Directives
items.text:
Block directives such as > instructions: use indented continuation text:

> instructions:
    Act as a release engineer.
    Prefer evidence from tools over assumptions.
    Keep the final answer concise.

Directive-specific substitution rules are documented with each directive. System instruction text can include variable and inline Python substitutions; output fields and procedure calls are not declarations there.

items.title: Multiline Python
items.text:
Fenced Python opening and closing markers must be alone on their lines and align with the surrounding Kedi scope. The Python source aligns with those fences:

@summarize(values: list[int]) -> dict[str, float]:
  = ```
  total = sum(values)
  return {
      "total": total,
      "average": total / len(values),
  }
  ```

Kedi dedents the block relative to its Kedi indentation before Python executes. Do not indent the Python an extra level merely because it is inside a fence.

Use fenced blocks for statements. A single backtick line is a side-effect statement; backticks inside an initialization, assignment, or return are expressions.

items.title: Return Continuations
items.text:
A rendered return uses a trailing backslash:

@message(name: str) -> str:
  = Hello <name>, \
    the deployment completed.

This joins physical lines into one return expression. It is not model-template continuation. The source whitespace around the backslash, at the end of one line and the start of the next, becomes a single space. Escaped whitespace next to it is content and stays: = a\s \ followed by 1 returns a 1. Use \\ when the output must contain a literal backslash.

items.title: Escapes
items.text:
Backslash escapes syntax characters in text:

Escape Result \< / \> Literal < / > \[ / \] Literal [ / ] \= Literal = \@ Literal @ \, Literal comma, especially inside a call argument \\ Literal backslash \# Literal # rather than a comment \~ or ~~ Literal ~ \` Literal backtick \( / \) Literal parentheses \t / \n / \s Tab, newline, or one preserved space 
@literal() -> str:
  = Use \<tag\>, \[field\], and contact\@example.com.

The same delimiter escapes work inside substitutions, output expressions, and call-argument text where applicable. A backslash before an unsupported character is an error rather than an implicit literal.

items.title: Comments and Literal Hashes
items.text:
An unescaped # begins a line or inline comment outside Python:

[mode] = strict  # Used by the reviewer
= mode\=<mode>

Use \# for visible hash text:

= Issue \#42

Inside Python fences, Python's own comment rules apply.

items.title: Block Comments and Docstrings
items.text:
Triple hashes delimit multiline comments:

###
This block is ignored by execution.
Kedi syntax inside it is not parsed as program statements.
###

When this is the first statement inside a procedure or profile, its contents become that declaration's docstring. In any later position it is only a comment.

items.title: Code Fences in Markdown and Generated Text
items.text: Kedi's Python fence is exactly three backticks on a line. When documenting it in Markdown, wrap the example in four backticks as this reference does. Within a Kedi string, escape a literal backtick with \`. Do not place language labels such as python after a Kedi runtime fence.

items.title: Whitespace Preservation
items.text:
Kedi trims ordinary whitespace at text boundaries and preserves internal spacing. Escaped whitespace from \s, \t, and \n remains significant even at a boundary:

= \tIndented\n

Indentation itself defines lexical scope, so tabs and inconsistent widths should not be used for layout. Keep one project-wide indentation style; the examples use two spaces for Kedi blocks and four spaces inside nested Python syntax after dedenting.

items.title: Multimodal Input
items.text:
Images, audio, video and documents reach a model by reference. A prompt writes <<name>>: the text gets the name, and the value is attached to the model's context under it.

> import: media

[cat_image: Image] = `image("photos/cat.png")`
[dog_image: Image] = `image("photos/dog.png")`

>> Compare <<cat_image>> and <<dog_image>>. Is <<cat_image>> the happier one? [answer: bool]
>> Extract the total of the receipt in <<image(photos/receipt.png)>> as [total: float].

<cat_image> would be a type error: <...> always renders text, and an image has no text form. See Substitutions and Calls for the rules every reference follows.

items.title: Loading Media
items.text:
> import: media exports four loaders, save and five types:

Name Kind image(source) loads an Image audio(source) loads an Audio value video(source, start=, end=, fps=, resolution=) loads a Video; the settings are optional and Gemini-only document(source) loads a Document save(media, path) writes a media value to a file and returns the path Media, Image, Audio, Video, Document types for annotations

A loader takes a path relative to the working directory, an http(s) URL or a data: URI. Paths follow the filesystem module's rules: with KEDI_WORKSPACE_POLICY=strict, the default, a path cannot leave the working directory, and .env files are refused. A media value is limited to 20 MB.

To send smaller media, set media_limit in > settings:. It takes 5MB, 512KB or a number of bytes (KB and MB are binary), and applies to the requests in its scope on Pydantic AI and LangChain:

> settings:
    media_limit: 5MB

A larger attachment fails before the request, naming it. The setting overrides PydanticAdapter(media_limit=...) and LangChainAdapter(media_limit=...). It is not sent to the model provider, and values held as a URL or a provider file ID have no local size, so they are not checked.

Loading is always explicit. Keep a loaded value with single-backtick Python, [photo: Image] = `image("cat.png")`, or reference a loader call directly in a prompt, <<image(cat.png)>>. A binding, parameter or capture typed Image accepts media values only: a string is never read as a path or URL, so [photo: Image] = cat.png and <caption(cat.png)> for a parameter typed Image are type errors.

Kind Formats Reaches the model as Image PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP <image> with the image Audio WAV, MP3, OGG, FLAC, AIFF, AAC <audio> with the audio Video MP4, MOV, WebM, MKV, FLV, MPEG, WMV, 3GP; YouTube URLs <video> with the video Document PDF <document> with the PDF Document UTF-8 text, Markdown, CSV, HTML, JSON, XML, YAML, TOML <document> with the text

Office files (docx, xlsx, pptx) are rejected: convert them to PDF or text.

items.title: What the Model Receives
items.text:
Every referenced value becomes an attachment. The attachments come first, inside one <attachments> element, each tagged with its ID and media type; the prompt text follows and shows only the IDs. The first template above sends one user message:

<attachments>
<image id="cat_image" type="image/png">
[the image]
</image>
<image id="dog_image" type="image/png">
[the image]
</image>
</attachments>
... Compare cat_image and dog_image. Is cat_image the happier one? [answer]

Coding agents and providers use the same pattern: Codex tags each image with its name, and Anthropic recommends XML-tagged documents placed before the question. The prompt text stays a single string for hooks, telemetry and prefix caching. The same rules apply to >> templates, << raw invokes and typed captures, and > if: template conditions.

The ID is, in order:

  1. a name given in Python: Image.from_path(path, name="cat");
  2. the binding name; a list[Image] binding photos gives photos_1, photos_2, ...;
  3. <proc>_result_1, <proc>_result_2, ... for a call such as <<image(photos/receipt.png)>>.

File names never reach the model, because a name such as invoice_1250USD.png can leak an answer. Within one prompt each content is attached once, and a second name for the same content renders the first ID.

A text document reaches every model as text inside its element:

<document id="notes" type="text/markdown">
...
</document>

The content is not escaped. A referenced document is attached in full whatever its size: the artifact threshold never turns referenced content into an artifact.

items.title: Provider Support
items.text:
With the Pydantic AI and LangChain adapters:

Provider Image Text document PDF Audio Video OpenAI yes yes yes audio models; WAV and MP3 no Anthropic yes yes yes no no Google Gemini yes yes yes yes yes, including YouTube URLs AWS Bedrock yes yes yes no Nova models

Kedi fails before the model call when a known provider cannot take an attachment, for example video on OpenAI or an OGG file on OpenAI. With LangChain it also honors the model profile flags image_inputs, pdf_inputs, audio_inputs and video_inputs. Kedi never transcribes or describes media for a model that cannot read it.

Agent harnesses take part of this:

Harness Media Sent as Claude Agent SDK images and PDFs content blocks, from data or an http(s) URL Codex images data as a temporary local file for the turn, an http(s) URL or an OpenAI file id ACP what the agent's promptCapabilities allow image and audio blocks; PDFs and video as embedded resources; URLs are downloaded first A2A the media types the agent card's defaultInputModes list raw parts for data, url parts for http(s) URLs, each with its media type and file name

Text documents go inline on all four. Other media, and media the ACP agent or A2A card does not advertise, fails before the call. None replays its history through Kedi, so each turn of a continued conversation sends the media it references. Kedi's own A2A server lists only text/plain, so it is refused media.

WebGPU does not accept media: a prompt with media fails before model I/O. The editor reports media prompts on adapters without media input; it does not check which kinds a harness reads. See the capability matrix.

Decision models read less. Jev (typesafe/...) reads images and text documents: images reach TypeSafe as image assets, and Kedi downloads image URLs first. TypeSafe image input is experimental and takes PNG or JPEG images of 16 MiB at most, each side 280 to 1568 pixels (TypeSafe image limits); Kedi checks these before the call. Laya reads text documents; its engine checkpoint laya/vega (laya 0.5+, PyTorch) also reads one image, audio or video per decision, sent as data with the prompt text as context for each question. Kedi rejects any other attachment for them before the call.

URLs go to the provider as URLs when the model accepts them. Otherwise Kedi downloads them over http(s) only, with private and cloud-metadata addresses blocked. YouTube URLs are never downloaded, and only Gemini reads them. s3:// and gs:// URIs pass through unchanged. Do not build media URLs from untrusted input.

items.title: Video Settings
items.text:
Gemini reads a clip of a video: start and end offsets in seconds, fps (frames sampled per second, above 0 and at most 24) and resolution (low, medium or high, Gemini 3 and later). Pass them to video():

> import: media

[intro: Video] = `video("talk.mp4", start=0, end=30, fps=2, resolution="low")`
[talk: Video] = `video("https://youtu.be/abc123", start=60, end=90)`
[reply] << Compare <<intro>> with <<talk>>.
= <reply>

In Python, Video.with_settings(start=..., end=..., fps=..., resolution=...) returns a copy. A setting it omits is kept, and None clears one.

  • Settings are part of the value's identity. Two clips of one file are two attachments; a different clip is sent again in history; a cached call with a different clip calls the model again.
  • Only Gemini reads them. Kedi refuses a video with settings for any other provider, including one it does not recognize, instead of sending the whole video. resolution on Gemini 2.x is refused too, because those models ignore it.
  • A clipped YouTube URL still goes to Gemini as a URL; a downloaded URL keeps its settings.
  • JSON serialization of a Video keeps only its source, not its settings.

items.title: Media Outside Prompts
items.text:
A media value is a native value. Single backticks keep it:

  • bindings: [copy: Image] = `cat_image`;
  • parameters typed Image, Audio, Video, Document or Media;
  • call arguments: <caption(`cat_image`)>.
> import: media

@caption(photo: Image) -> str:
  [text] << Describe <<photo>> in one sentence.
  = <text>

[invoice: Image] = `image(args.invoice)`
= <caption(`invoice`)>

<cat_image> anywhere is a type error, and the editor reports it as K-SUBSTITUTION-TYPE. <<cat_image>> outside a model prompt, for example in an assignment, a return, > show:, > instructions: or > send input, is a parse error (K-REFERENCE-CONTEXT). A > task prompt is a model prompt: its references go to the child (see Native Tasks). > show: `cat_image` and Python str() display a byte-free label such as <image cat.png · image/png · 48 KB>.

items.title: Media Inside a Value
items.text:
Media in a dict, a model, a dataclass or a mixed list are attached each under a name derived from its path, and the value goes as JSON with a placeholder naming each one:

> import: media

[cat: Image] = `image("cat.png")`
[report: dict] = `{"title": "Q3", "photo": cat, "pets": [cat, "note"]}`
[reply] << Summarize <<report>>.
= <reply>

The model receives one image, report_photo, and the document report: {"title":"Q3","photo":"<image report_photo>","pets":["<image report_photo>","note"]}.

  • Names come from the path: report_photo, report_pets_1 for the first item of pets, pick_result_2 for the second item of <<pick()>>.
  • An image also referenced directly keeps its first name, so Compare <<cat>> with <<report>> sends the image once and the JSON says <image cat>.
  • Only media the value's serialization writes are attached: a model field with exclude=True is neither written nor sent.
  • <report> still renders text, so substituting a value that holds media is an error, as it is for a media value.

save writes a value's bytes to a file and returns the path:

> import: media

[photo: Image] = `image("photos/cat.png")`
[copy] = <save(`photo`, out/cat.png)>

In Python, photo.save("out/cat.png") does the same. The path follows the same rules as loading: it starts at the working directory, cannot leave it with KEDI_WORKSPACE_POLICY=strict, and is never a .env file. Parent directories are created and an existing file is replaced. A value held as a URL or an uploaded file has no bytes and cannot be saved.

In Kedi Notebook (host mode), > show: `photo` displays an image inline and gives audio a player instead of printing the label.

items.title: Media From Tools
items.text:
A tool that returns media gives it to the model as media:

> import: media

@snap() -> Image:
  = `image("camera/latest.jpg")`

> approval: allow
> use: snap
[reply] << Take a photo and say which color fills it.
= <reply>

The tool result is a placeholder, <image snap_result_1>, and the image follows natively. A dict, a model or a list holding media becomes JSON with a placeholder for each one, as <<x>> does. Names stay unique across the tool calls of one request, and across the requests of a conversation (see History), and never take an attachment's name. The model can answer with these media by name, and pass them to other tools: see Media in Outputs.

Adapter Where the media go Pydantic AI inside the tool result where the provider takes it (Anthropic, Gemini 3), otherwise in a following user message (OpenAI, Gemini 2.x) LangChain in the tool message when the model profile sets image_tool_message or pdf_tool_message, otherwise in a user message after the tool messages Claude Agent SDK, Codex, WebGPU not sent: the tool bridge carries text, so the model reads a tool error saying so
  • Provider rules and media_limit apply as for prompt media; audio from a tool fails on Anthropic models, for example.
  • Media are never stored as artifacts, whatever their size.
  • In CodeMode, code receives the placeholders. Media its result names are attached to that result.
  • PostToolUse hooks see the result as the adapter sends it, media included.

items.title: Image Output
items.text:
A typed raw invoke with Image asks the model for an image. An image model draws it:

> import: media

[img: Image] << Draw a cat in a spacesuit, flat colors.
[path] = `save(img, "out/cat.png")`
[caption] << Describe <<img>> in one sentence.
= <caption>

img is an ordinary Image: reference it, save it, or show it in Kedi Notebook.

Adapter Models that draw Pydantic AI image models such as google:gemini-2.5-flash-image, and OpenAI Responses models, which get the image generation tool LangChain chat models whose profile sets image_outputs, such as Gemini image models
  • Any other model names an image of its request instead: see Media in Outputs. An OpenAI Responses model may draw or name one when there is one to name.
  • A model that cannot draw fails before the call, with an error naming it, when nothing could be named: no image attached, and no tool, MCP server or archived history that could return one.
  • Adapters without image output (Claude Agent SDK, Codex) can only name an attached image. Without one, and on WebGPU, ACP and A2A, the call fails before it starts. The editor reports [x: Image] << on adapters without image output unless the prompt attaches media.
  • Image models take no tools, so Kedi leaves its artifact tools out for them. A program that turns artifacts on explicitly gets an error instead, and so does a call with > use: tools.

items.title: Media in Outputs
items.text:
A model never writes media. Where its answer holds media (the output itself, a template field, a list item or a model field), it names one of its request's media, an attachment or a tool result, and Kedi binds that value:

> import: media

@satellite(region: str) -> Image:
  = `image("tiles/" + region + ".png")`

> approval: allow
> use: satellite
[tile: Image] << Fetch the satellite image of Ankara.
[photos: list[Image]] = `[image("a.png"), image("b.png")]`
>> Pick the sharpest of <<photos>> as [best: Image] and say why as [reason].
  • The model writes the name the request gives the media (satellite_result_1, photos_2) or its placeholder (<image satellite_result_1>).
  • Any other string is refused, made-up URLs and data URIs included. The model reads the names it can use and answers again.
  • Requests whose output holds media, or that offer a tool taking media, and that attach media or offer tools, get one instruction that says so.
  • In a conversation (> history: enabled), the model can also name media of its earlier requests.
  • Pydantic AI, LangChain, the Claude Agent SDK and Codex resolve names. The harnesses' tool bridges send text only, so there the model names attachments.
  • [x: Audio] << names an audio when the prompt attaches media or a tool in scope declares an audio return type; otherwise it speaks (see Speech Output).
  • Tool arguments take names the same way: the model hands a tool an image of its request (@crop(photo: Image) called with photo: satellite_result_1). A wrong name fails the tool call with the names it can use.
  • A > task capture typed with media names one of the child's media, and the program gets the value. A delegate_task result goes to the parent model and to workflows as JSON, so it names none.

items.title: Speech Output
items.text:
A typed raw invoke with Audio asks the model itself to speak:

> import: media

> settings:
    voice: Kore

[speech: Audio] << Say good morning to the team in one sentence.
[path] = `save(speech, "out/morning.wav")`
= `speech.transcript`

speech is an ordinary Audio value in WAV: reference it, save it, or play it in Kedi Notebook. speech.transcript holds what the model said, when the model reports it, and is None otherwise.

Adapter Models Pydantic AI realtime models such as google:gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview and openai:gpt-realtime; Kedi opens a one-shot realtime session, sends the prompt, keeps the reply's speech and closes the session LangChain Gemini TTS models such as gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts, which read the prompt aloud, and OpenAI audio models such as gpt-audio
  • voice in > settings: picks the voice: Kore and the other Gemini voices, alloy and the other OpenAI voices. On LangChain, a chat model that declares a voice field, such as a local TTS model wrapped as a chat model, gets it. LangChain's Gemini models take no voice setting, so setting one there is an error.
  • A speech request sends text only and offers no tools. Only the program's own > instructions: go with it, and a Gemini TTS model, which reads its prompt aloud, gets none.
  • A prompt that attaches media, or a call with a tool in scope that declares an audio return type (-> Audio, -> list[Audio], -> Media), does not speak: the model names an audio of its request instead (see Media in Outputs), and the call is an ordinary turn of the conversation. With no audio attached and no such tool, it fails before the call. Other tools leave the call speech.
  • A speech request stays outside the conversation: with > history: enabled it neither reads nor records history, so later text turns do not see it.
  • It counts as one model request for > budget:. Fallback models are not tried for it.
  • Any other model fails with an error naming it. Adapters without speech output (Claude Agent SDK, Codex, WebGPU, ACP, A2A) fail before the call, and the editor reports [x: Audio] << on them unless the prompt attaches media.
  • Only [x: Audio] << produces speech. Live voice sessions, with microphone input and interruptions, are not part of Kedi yet.

items.title: History
items.text:
With > history: enabled, an attachment that the replayed history already holds under the same ID and content is not sent again; the prompt text still writes the ID.

Names are unique across the conversation's requests, so an ID never means two media:

  • A binding rebound to new content, for example in a loop, gets a new ID (photo_2), and the same content keeps its first ID.
  • A tool's second image in the conversation is snap_result_2.
  • With the parallel engine, which of two requests composed at once gets the _2 suffix can differ between runs; names stay unique.
  • A conversation restored from a checkpoint keeps its names but not their media: new media get new names, and an earlier name can no longer be named.
  • To resolve names, a conversation keeps every media it named in memory for its lifetime, including media that history archiving or compaction has dropped from the history.

With a history processor, native compaction or history archiving, Kedi cannot tell what the model still sees, so it attaches references on every turn.

History archiving keeps media out of the archived transcript:

  • Each image, audio, video or PDF of the archived turns is stored once as an artifact of its own, marked sensitive like the transcript.
  • The transcript names it by reference (kedi-artifact:<ref>), and the checkpoint lists it by name and reference.
  • read_artifact on that reference returns the media itself, so the model can look at an archived image again; Pydantic AI and LangChain send it natively.
  • URLs and uploaded files stay as they are, and media in the turns that are kept are not moved. If storing a media artifact fails, the turns are not archived.

items.title: Python
items.text:
kedi.media provides the same types:

from kedi.media import Document, Image, Media

Image.from_path("photos/cat.png")
Image.from_url("https://example.com/cat.png")
Image.from_bytes(data, "image/png")
Document.from_path("notes.txt", encoding="cp1254")  # re-encoded to UTF-8
Media.from_path("clip.mp4")  # picks Video from the media type

References also accept Pydantic AI BinaryContent, ImageUrl, AudioUrl, VideoUrl, DocumentUrl and UploadedFile objects and PIL images.

Hooks see the attachments read-only in UserPromptSubmitRequest.media: name, kind, media type, size and SHA-256. An edit decision replaces only the prompt text. Telemetry and debugger events record the same metadata and never the bytes.

items.title: Outputs, Initialization, and Assignment
items.text: Square brackets are write syntax in Kedi. In a >> template they declare fields the model must produce; on the left of = they initialize variables with deterministic values. Neither form is the same as <name>, which reads a value.

items.title: Output Fields as L-Values
items.text:
An output field embedded in a template is an L-value:

>> The incident severity is [severity: str]. The summary is [summary: str].
= <severity>: <summary>

Kedi builds a structured output schema, asks the active adapter to fill it, and stores each field in the current environment. Output names must be valid Python identifiers: they start with a letter or underscore and contain only letters, digits, and underscores.

Use model outputs for semantic extraction or generation. Do not use them for values that Python can determine exactly.

items.title: Simple and Typed Outputs
items.text:
An untyped output defaults to str:

>> A concise headline is [headline].

A typed output asks the adapter for a native value and validates it:

>> The priority is [priority: int]. The owners are [owners: list[str]]. It is [blocked: bool] that the work is blocked.

Kedi does not merely include the annotation in the prompt. It resolves the type, creates the provider schema, and validates the returned value. Unsupported provider schema formats fail before a model call where the adapter can detect them.

items.title: Inline Python Output Types
items.text:
Wrap a type expression in backticks when the type comes from runtime Python state:

```
from typing import Literal
Priority = Literal["low", "medium", "high"]
```

>> The ticket priority is [priority: `Priority`].

For ordinary built-in or custom Kedi types, prefer the direct form [priority: Priority]. Runtime expressions are useful for types created by a prelude, import, or factory, but they make static tooling less certain.

items.title: Field Description Metadata
items.text:
Use Annotated[T, "description"] to explain a field to the model while keeping T as its runtime type:

>> The country code is [code: Annotated[str, "Uppercase ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code"]].

The description becomes JSON Schema metadata for adapters that expose schemas. The native description form uses a single-line string literal. Annotated[T] is accepted as T but triggers an editor warning because it carries no description. Python type aliases can carry additional non-string validation or decision metadata; Kedi preserves that metadata. See Validation Constraints.

Use descriptions for constraints the base type cannot express clearly. Do not repeat obvious information such as Annotated[int, "An integer"].

items.title: Multiple Outputs and Same-Scope Initialization
items.text:
One template can fill several fields:

>> Version [version: str] was released on [date: date].
It includes [changes: list[str]].

All continuation lines in that >> block belong to one model request and one combined schema. A later output or = initialization with the same name replaces the value in the current scope:

[status] = draft
>> The document status after review is [status: str].
= <status>

This does not update an outer lexical binding. Prefer a new name such as reviewed_status when both values matter.

items.title: Variable Initialization
items.text:
Initialization does not contact a model:

[title] = Release <version>
[attempts: int] = `2 + 1`
[copy] = <title>

The right-hand side has two evaluation modes:

  • A sole native Python segment preserves its native result.
  • A sole procedure call preserves that procedure's native result.
  • Mixed literal text and substitutions render to str.

This distinction matters:

[native: int] = `40 + 2`
[rendered] = Answer: <`40 + 2`>

native is the integer 42; rendered is the string "Answer: 42".

= always declares in the current lexical scope. A declaration inside an if, else, or loop iteration shadows a visible outer name and disappears when that child scope ends.

items.title: Assignment
items.text:
Use := to assign a new value to the nearest visible Kedi binding instead of shadowing it:

[attempts: int] = `0`

> if: `True`:
  [attempts] := `attempts + 1`

= `attempts`

The target must already exist. := does not accept a type annotation because the existing binding owns its type contract; Kedi validates the new value against that contract. Unknown and reserved targets fail.

A fenced Python result can be assigned without changing the target type:

[total: int] = `0`
[total] := ```
return sum([1, 2, 3])
```

items.title: Typed Initialization
items.text:
A typed initialization validates the resulting value without coercing it:

[ports: list[int]] = `[8000, 8001]`
[enabled: bool] = `True`

[count: int] = five fails instead of converting text. If parsing user text is required, do it explicitly in Python:

[raw_count] = 5
[count: int] = `int(raw_count)`

items.title: Initialization from a Python Block
items.text:
Use a fenced block when computing a value requires statements:

[durations: list[int]] = `[14, 8, 21]`
[p95: int] = ```
ordered = sorted(durations)
index = round(0.95 * (len(ordered) - 1))
return ordered[index]
```

= p95\=<p95>

The block must execute return to supply the initialization value. New helper names inside the block remain local; the initialized result is the supported way to surface one of them.

items.title: Output Capture versus Raw Capture
items.text:
Use >> output fields when you need typed or multiple structured values:

>> The detected language is [language: str]. The confidence is [confidence: float].

Use raw capture when the complete model response should remain an unstructured string:

[explanation] << Explain why the build failed in one paragraph.

Raw capture accepts no embedded output fields and no type other than optional str. A plain >> request with no output fields runs the model and discards its response.

items.title: Resolution and Validation Errors
items.text:
Kedi rejects duplicate output names within an invalid schema, malformed identifiers, unknown types, values that do not match their initialization or assignment contracts, and adapter schemas the active backend cannot represent. Type validation is strict: a numeric-looking string is still a string.

Choose annotations that match the wire capability of the selected adapter. For example, a descriptive Annotated[str, "..."] can be more portable than a provider-specific URL or regex format.

items.title: Parameters and Returns
items.text: Procedure signatures define the native contract between Kedi, Python, tools, tests, and evals. An omitted annotation is not Any: it defaults to str.

items.title: Positional and Typed Parameters
items.text:
@render_issue(id: int, title: str, tags: list[str]) -> str:
  = \#<`id`> <title> \[<`", ".join(tags)`>\]

Kedi validates each argument against its annotation. It does not coerce a rendered "42" into 42, and it does not accept a dict where a custom model is required.

Direct type names and runtime Python type expressions are equivalent:

@first(items: `list[str]`) -> `str`:
  = `items[0]`

Prefer direct annotations when possible because the LSP can resolve and explain them statically. Use backtick annotations for a type supplied by Python state.

items.title: Default Parameters
items.text:
Defaults are single-line Python expressions:

@format_count(count: int, label: str = `"items"`, compact: bool = `False`) -> str:
  = `f"{count}{label}" if compact else f"{count} {label}"`

= <format_count(`3`)>

Required parameters must precede defaulted parameters. Duplicate parameters and fenced block defaults are parse errors.

Defaults are evaluated when the procedure is defined, not on each call:

```
seed = 1
```

@value(current: int = `seed`) -> int:
  = `current`

`seed = 9`
= `value()`  # 1

Untyped defaults retain their native Python value, but the parameter itself still follows the signature contract. Annotate non-string defaults explicitly for clarity.

items.title: Call Arguments
items.text:
Kedi angle-call syntax is positional:

= <format_count(`3`, records, `True`)>

Use single backticks to pass a native Python result. Plain text and mixed template arguments render to str. Escape text commas as \,.

Named arguments are available through Python because compiled Kedi procedures have real Python signatures:

= `format_count(count=3, compact=True, label="records")`

Use angle calls for normal Kedi composition. Use Python keyword calls when argument order would be unclear or values are already native.

items.title: Declared Return Types
items.text:
Return annotations are enforced:

~Row(id: int, active: bool)

@active_ids(rows: list[Row]) -> list[int]:
  = `[row.id for row in rows if row.active]`

Without -> ..., a procedure has a str return contract. Returning a native integer, list, or model from an untyped procedure is an error. Annotate every procedure that intentionally returns a non-string.

Kedi validates rather than coerces return values. = "5" cannot satisfy -> int; use = `5` or parse explicitly.

items.title: Rendered and Native Returns
items.text:
A rendered return starts with = and combines literal text, substitutions, calls, and inline Python:

@status(name: str, healthy: bool) -> str:
  = <name>: <`"healthy" if healthy else "degraded"`>

A sole backtick expression returns its native result:

@total(values: list[int]) -> int:
  = `sum(values)`

A fenced block can return a value after several statements:

@median(values: list[float]) -> float:
  = ```
  ordered = sorted(values)
  middle = len(ordered) // 2
  if len(ordered) % 2:
      return ordered[middle]
  return (ordered[middle - 1] + ordered[middle]) / 2
  ```

Choose a rendered return for human-facing text and a native return for values that callers will calculate with, validate, serialize, or pass to tools.

items.title: Multiline Returns
items.text:
Use a trailing backslash to continue one rendered return across physical lines:

@notice(name: str) -> str:
  = Hello <name>, \
    your report is ready.

Return continuation is a text feature. It is not how multiline model prompts work; >> prompts use same-indentation continuation lines instead. Use \\ for a literal backslash.

Kedi trims line-end whitespace while preserving meaningful internal spacing. Escaped whitespace (\s, \t, and \n) remains significant even at a boundary.

items.title: Early Return and No Return
items.text:
The first evaluated = ends the enclosing procedure or regular program. Different reachable branches may each return; this is not a one-return-per-file restriction. Statements after a definitely terminal path are rejected before execution. A Python return inside a fenced block still exits that Python block only.

@choose(value: int) -> int:
  > if: `value < 0`:
    = `0`
  = `value`

= `choose(-1)`

This returns 0. Work after a taken return is not started. Already scheduled work is drained normally; its failures are not hidden by return.

items.title: Display Without Returning
items.text:
[city] = Ankara
> show: The selected city is <city>.
> show: `len(city)`
= <city>

> show: evaluates once, displays with a newline, and continues without changing the return value. It supports literal text, substitutions and inline Python, but cannot declare output captures. It does not implicitly generate model output or append display text to model history.

Notebook and IDLE roots reject = before execution, even in nested control flow. Use > show: there; procedure returns remain valid. IDLE also accepts :show as an alias. When migrating old repeated returns, convert intended displays only; do not automatically print discarded computations or sensitive values.

An untyped procedure with no returned value produces "". Relying on that is appropriate only for side-effect-oriented helpers. Public procedures should return deliberately and declare the contract.

items.title: Errors
items.text: Kedi reports missing and extra arguments, invalid default ordering, unresolved types, parameter mismatches, and return mismatches. These errors occur at the boundary where the contract is violated, before an invalid value silently propagates into later model or tool calls.

items.title: Procedures
items.text: Procedures package Kedi statements into typed, reusable callables. They are also the unit exposed to tools, tests, evals, optimization, generated code, and the Python API.

items.title: Define and Call a Procedure
items.text:
Declare a procedure with @name(parameters): and indent its body:

@greet(name: str) -> str:
  = Hello, <name>.

= <greet(Ada)>

The name must be a valid Python identifier. The body can contain variable initializations, assignments, templates, Python blocks, directives, nested types, nested procedures, and a return. Call it with <greet(Ada)> in rendered Kedi text or greet("Ada") in a Python expression.

items.title: Procedure Bodies and Returns
items.text:
Statements execute in source order. A return statement starts with =:

@summarize(text: str) -> str:
  >> A one-sentence summary of <text> is [summary: str].
  = <summary>

The first evaluated = ends the current procedure immediately. Statements after an unconditional return are rejected as unreachable; returns in different if/else branches are valid because only one branch is evaluated. If an untyped procedure reaches the end without a value, it returns an empty string. For non-string behavior, add an explicit return annotation and return a native value.

Keep deterministic transformation in Python and model judgement in >> templates. A procedure may combine both, but its name and return type should still describe one coherent operation.

items.title: Local Variables
items.text:
Parameters and variable initializations belong to the procedure invocation:

[prefix] = global

@format(value: str) -> str:
  [prefix] = local
  [result] = <prefix>: <value>
  = <result>

= <format(item)> / <prefix>

The procedure returns "local: item" while the top-level prefix remains "global". New local names do not leak to callers.

Parameters are read-only bindings for lexical assignment purposes. Reuse a new local name when deriving from a parameter rather than treating the parameter as shared mutable state.

items.title: Calling Other Procedures
items.text:
Procedures can form pipelines:

@normalize(value: str) -> str:
  = `value.strip().lower()`

@classify(value: str) -> str:
  >> The category of <value> is [category: str].
  = <category>

@process(value: str) -> str:
  [normalized: str] = <normalize(<value>)>
  = <classify(<normalized>)>

An angle call always renders text, also as the whole right-hand side of an initialization or assignment, so it suits procedures that return text. To keep the called procedure's native return type, call it with single-backtick Python: [profile: Profile] = `get_profile("Ada")`.

items.title: Nested Procedures
items.text:
A procedure can declare helpers visible only during that invocation:

@invoice_total(lines: list[float]) -> float:
  @subtotal(values: list[float]) -> float:
    = `sum(values)`

  = `round(subtotal(lines), 2)`

The nested subtotal is not visible after invoice_total returns. A nested definition shadows an outer procedure with the same name only inside its lexical scope.

Use nested procedures for helpers that are meaningful only to one operation or that need to capture invocation state. Use a top-level procedure when several features should call it or when it should be exported, tested, optimized, or exposed as a tool independently.

items.title: Lexical Closures
items.text:
Nested procedures capture the surrounding invocation and observe the latest outer value:

@make_report(title: str) -> str:
  [state] = draft
  @render() -> str:
    = <title>: <state>
  [state] = approved
  = <render()>

Calling make_report("Release") returns "Release: approved", not "Release: draft". Closure lookup walks the current local scope, outer procedure scopes, imports, and top-level globals. A nested parameter shadows a captured name.

An explicit := assignment made through nested lexical scopes can update a captured Kedi binding. This is different from Python block rules, where rebinding from a nested Python function requires global.

items.title: Recursion
items.text:
Compiled procedures are ordinary callable values and can be called from Python, including recursively:

@factorial(n: int) -> int:
  = `1 if n <= 1 else n * factorial(n - 1)`

= `factorial(5)`

Use recursion only when it improves the domain model. Iteration in a Python block is usually clearer for large collections and avoids Python's recursion limit. Model-calling recursion can also multiply cost and latency; bound it explicitly.

items.title: Procedure Documentation
items.text:
Place a ### block first in the body to define the procedure docstring:

@lookup_order(order_id: str) -> str:
  ###
  Return the canonical status for one order.

  Args:
    order_id: External order identifier.
  ###
  = pending

Kedi surfaces this text in editor hover, generated Python stubs, procedure JSON schemas, and tool descriptions. A block comment after another statement remains a comment and does not become the procedure docstring.

items.title: Structured Docstrings and JSON Schema
items.text:
Kedi follows the summary-and-body convention from PEP 257 and recommends Google-style Python docstrings for structured Args: and Returns: sections. PEP 257 defines general docstring conventions but does not prescribe those section names; Args: and Returns: come from the Google-style convention.

When a procedure is exposed as a tool, Kedi parses the leading docstring and adds its descriptions to the generated JSON Schemas:

@quote_shipping(destination: str, weight_kg: float, express: bool = `False`) -> float:
  ###
  Calculate a shipping quote for one destination.

  Args:
      destination: Country or region receiving the shipment.
      weight_kg: Package weight in kilograms; must be greater than zero.
      express: Whether to use the faster express service.

  Returns:
      Estimated shipping price in US dollars.
  ###
  = `0.0`

The procedure signature and docstring produce this input schema:

{
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "destination": {
      "title": "Destination",
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Country or region receiving the shipment."
    },
    "weight_kg": {
      "title": "Weight Kg",
      "type": "number",
      "description": "Package weight in kilograms; must be greater than zero."
    },
    "express": {
      "default": false,
      "title": "Express",
      "type": "boolean",
      "description": "Whether to use the faster express service."
    }
  },
  "required": ["destination", "weight_kg"],
  "title": "quote_shipping",
  "type": "object",
  "description": "Calculate a shipping quote for one destination. Returns `float` instance."
}

Kedi emits the return contract separately:

{
  "type": "number",
  "description": "Estimated shipping price in US dollars."
}

Types, required fields, and defaults come from the procedure signature. Descriptions under Args: are matched to parameters by name, while the Returns: text describes the return schema. Docstring text documents the contract; it does not override its types. Kedi also accepts common reStructuredText forms such as :param name: and :return:, but Google style is the recommended form for new code.

Document externally visible procedures and every procedure exposed with > use:. Include semantic constraints that types cannot express; do not duplicate the signature verbatim.

items.title: Failure Behavior
items.text: Calling a procedure fails when arguments are missing or excessive, a native value violates a parameter annotation, the body raises, or the return violates its annotation. Kedi retains source spans across nested calls so the reported failure points back to the relevant .kedi statement.

items.title: Scopes and Binding Lifetime
items.text: A binding belongs to the scope that declares it. A procedure invocation, a selected branch, and each loop iteration have their own value environments. Visibility is not ownership: seeing an outer value does not make a new local declaration overwrite it.

items.title: Initialization versus Assignment
items.text:
[status] = pending
[visits: int] = `0`

> if: `True`:
  [status] = local review
  [visits] := `visits + 1`
  [scratch] = temporary

= `(status, visits)`

The result is ("pending", 1). status inside the branch shadows the outer binding. visits := updates the nearest existing owner. scratch disappears with the branch. Assigning an unknown name with := fails; adding a type annotation to := is invalid because the owner already defines the contract.

items.title: Python Write-Back
items.text:
[flag: bool] = `False`

> if: `True`:
  ```
  flag = True
  scratch = "not a Kedi binding"
  ```

= `flag`

The existing flag can be updated. New Python locals such as scratch are not exported into the Kedi environment. If no outer Kedi flag existed, writing a Python local of that name would not create a global Kedi binding. Parameters and reserved names are not writable through lexical assignment.

items.title: Mutable Objects and Aliases
items.text:
Lexical isolation is not an object-memory sandbox. A visible list can be mutated in place, and aliases can observe that mutation. Binding validation does not prove that arbitrary Python code cannot mutate the interior of an object into an invalid shape. Revalidate external or mutated data when it crosses a typed boundary; copy it explicitly when ownership must be isolated.

Scheduled model requests have their own input snapshot behavior. Do not infer ordinary Python alias behavior from Concurrency.

items.title: Procedure and Type Definitions
items.text:
Value bindings follow the scopes above; procedure and Kedi type definitions do not. A definition inside > if:, > loop:, > map:, or another control block belongs to the enclosing procedure invocation or, at top level, to the program, so it stays visible after the block:

> if: `True`:
  @double(n: int) -> int:
    = `n * 2`

= `double(4)`

The result is 8. Top-level types are registered before the program runs, so a top-level type's field types cannot name top-level variables. Declare such a type inside a procedure, where field types resolve local aliases.

items.title: Iteration and Captures
items.text:
Each iteration gets a fresh binder and local declarations. An outer name with the same spelling survives unchanged. A map continuation retains its own iteration environment until its stage is joined. See Loops and Map for nested execution and shared side effects.

Nested procedures can read enclosing value bindings. Model/profile configuration is captured at definition and local directives affect following calls in that scope. Value lookup, configuration capture, and definition-time parameter defaults are different rules; see Procedures and Parameters and Returns.

items.title: Statements and Source Order
items.text:
Kedi preserves source order for declarations and executable statements. Imports publish their exported bindings at the position of the import, and later writes replace earlier bindings:

[label] = draft
> import: labels
[label] = final

= <label>

The final same-scope initialization wins. The same rule applies when a procedure, type, value, or import reuses a name. Prefer unique public names; relying on replacement is mainly useful for deliberate overrides.

items.title: Indentation and Lexical Blocks
items.text:
Indentation opens procedure, profile, directive, test, eval, and Python-owned blocks. Tabs count as width four when indentation is compared, but spaces are recommended so editor rendering cannot alter perceived scope.

@greet(name: str) -> str:
  [prefix] = Hello
  = <prefix>, <name>

The body must be indented relative to @greet. A dedent ends the block.

items.title: Top-Level and Procedure Scope
items.text:
Top-level values are visible to following statements and procedures compiled in that environment. Procedure parameters and local initializations live in the procedure frame. Inner scopes may shadow outer values without permanently changing the caller's frame; := explicitly assigns through that lexical chain.

Agent configuration has capture semantics in addition to normal lexical scope: top-level directives are captured by following procedure definitions, while directives inside a procedure affect following model calls in that procedure.

items.title: Blank Lines
items.text: Blank lines do not close a block. Dedentation determines block boundaries. Within a multiline >> template, continuation rows are part of one prompt only while they remain adjacent continuation syntax at the same Kedi indentation.

items.title: Line Comments
items.text:
# starts a line comment outside Python blocks:

[limit: int] = `10`  # Runtime limit

Escape a literal hash in Kedi text as \#:

= Ticket \#<`42`>

Python blocks use Python's own comment rules because their contents are parsed as Python rather than Kedi.

items.title: Block Comments
items.text:
Matching lines containing only ### open and close a block comment:

###
This workflow is intentionally deterministic after classification.
The block can span multiple lines.
###

The delimiters may be indented with their surrounding Kedi block. They must be paired, must occupy their own lines, and ### cannot appear inside the comment body as ordinary text.

items.title: Procedure Docstrings
items.text:
When the first statement in a procedure body is a block comment, that comment becomes the procedure's docstring:

@slugify(value: str) -> str:
  ###
  Convert a display label into a stable lowercase slug.
  ###
  = `value.strip().lower().replace(" ", "-")`

Procedure docstrings feed Python introspection, editor hovers, virtual stubs, and tool descriptions when the procedure is exposed as an agent tool. A block comment after another body statement remains a normal comment.

items.title: Profile Docstrings
items.text:
Profiles also support a docstring when the first member is a block comment:

> profile: reviewer:
    ###
    Review a change against repository evidence.
    ###
    > instructions: Cite evidence for each finding.

This documents the profile; it is not a system instruction. A later block comment remains an ordinary comment. See Profile Documentation for its use in editor hovers and subagent descriptions.

items.title: Reserved Names
items.text:
args is the default runtime-owned command-line argument binding and cannot be assigned or removed. Embedders can change the identifier through the compiler environment before compilation, but ordinary programs should treat it as reserved.

Directive names and output identifiers are also validated. Unknown > directives fail instead of being treated as prompt text.

items.title: Substitutions and Calls
items.text: Substitutions are Kedi's read syntax. <...> inserts an existing value, a procedure result, or a Python expression into rendered text. A model prompt can also pass a value by reference with <<...>>. Neither declares an output.

items.title: Variable Substitutions
items.text:
Use <name> to read a value from the current lexical environment:

[project] = Atlas
[status] = ready

> show: Project <project> is <status>.

Substitution always renders the value as text at that position. It is therefore appropriate for prompts, messages, paths, and final text.

<...> renders a value that has a text form: text that comes from the value's data alone, in one canonical form, without running a __str__ or __repr__.

Value Renders as str the text itself int, float, Decimal the number: 3, 1.5, 1.10; NaN and infinities are errors bool true, false datetime, date, time ISO 8601: 2026-11-16T10:00:00Z, 2026-11-16, 09:05:00 UUID its canonical form an Enum member its value, by these rules list, tuple, dict with str keys compact JSON, checked item by item: ["a",1], {"k":[1,null]}

None inside a container renders as null, and a Decimal, date, time or UUID inside one is a JSON string (["1.10"]). > show: <flag> displays true; > show: `flag` displays the Python value itself, True. Any other value is a type error that names the offending part, for example <order> renders text, but order["items"][2] is of type Client: None itself, media, bytes, sets (no stable order: <`sorted(ids)`>), paths (<`str(path)`>), timedelta, complex, NamedTuples, dict and list subclasses, models, ~Type values, dataclasses, clients and other objects. Rendering them through repr would be opaque and could leak data, such as an API key held by a client object. The editor reports K-SUBSTITUTION-TYPE when a declared type decides it, such as [ids: set[int]]. A value stored as an artifact renders its text, never an artifact reference. Convert explicitly when you want text, <`str(value)`> or <`report.title`>, or pass the value to a model by reference. If the next operation needs the original int, list, model, or other Python object, use the value by bare name inside Python or pass it as a native call argument.

[retries: int] = `3`

# Text rendering
> show: Retries: <retries>

# Native arithmetic
> show: `retries + 1`

An unknown name is an error. Kedi does not silently render a missing substitution as an empty string.

items.title: Procedure Calls
items.text:
Call a Kedi procedure inside angle brackets:

@display_name(first: str, last: str) -> str:
  = <first> <last>

> show: Owner: <display_name(Ada, Lovelace)>

Angle-call arguments are positional. Kedi does not provide a name=value form in this syntax. When keyword calling is important, call the compiled Kedi procedure from Python:

@label(name: str, prefix: str = `"Issue"`) -> str:
  = <prefix>: <name>

> show: `label(name="Parser", prefix="Bug")`

Use the ordinary angle-call form for readable prompt composition. Use a Python call when you specifically need keyword arguments or already have native Python objects.

items.title: Nested Calls
items.text:
Calls can be nested directly:

@trim(value: str) -> str:
  = `value.strip()`

@slug(value: str) -> str:
  = `value.lower().replace(" ", "-")`

= <slug(<trim(  Release Notes  )>)>

The inner call completes before its value becomes the outer argument, as text: an angle call always renders text, even as a whole argument. Pass a native value with a backtick argument, <double(`count(items)`)>, or call from Python as below.

@count(items: list[str]) -> int:
  = `len(items)`

@double(value: int) -> int:
  = `value * 2`

= `double(count(["a", "b", "c"]))`

For native collections, the direct Python form above is usually clearer than embedding several backtick expressions in angle-call syntax.

items.title: Native and Rendered Arguments
items.text:
A single-backtick argument passes the evaluated Python value without converting it to text. Every ordinary literal or mini-template argument is rendered as a string:

@describe(count: int, label: str) -> str:
  = <label>: <`str(count)`>

= <describe(`2 + 3`, Open items)>

Here 2 + 3 arrives as the integer 5; Open items arrives as a string. Without backticks, <describe(5, Open items)> passes "5" and fails the int parameter check. Kedi validates rather than coercing "5" to 5.

These argument forms are distinct:

Form Value passed plain text Rendered str <name> Rendered str <procedure()> Rendered str <`expression`> Rendered str prefix <name> Rendered str `expression` Native Python result

Prefer a native argument when the parameter is typed as anything other than str. Prefer rendered arguments for human-language content.

items.title: Bindings Are Text Unless Backticked
items.text:
A template is text wherever it appears, including a binding or a return whose right-hand side is a single call:

[profile: Profile] = `get_profile("Ada")`   # the Profile value
[label] = <get_profile(Ada)>                 # error: a Profile has no text form
[n: int] = <count>                           # error: text is not an int

Native values come from single-backtick Python only. Strings are never converted to other types implicitly.

items.title: References
items.text:
A model prompt passes a value by reference with <<name>> or <<procedure(...)>>. The text gets the value's ID, and the value is attached to the model's context under that ID, before the prompt text:

[spec] = `read_text("spec.md")`
>> Does the change follow <<spec>>? Check <<spec>> section by section. [ok: bool]
<attachments>
<document id="spec" type="text/plain">
...contents of spec.md...
</document>
</attachments>
Does the change follow spec? Check spec section by section. ...
  • A binding's ID is its name. A call gets <procedure>_result_1, <procedure>_result_2, ... within the prompt.
  • Each content is attached once; every mention writes <<...>> again and gets only the ID.
  • Media go as native parts (Multimodal Input). Any other value goes as its text form, the text <value> renders: scalars as text/plain, lists, tuples and dicts as JSON (application/json). Models, ~Type values and dataclasses are accepted too, written as JSON by their own schema; a set of two or more items or a non-finite number inside one is an error. None and values without a text form are errors.
  • References are valid only in model prompts: >> templates, [x] << ... and [x: T] << ... invokes, and > if: / > loop: template conditions. Elsewhere <<...>> is a parse error (K-REFERENCE-CONTEXT).
  • A value that already is an artifact goes as its reference (<artifact id="log">) when the call has artifact tools, and in full otherwise. Plain values are attached in full however large they are, and <log> always writes the text itself: size never decides.
  • Attached content is not escaped. Do not treat referenced content as instructions.

<items> writes a list into the text; <<items>> attaches it as a JSON document. Which one fits is your choice.

items.title: Inline Python Substitutions
items.text:
Evaluate one Python expression with <`expression`>:

[items: list[str]] = `["parser", "runtime", "lsp"]`
= Components: <`", ".join(items)`>; total: <`len(items)`>.

The expression can read the prelude, imports, custom types, procedures, global values, and the current procedure environment. It must be a single expression, not a statement suite. Use a fenced Python block for imports, loops, exception handling, or several statements.

items.title: Bare Inline Python Segments
items.text:
Inside rendered text, a bare backtick segment also evaluates and inserts Python:

[limit: int] = `4`
= Processing `limit * 2` records.

This is equivalent to using <`limit * 2`> for insertion. Bare segments can be easier to read when an expression contains angle brackets or square brackets. Use angle-wrapped Python when the model boundary should be visually explicit; use bare segments sparingly in prose so code and literal text remain easy to distinguish.

items.title: Commas and Argument Boundaries
items.text:
Commas separate call arguments. Escape a comma that belongs to rendered text:

@echo(value: str) -> str:
  = <value>

= <echo(alpha\, beta\, gamma)>

The procedure receives one string, "alpha, beta, gamma". A comma inside a backtick Python expression follows Python syntax and does not need Kedi's text escape.

items.title: Evaluation Order
items.text:
Kedi evaluates substitutions from left to right while rendering an expression. Nested calls are evaluated before the containing call. If one procedure call is referenced both while constructing a structured prompt and while rendering that same prompt's result, Kedi memoizes it for that expression so it is not invoked twice.

Do not rely on model calls for deterministic side-effect ordering. Keep side-effecting work in explicit statements or Python blocks, and treat substitutions as value-producing expressions.

items.title: Missing and Invalid Substitutions
items.text:
Kedi reports an error when:

  • a variable or procedure is not visible in the lexical scope;
  • a procedure receives too few or too many positional arguments;
  • an argument fails its declared parameter type;
  • an inline Python expression raises;
  • delimiters are unbalanced or an unsupported escape is used.

The error retains the Kedi source location. Do not add fallback values merely to hide missing names; declare a procedure default or compute an explicit fallback instead.

items.title: Template Lines with >>
items.text:
>> opens a model template at top level or inside a procedure:

@extract_owner(issue: str) -> str:
  >> Issue: <issue>
  The [owner: str] team owns the next action.
  = <owner>

Literal text is sent as written after substitutions are rendered. Output fields describe values the model must produce.

items.title: Multiline Template Blocks
items.text:
Continuation rows at the same indentation are newline-joined into one model request:

>> Incident: <incident>.
The affected service is [service: str].
The severity is [severity: Literal["low", "medium", "high"]].

Do not prefix every continuation row with >> unless separate model calls are intended.

items.title: One Model Call per Block
items.text:
The previous example starts one logical adapter operation with two output fields. Tools, validation retries, or transport recovery can require more than one provider request inside that operation. Starting a second block starts a dependency-aware second operation:

>> Incident <incident> affects [service: str].
>> To restore <service>, follow [steps: list[str]].

The second call can substitute service because the first call completed and captured it. In parallel mode Kedi derives dependencies from these reads and writes; no special concurrency syntax is needed.

items.title: Raw Model Invokes with <<
items.text:
Use a capture target before << when the entire response should be retained as text:

[explanation] << Explain <concept> for an experienced Python developer.
= <explanation>

An untyped capture is a string. [explanation: str] is accepted but redundant.

Give the capture another type when the whole response should be that type:

~Report(title, risks: list[str], score: int)

[report: Report] << Review <diff> and report the main risks.
[count: int] << How many services does <spec> describe?

Kedi sends the prompt unchanged and asks the adapter for the capture type through its native structured output. No field-filling rules are added, and the response schema is the type itself, not an object with one property per field. The value is validated like a template output and keeps its declared type, so a later := is checked against it. A typed capture is a structured model call: the adapter must support structured output, and hooks and telemetry report it as structured rather than raw.

A raw prompt cannot contain output fields such as [count: int].

items.title: Structured and Text Results
items.text:
Choose >> with output fields when:

  • downstream code needs named or typed values;
  • multiple fields must be captured from one call;
  • schema descriptions improve model behavior;
  • invalid output should trigger adapter validation or retry behavior.

Prefer >> with [name: str] even for one piece of prose when the result is a declared part of program dataflow. Choose [name] << ... only when deliberately retaining an opaque, provider-native text response without an output schema. Choose [name: Type] << ... when one typed value is the whole answer and the prompt should reach the model exactly as written. Do not parse a predictable structured response from raw text when a typed output can express the contract directly.

items.title: Procedure-Local Backend State
items.text: Templates use the active adapter or harness, model, effort, instructions, settings, tools, MCP servers, skills, and approval policy at their source location. Procedures capture applicable outer configuration when defined, and inner directives can override following calls.

items.title: Template Failure Behavior
items.text:
A plain >> prompt with no output fields is still sent to the model, but its response is discarded:

>> Record a concise acknowledgement of <event>.

Use this only when discarding the response is intentional. To keep it, use a raw capture. Structured calls can fail before contacting the model when types or adapter schema capabilities are unsupported; provider, validation, retry, and approval failures surface as execution errors rather than empty outputs.

items.title: Types
items.text: Kedi types are runtime contracts, provider schemas, and editor information. They are used in output fields, variable initializations, procedure signatures, custom fields, tool schemas, evals, and the Python API. Assignments reuse the target binding's established type contract.

items.title: Built-In Types
items.text:
The type environment includes model-facing Python and typing primitives such as:

  • str, int, float, bool, and bytes;
  • list[T], dict[K, V], and set[T];
  • Union, Optional, Literal, and Annotated;
  • datetime, date, time, and timedelta;
  • Regex, Email, HttpUrl, and FileUrl.
~Window(start: datetime, duration: timedelta)

@window(start: datetime, duration: timedelta) -> Window:
  = `Window(start=start, duration=duration)`

Native Kedi annotations reject tuple, Tuple, Sequence, Mapping, Iterable, object, bytearray, slice, and range. They remain available to ordinary Python expressions and blocks; only their use as Kedi type contracts is rejected. Use list, dict, or a named custom type for model-facing schemas.

Unannotated outputs, variable initializations, parameters, returns, and custom fields default to str. Add an annotation whenever a value is intentionally not text.

items.title: Container, Union, and Literal Types
items.text:
Types can be nested:

>> The model scores are [scores: dict[str, list[float]]].
>> The current state is [state: Literal["open", "closed", "blocked"]].
>> The responsible owner is [owner: str | None].

Choose a shape that the model and adapter can reliably represent. Deeply nested unions may be valid Python but poor model interfaces; a named custom type often produces a clearer schema.

items.title: Inline Python Type Expressions
items.text:
Backtick-wrapped annotations are evaluated at runtime:

```
from typing import Literal
Severity = Literal["low", "medium", "high"]
```

@triage(level: `Severity`) -> `Severity`:
  = `level`

They have the same validation behavior as direct annotations. Prefer direct syntax for built-ins and Kedi custom types. Use runtime expressions only when the type is computed or imported through Python.

items.title: Define Custom Types
items.text:
Declare a Pydantic-compatible model with ~Name(fields):

~Owner(
  name: Annotated[str, "Human-readable display name"],
  email: Email
)

~Issue(
  id: int,
  title: str,
  owner: Owner | None,
  labels: list[str] = `[]`
)

Fields without annotations are str. Field names must be unique valid identifiers. Required fields must come before fields with defaults, and a defaulted custom field must have an explicit annotation.

Custom types are lexically scoped. A type declared inside a procedure is visible to that procedure and nested scopes, but not after the call. A nested type may shadow an outer type with the same name.

items.title: Defaults
items.text:
Field defaults are single-line Python expressions evaluated at definition time:

~Job(name: str, retries: int = `3`, tags: list[str] = `[]`)

Kedi deep-copies mutable defaults for each model instance, so instances do not share the same list or dict. Required-after-default and untyped-default fields are parse errors.

items.title: Field Description Metadata
items.text:
Annotated[T, "description"] keeps T as the runtime type and adds the string to the generated schema:

~Finding(
  path: Annotated[str, "Repository-relative POSIX path"],
  confidence: Annotated[float, "Value from 0.0 through 1.0"]
)

Descriptions should state semantic constraints or interpretation. They are forwarded to model-facing schemas. Annotated[T] works as T but lacks useful metadata and is warned about. The first string metadata item supplies the field description when it is the first metadata argument. Non-string metadata from Python type aliases is preserved for validation and integrations; it is not discarded. Descriptions guide the model but do not enforce a numeric range.

items.title: Validation Constraints
items.text:
Import kedi.Constraints when bounds must be enforced. In a native Annotated, wrap the metadata constructor call in backticks:

```
from kedi import Constraints
```

~Review(
  confidence: Annotated[
    float,
    "Confidence of the review",
    `Constraints(ge=0, le=1)`
  ]
)
[review: Review] = `Review(confidence=0.9)`
> show: `review.confidence`

This also works inside nested lists, dictionaries, optional and union types. The metadata expression produces a value, while the first Annotated argument must still be a type. Constraints is not an implicit global.

Alternatively, define the whole annotation as a Python alias:

```
from typing import Annotated
from kedi import Constraints

Rating = Annotated[
    float,
    "Rating on a zero-to-two scale",
    Constraints(ge=0, le=2),
]
```

[rating: `Rating`] = `1.5`
= `rating`

The Python alias supplies actual validation metadata. Kedi's native annotation grammar does not accept arbitrary constructor calls such as Annotated[float, Constraints(ge=0)]; use a backtick metadata expression or reference a Python alias through a backtick type expression. These constraints validate values, not the truth of model judgements. See Jev for decision metadata and supported schemas.

items.title: Pydantic-Compatible Models
items.text:
Generated custom types subclass Pydantic BaseModel. Construct them with positional fields in declaration order, keyword arguments, or a mixture:

~Person(age: int, name: str, city: str)

[person: Person] = `Person(30, name="Ada", city="London")`
= `person.model_dump_json()`

Pydantic APIs such as model_dump(), model_dump_json(), and model_json_schema() are available. Prefer keyword construction in public code because it remains readable if field order changes.

items.title: Custom Types in Model Outputs
items.text:
Use a custom type when one output has a meaningful structured shape:

~Decision(
  approved: bool,
  reason: str,
  conditions: list[str] = `[]`
)

>> The request review decision is [decision: Decision].
= `decision.model_dump_json()`

The adapter receives the nested JSON schema and Kedi validates the model response. Use multiple primitive outputs when the fields are local and simple; use a named type when the structure is reused, nested, returned, or exposed to a tool.

items.title: Custom Types in Procedures
items.text:
Custom types can cross procedure boundaries natively:

~Ticket(id: int, title: str)

@format_ticket(ticket: Ticket) -> str:
  = \#<`ticket.id`> <`ticket.title`>

= `format_ticket(Ticket(id=7, title="Parser error"))`

Passing rendered JSON text is not equivalent to passing a Ticket. Construct or validate the model in Python when converting external data.

items.title: Adapter Schema Compatibility
items.text:
Provider support is narrower than Python's type system. Kedi validates known schema limitations before contacting the model:

  • Codex supports formats including date, date-time, duration, email, and time.
  • Codex rejects Regex, HttpUrl, and FileUrl model-output schemas.
